title: Where does each common carotid artery arise?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does each common carotid artery arise?
body.back: Right: from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the sternoclavicular joint. Left: directly from the arch of the aorta behind the manubrium sterni.

title: Describe the course of the facial artery.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the course of the facial artery.
body.back: Arises from the external carotid in the carotid triangle at the level of the hyoid. It travels superiorly and obliquely, under the digastric and closely related to the posterior surface of the submandibular gland, then curves up over the body of the mandible along the anterior border of the masseter, deep to the platysma, and runs tortuously toward the angle of the mouth.

title: Branches of the facial artery in the neck and on the face.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Branches of the facial artery in the neck and on the face.
body.back: Neck: ascending palatine (soft palate, palatine tonsils), tonsillar (palatine tonsils), submental (floor of mouth and sublingual gland) and glandular (submandibular gland). Face: superior and inferior labial (upper and lower lips) and, as its termination, the angular artery (external nose, lower eyelid, orbicularis oculi, lacrimal sac).

title: Occipital artery: origin and what it supplies.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Occipital artery: origin and what it supplies.
body.back: Arises in the carotid triangle from the posterior aspect of the external carotid about 2 cm from its origin. It passes backward and upward under cover of the posterior belly of digastric, crossing the internal carotid, internal jugular vein and the hypoglossal and accessory nerves. It supplies sternocleidomastoid, the posterior neck and deep back muscles, the posterior part of the auricle, the scalp and occipital muscles, and gives mastoid and meningeal branches to the dura.

title: Ascending pharyngeal artery: size, course and branches.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Ascending pharyngeal artery: size, course and branches.
body.back: The smallest branch, arising posteriorly near the origin of the external carotid. It ascends to the base of the skull between the wall of the pharynx and the internal carotid. Branches: pharyngeal (pharynx, constrictors, stylopharyngeus, soft palate, tonsils, auditory tube), inferior tympanic (medial wall of the middle ear) and meningeal (dura mater and several cranial nerves).

title: Posterior auricular artery: what does it supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Posterior auricular artery: what does it supply?
body.back: The back of the auricle, external ear, middle ear and the muscles around the mastoid process. Branches: auricular (back of the pinna and extrinsic auricular muscles), stylomastoid (enters the stylomastoid foramen to supply the middle and inner ear and the facial nerve), occipital (sternocleidomastoid, digastric, stylohyoid) and posterior tympanic.

title: Superficial temporal artery: course and main branches.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Superficial temporal artery: course and main branches.
body.back: A terminal branch of the external carotid. It divides into frontal (anterior) and parietal (posterior) branches supplying the scalp and forehead. Other branches include the transverse facial, zygomatico-orbital, anterior auricular and middle temporal arteries.

title: Maxillary artery: origin, course and parts.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Maxillary artery: origin, course and parts.
body.back: The larger terminal branch of the external carotid, arising behind and below the mandibular neck in the substance of the parotid gland. It runs forward medial to the neck of the mandible into the pterygopalatine fossa. Three parts: mandibular, pterygoid and pterygopalatine, conventionally divided by the lateral pterygoid muscle, with five branches from each part.

title: What does the maxillary artery supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the maxillary artery supply?
body.back: The upper and lower jaws, the muscles of mastication, the nose, the palate and the meninges inside the skull, through the middle meningeal artery, which enters the foramen spinosum.

title: How is the facial vein formed, and where does it drain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How is the facial vein formed, and where does it drain?
body.back: The supratrochlear and supraorbital veins merge at the medial angle of the eye to form the angular vein, which becomes the facial vein as it descends the face. At the angle of the mandible it joins the anterior division of the retromandibular vein to form the common facial vein, which drains into the internal jugular vein, generally at the level of the hyoid bone.

title: Which tributaries does the facial vein receive?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which tributaries does the facial vein receive?
body.back: Tributaries mirroring the branches of the facial artery, including the superior and inferior labial veins and the submental vein. It passes over the masseter muscle and superficial to the submandibular gland.

title: Where does the common carotid artery divide, and into what?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does the common carotid artery divide, and into what?
body.back: In the carotid triangle, at the upper border of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage, opposite the disc between C3 and C4, into the external and internal carotid arteries.

title: Why is the facial vein clinically dangerous?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why is the facial vein clinically dangerous?
body.back: It connects through the ophthalmic veins with the cavernous sinus, and the deep facial vein drains the buccal space and connects with the pterygoid venous plexus, which in turn connects with the cavernous sinus. These are potential routes for infection from the face to spread to the brain.

title: How is the retromandibular vein formed and what does it divide into?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How is the retromandibular vein formed and what does it divide into?
body.back: Formed in the parotid gland by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins. On leaving the gland it divides into an anterior division, which joins the facial vein to form the common facial vein, and a posterior division, which joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.

title: External jugular vein: formation, course and drainage.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: External jugular vein: formation, course and drainage.
body.back: Formed behind the angle of the jaw by the union of the posterior auricular vein with the posterior division of the retromandibular vein. It descends over the sternocleidomastoid and beneath the platysma, and drains into the subclavian vein behind the middle of the clavicle.

title: Internal jugular vein: where does it start and end?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Internal jugular vein: where does it start and end?
body.back: It starts as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus and leaves the skull through the jugular foramen. It descends in the carotid sheath, lateral to the vagus nerve and to the internal and common carotid arteries, and ends by joining the subclavian vein behind the medial end of the clavicle to form the brachiocephalic vein.

title: What does the internal jugular vein drain, and name its tributaries.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the internal jugular vein drain, and name its tributaries.
body.back: It drains the brain (through the dural venous sinuses), the face, the thyroid gland and the neck. Tributaries: inferior petrosal sinus, facial vein, pharyngeal veins, lingual vein, superior thyroid vein and middle thyroid vein.

title: Name the three primary lymph node groups of the face and what drains to each.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three primary lymph node groups of the face and what drains to each.
body.back: Preauricular (superficial parotid) nodes: upper face, forehead and lateral eyelids. Submandibular nodes: central face, cheeks and lateral nose. Submental nodes: lower lip, chin and apex of the tongue.

title: Trace lymph from the face back to the bloodstream.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace lymph from the face back to the bloodstream.
body.back: From the primary facial groups, lymph flows to the superficial and deep cervical nodes in the neck, then to the supraclavicular nodes, then through the jugular trunks into the large veins at the root of the neck, emptying into the thoracic duct on the left or the right lymphatic duct.

title: Describe the course of the external carotid artery.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the course of the external carotid artery.
body.back: It begins lateral to the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the level of the C3 to C4 disc, anteromedial to the internal carotid. It ascends in a gentle spiral, first slightly forward then backward and laterally, passing between the mastoid tip and the mandibular angle, and ends lateral to the internal carotid.

title: Where does the external carotid artery end?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does the external carotid artery end?
body.back: In the substance of the parotid gland, behind the neck of the mandible, dividing into the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries.

title: Name the eight branches of the external carotid artery in order.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the eight branches of the external carotid artery in order.
body.back: Superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, superficial temporal and maxillary.

title: What are the relations of the external carotid in the neck?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the relations of the external carotid in the neck?
body.back: Medially: the wall of the pharynx and the internal carotid artery. The stylopharyngeus and styloglossus muscles, the glossopharyngeal nerve and the pharyngeal branch of the vagus pass between the external and internal carotid arteries.

title: What are the relations of the external carotid on the face?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the relations of the external carotid on the face?
body.back: Anterolaterally it is overlapped at its beginning by the sternocleidomastoid; above this it is superficial, covered by skin and fascia. It is crossed by the hypoglossal nerve, the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, and within the parotid gland by the facial nerve. The internal jugular vein lies first lateral, then posterior to it.

title: Superior thyroid artery: origin and four branches.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Superior thyroid artery: origin and four branches.
body.back: Arises from the front of the external carotid below the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid. At the thyroid gland it divides into infrahyoid, superior laryngeal, cricothyroid and glandular branches, supplying the thyroid, infrahyoid muscles, upper larynx and cricothyroid.

title: Lingual artery: origin and four main branches.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Lingual artery: origin and four main branches.
body.back: The principal artery of the tongue. Arises anteromedially from the external carotid opposite the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid, between the superior thyroid and facial arteries, and is divided into three parts by the hyoglossus. Branches: suprahyoid (suprahyoid muscles), dorsal lingual (back of tongue and throat), sublingual (sublingual gland) and deep lingual (body and tip of the tongue).

title: Which artery is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which artery is highlighted?
body.back: The external carotid artery. It begins at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, anteromedial to the internal carotid, and ends in the parotid gland.

title: Which terminal branch is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which terminal branch is at the arrow?
body.back: The superficial temporal artery, the other terminal branch, supplying the scalp and temporal region.

title: Which vessel is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which vessel is highlighted?
body.back: The common carotid artery. It divides in the carotid triangle at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, opposite the C3 to C4 disc.

title: Which artery is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which artery is highlighted?
body.back: The internal carotid artery. It gives no branches in the neck and enters the carotid canal to supply the brain.

title: Which branch is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which branch is at the arrow?
body.back: The superior thyroid artery, the first branch, arising from the front of the external carotid below the greater cornu of the hyoid.

title: Which branch is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which branch is at the arrow?
body.back: The lingual artery, the principal artery of the tongue. It is divided into three parts by the hyoglossus.

title: Which branch is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which branch is at the arrow?
body.back: The facial artery. It arises in the carotid triangle, crosses the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter, and ends as the angular artery.

title: Which branch is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which branch is at the arrow?
body.back: The occipital artery, arising from the posterior aspect of the external carotid about 2 cm from its origin, supplying the back of the scalp and neck.

title: Which branch is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which branch is at the arrow?
body.back: The ascending pharyngeal artery, the smallest branch of the external carotid, ascending between the pharynx and the internal carotid.

title: Which branch is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which branch is at the arrow?
body.back: The posterior auricular artery, supplying the back of the auricle, the external and middle ear, and giving the stylomastoid branch.

title: Which terminal branch is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which terminal branch is at the arrow?
body.back: The maxillary artery, the larger terminal branch, supplying the jaws, muscles of mastication, nose, palate, and the meninges via the middle meningeal artery.

title: What is the brainstem, and what does it do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the brainstem, and what does it do?
body.back: It connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum. Three parts, descending: midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata. Ten of the twelve cranial nerves arise from its nuclei. It controls vital functions: breathing, consciousness, blood pressure, heart rate and sleep.

title: Which cranial nerves emerge from the pons?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cranial nerves emerge from the pons?
body.back: CN V from the lateral mid-pons; CN VI at the pontomedullary junction near the midline; CN VII at the cerebellopontine angle; CN VIII lateral to CN VII.

title: Describe the floor of the fourth ventricle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the floor of the fourth ventricle.
body.back: Formed by the back of the pons and medulla. The medial eminence marks the midline. The facial colliculus is a bulge of facial nerve fibres looping round the abducens nucleus. The stria medullaris crosses transversely and marks the border between pons and medulla.

title: What is the cerebellopontine angle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the cerebellopontine angle?
body.back: The angle at the junction of pons, medulla and cerebellum, where the flocculus, the choroid plexus and the emerging CN VII and VIII surround the lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle, the foramina of Luschka.

title: Describe the ventral surface of the medulla.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the ventral surface of the medulla.
body.back: The ventral median fissure, continuous with the cord's, whose lower part is marked by the decussation of 75 to 90 percent of corticospinal fibres. The pyramid on each side, made by the corticospinal tract. The olive lateral to it, made by the inferior olivary nucleus, important in movement control.

title: Which nerves emerge from the medulla?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which nerves emerge from the medulla?
body.back: Four: CN XII from the sulcus between pyramid and olive; CN IX, X and the cranial part of XI, from above downwards, from the sulcus behind the olive.

title: Give the general internal organisation of the brainstem.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the general internal organisation of the brainstem.
body.back: As in the cord: white matter with descending motor and ascending sensory pathways; an ependymal cavity, the fourth ventricle and aqueduct of Sylvius; and grey matter, the cranial nerve nuclei and the reticular formation.

title: Summarise the emergence of the cranial nerves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Summarise the emergence of the cranial nerves.
body.back: Anterior surface: III between the peduncles; V from the pons; VI, VII, VII bis and VIII at the bulbopontine groove, from medial to lateral; XII opposite the olive. Lateral surface, behind the olive: IX, X and XI. Posterior surface: IV, the only nerve emerging dorsally.

title: Two rules about the cranial nerves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Two rules about the cranial nerves.
body.back: All arise from the brainstem except the optic and olfactory nerves. All emerge from the anterolateral surface except the trochlear nerve, which emerges dorsally from the midbrain.

title: What is the reticular formation?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the reticular formation?
body.back: A mixture of neuronal cell bodies and small bundles of axons running in many directions, without distinct boundaries, spread through the brainstem from the cord to the thalamus. It integrates vital systems: arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, motor coordination, cardiovascular and respiratory control, pain modulation and habituation.

title: Name the tracts running through the brainstem.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the tracts running through the brainstem.
body.back: Descending: the motor pathway, corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, for voluntary movement of body and face. Ascending conscious: the dorsal column-medial lemniscus (touch, proprioception, vibration) and the anterolateral or spinothalamic system (crude touch, pain, temperature). Ascending unconscious: the spinocerebellar tracts.

title: Where does the brainstem lie?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does the brainstem lie?
body.back: In the posterior cranial fossa, on the clivus of the occipital bone, under the tentorium cerebelli: above the spinal cord, below the cerebrum and in front of the cerebellum.

title: Describe the fourth ventricle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the fourth ventricle.
body.back: Roof: the superior and inferior medullary vela over the cerebellum. Floor: the rhomboid fossa. Side walls: the vela and cerebellar peduncles. Its peak in the cerebellum is the fastigium; its caudal tip the obex; widest at the pontomedullary junction. Choroid plexus lines the roof, and CSF leaves by the median foramen of Magendie and two lateral foramina of Luschka.

title: Describe the blood supply of the brainstem.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the blood supply of the brainstem.
body.back: The basilar artery and its branches: the posterior cerebral artery and its peduncular branch, the superior cerebellar artery, the posterior choroidal artery and the interpeduncular branches.

title: List the functions of the brainstem.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: List the functions of the brainstem.
body.back: A pathway for tracts between cortex and cord; the site of origin of the nuclei of CN III to XII; the site of emergence of CN III to XII; and the reticular formation, controlling consciousness, pain perception and cardiovascular and respiratory regulation.

title: What is an alternating syndrome?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is an alternating syndrome?
body.back: A peripheral cranial nerve lesion associated with a hemiplegia on the opposite side. It locates the level of the lesion in the brainstem.

title: Where are the respiratory and cardiovascular centres?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where are the respiratory and cardiovascular centres?
body.back: In the medulla oblongata, which is why a lesion there is life-threatening.

title: Give the embryological origin of each part.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the embryological origin of each part.
body.back: Medulla from the myelencephalon (fifth vesicle), pons from the metencephalon (fourth vesicle), midbrain from the mesencephalon (third vesicle). The growing neural tube bends at the cephalic and mesencephalic flexures.

title: How does the brainstem connect to its neighbours?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How does the brainstem connect to its neighbours?
body.back: Above: the diencephalon, by the transverse fissure of Bichat. Behind: the cerebellum, by the cerebellar peduncles. Below: the spinal cord, through the foramen magnum.

title: Which cerebellar peduncle goes where?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cerebellar peduncle goes where?
body.back: Superior: midbrain. Middle: pons. Inferior: medulla oblongata.

title: Describe the midbrain.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the midbrain.
body.back: The smallest part, about 2 cm, passing through the tentorial opening, the foramen of Pacchioni. Two parts: the tectum behind the cerebral aqueduct and the paired cerebral peduncles in front.

title: Describe the tectum.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the tectum.
body.back: Four colliculi, two superior and two inferior, just below the pineal gland. The superior brachium links the superior colliculus with the retina (vision); the inferior brachium carries lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus fibres to the medial geniculate body (hearing). CN IV emerges just below the colliculi.

title: Describe the cerebral peduncles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the cerebral peduncles.
body.back: Paired, running from the hemispheres to converge at the pons, separated in front by the interpeduncular fossa. CN III exits between them; the optic tract runs round the upper border of the midbrain.

title: Describe the anterior surface of the pons.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the anterior surface of the pons.
body.back: The largest part of the brainstem, from the metencephalon with the cerebellum, linking cerebrum and cerebellum. Its ventral bulge is made by transverse pontocerebellar fibres, about 2.5 cm. The basilar groove in the midline holds the basilar artery. The pontomedullary junction is a key landmark.

title: Which part of the brainstem is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the brainstem is at the arrow?
body.back: The midbrain, the smallest part, about 2 cm, containing the tectum and cerebral peduncles.

title: Which part of the brainstem is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the brainstem is at the arrow?
body.back: The pons, the largest part, its bulge made by transverse pontocerebellar fibres.

title: Which part of the brainstem is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the brainstem is at the arrow?
body.back: The medulla oblongata, with the pyramids and olives, housing the respiratory and cardiovascular centres.

title: Which elevation is at the arrow, and what makes it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which elevation is at the arrow, and what makes it?
body.back: The pyramid, made by the corticospinal tract, whose fibres mostly cross in the lower medulla.

title: Which elevation is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which elevation is at the arrow?
body.back: The olive, lateral to the pyramid, made by the inferior olivary nucleus.

title: Which cranial nerve emerges at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cranial nerve emerges at the arrow?
body.back: The trigeminal nerve (CN V), from the lateral aspect of the mid-pons.

title: Which cranial nerve emerges at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cranial nerve emerges at the arrow?
body.back: The oculomotor nerve (CN III), between the cerebral peduncles.

title: Which cranial nerve emerges at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cranial nerve emerges at the arrow?
body.back: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), from the sulcus between pyramid and olive.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dentate nucleus: the largest and most lateral deep nucleus; output of the cerebrocerebellum to the thalamus and motor cortex.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fastigial nucleus: the most medial deep nucleus; output of the vermis to the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation; balance and posture.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Flocculonodular lobe: the vestibulocerebellum (archicerebellum). Balance and eye movements.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intermediate zone: part of the spinocerebellum. Coordinates limb movements using spinal input.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Interposed nuclei (globose + emboliform): output of the intermediate zone; limb movements, via the red nucleus.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lateral hemisphere: the cerebrocerebellum, the largest division. Input from the cortex via the pontine nuclei; plans and times skilled movements.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vermis: part of the spinocerebellum. Axial muscles, posture and gait.

title: Where is the cerebellum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where is the cerebellum?
body.back: Posterior cranial fossa: under the tentorium cerebelli, behind the pons and medulla, separated from them by the fourth ventricle.

title: What are the three roles of the cerebellum in movement?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the three roles of the cerebellum in movement?
body.back: Control of muscle tone, maintenance of balance and coordination of voluntary movements (automatic regulation).

title: List the three layers of the cerebellar cortex, outside in, with their main cells.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: List the three layers of the cerebellar cortex, outside in, with their main cells.
body.back: Molecular (stellate and basket cells); Purkinje cell layer (Purkinje cells); granular (granule and Golgi cells).

title: What is special about Purkinje cells?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is special about Purkinje cells?
body.back: They are the only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and they are inhibitory, projecting to the deep nuclei.

title: Name the four deep cerebellar nuclei from lateral to medial.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the four deep cerebellar nuclei from lateral to medial.
body.back: Dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial (Don't Eat Greasy Food). Emboliform + globose = interposed nuclei.

title: Where do climbing fibres come from, and what do they do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where do climbing fibres come from, and what do they do?
body.back: Only from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus; each powerfully excites one Purkinje cell and signals movement errors for motor learning.

title: Where do mossy fibres come from, and where do they end?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where do mossy fibres come from, and where do they end?
body.back: Spinal cord, vestibular nuclei and pontine nuclei; they end on granule cells in the granular layer (glomeruli).

title: Which arteries supply the cerebellum, and where do they come from?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which arteries supply the cerebellum, and where do they come from?
body.back: SCA and AICA from the basilar artery; PICA from the vertebral artery.

title: Name the three functional divisions and their roles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three functional divisions and their roles.
body.back: Vestibulocerebellum: balance and eye movements. Spinocerebellum: tone, posture, trunk and limb coordination. Cerebrocerebellum: planning and timing of skilled movements.

title: A patient has a right cerebellar hemisphere lesion. Which side shows the signs?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: A patient has a right cerebellar hemisphere lesion. Which side shows the signs?
body.back: The right side: cerebellar signs are ipsilateral.

title: What does damage to the flocculonodular lobe cause?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does damage to the flocculonodular lobe cause?
body.back: Loss of equilibrium with an altered, unsteady gait.

title: What joins the two cerebellar hemispheres?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What joins the two cerebellar hemispheres?
body.back: The vermis, a median portion.

title: Which fissure separates the anterior and posterior lobes?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which fissure separates the anterior and posterior lobes?
body.back: The primary fissure.

title: Which fissure separates the posterior and flocculonodular lobes?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which fissure separates the posterior and flocculonodular lobes?
body.back: The posterolateral fissure.

title: What does the horizontal fissure (great circumferential sulcus of Vicq d'Azyr) separate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the horizontal fissure (great circumferential sulcus of Vicq d'Azyr) separate?
body.back: The superior surface from the inferior surface.

title: What are the cerebellar tonsils, and why do they matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the cerebellar tonsils, and why do they matter?
body.back: Rounded parts of the medial inferior hemispheres beside the inferior vermis. Herniation through the foramen magnum compresses the medulla and threatens breathing and circulation.

title: Name the three cerebellar peduncles and what each joins.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three cerebellar peduncles and what each joins.
body.back: Superior → midbrain; middle → pons; inferior → medulla oblongata.

title: Which peduncle is the largest, and what does it carry?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which peduncle is the largest, and what does it carry?
body.back: The middle peduncle (brachium pontis): pontocerebellar input from the contralateral pontine nuclei.

title: Which peduncle is mainly the output pathway, and where does it go?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which peduncle is mainly the output pathway, and where does it go?
body.back: The superior peduncle (brachium conjunctivum): to the red nucleus and thalamus (then motor cortex).

title: What is the cerebrum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the cerebrum?
body.back: The control centre of the body and the largest part of the brain, above and in front of the brainstem. Especially developed in humans, it is the highest level of the CNS hierarchy. It consists of the cerebral hemispheres and the diencephalon.

title: Describe the frontal lobe.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the frontal lobe.
body.back: About 40 percent of the hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus, crossed by two T-shaped sulci, with four gyri: precentral, superior, middle and inferior frontal.

title: Describe the parietal lobe.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the parietal lobe.
body.back: Between the central, lateral and parieto-occipital sulci. An interparietal furrow divides it into the postcentral gyrus, the superior parietal and the inferior parietal gyri. The inferior parietal gyrus, at the end of the first temporal furrow, forms Wernicke's area.

title: Describe the occipital lobe.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the occipital lobe.
body.back: At the back of the hemisphere, limited in front by the parieto-occipital sulci, with six gyri: superior, middle and inferior on the lateral face, the fourth and fifth on the underside, and the sixth, the cuneus, on the internal face.

title: Describe the temporal lobe.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the temporal lobe.
body.back: Below the frontal and parietal lobes and in front of the occipital, with five gyri: superior, middle, inferior, the fourth on the lower face, and the fifth, the hippocampal convolution, whose front curves into the uncus.

title: Describe the insula.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the insula.
body.back: At the bottom of the Sylvian fissure, divided by a deep groove into an anterior lobule with 3 convolutions and a posterior with 2.

title: Describe the corpus callosum.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the corpus callosum.
body.back: A white matter tract of about 200 million fibres connecting the two hemispheres. In front the genu ending in the rostrum; behind the splenium.

title: Describe the fornix.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the fornix.
body.back: A C-shaped white matter bundle on the medial hemisphere below the corpus callosum, in its concavity. The largest pathway of the hippocampus and part of the limbic system. Anterior columns join the mammillary bodies; posterior columns end at the hippocampus.

title: Name the telencephalic commissures and their role.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the telencephalic commissures and their role.
body.back: The corpus callosum, the fornix, the anterior white commissure in front of the fornix and callosal genu, and the posterior white commissure under the epiphysis in the back wall of the third ventricle. Functions: cognition, memory, emotions.

title: Grey matter versus white matter.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Grey matter versus white matter.
body.back: Grey matter is grey from its concentration of neuronal cell bodies, with glia and vessels. White matter is axons coated with myelin, a protein-lipid mixture that speeds conduction and protects the axon.

title: Where are grey matter, white matter and the ventricles in the hemisphere?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where are grey matter, white matter and the ventricles in the hemisphere?
body.back: Grey matter: the peripheral cortex and the deep basal ganglia. White matter: the centrum semiovale and the capsules. Ventricles: the lateral ventricles, communicating with the third ventricle through the foramina of Monro.

title: Give the anatomical classification of the CNS.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the anatomical classification of the CNS.
body.back: Cerebral hemispheres; diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus); brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla); cerebellum; spinal cord.

title: Describe the centrum semiovale and the three capsules.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the centrum semiovale and the three capsules.
body.back: The centrum semiovale is the white matter above the lateral ventricles and corpus callosum, under the cortex. Internal capsule: between thalamus and caudate medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. External: between lentiform nucleus and claustrum. Extreme: outside the claustrum.

title: Describe the cerebral cortex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the cerebral cortex.
body.back: Covering the hemispheres, 3 to 4 mm thick, about 10 billion neurons. It interprets sensory information, produces thought, controls behaviour and perceives the outside world.

title: What are the basal ganglia, and what do they need?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the basal ganglia, and what do they need?
body.back: Subcortical nuclei mainly for motor control, plus motor learning, executive functions, behaviour and emotion. Part of the extrapyramidal system, working with the pyramidal and limbic systems. They need dopamine at the input nuclei.

title: Name the five paired basal ganglia and the striatum.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the five paired basal ganglia and the striatum.
body.back: Caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus (diencephalon) and substantia nigra (mesencephalon). Dorsal striatum: caudate and putamen. Ventral striatum: nucleus accumbens and olfactory tubercle, part of the limbic system. Lentiform nucleus: putamen and globus pallidus.

title: Describe the caudate nucleus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the caudate nucleus.
body.back: C-shaped, in front of the thalamus, lateral to the lateral ventricle and medial to the internal capsule, with a head, body and tail. The head forms the lateral wall of the lateral ventricle; the tail the roof of its inferior horn, ending at the amygdala. Its front is continuous with the putamen.

title: Describe the putamen and globus pallidus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the putamen and globus pallidus.
body.back: Putamen: round, the most lateral basal ganglion on axial section, lateral to the globus pallidus and medial to the external capsule, separated from the caudate by the internal capsule. Globus pallidus: medial to the putamen, split by the internal medullary lamina into external and internal segments.

title: Describe the subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra.
body.back: Subthalamic nucleus (Luys' body): small, biconvex, at the junction of diencephalon and midbrain, below the thalamus; a neurostimulation target in Parkinson's disease. Substantia nigra: in the front of the midbrain between the cerebral peduncle and tegmentum, functionally part of the basal ganglia, with a pars compacta and pars reticulata.

title: How do the basal ganglia fine-tune movement?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How do the basal ganglia fine-tune movement?
body.back: They receive the plan for an upcoming movement from the cortex, process and adjust it, and send instructions to the thalamus, which relays them back to the cortex. The final command goes to the muscles via the pyramidal tracts. They also help with planning, memory, eye movements, reward and motivation.

title: How are the hemispheres specialised?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How are the hemispheres specialised?
body.back: Each controls the opposite side of the body. The left controls speech, comprehension, arithmetic and writing; the right creativity, spatial, artistic and musical skills. The left is dominant for hand use and language in about 92 percent of people.

title: Give the functions of each lobe.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the functions of each lobe.
body.back: Frontal: personality, behaviour, emotion, judgement, planning, speech (Broca), movement (motor strip), intelligence. Parietal: language interpretation, touch, pain and temperature (sensory strip), integrating senses, spatial perception. Occipital: vision. Temporal: language understanding (Wernicke), memory, hearing, sequencing. Insula: taste, visceral sensation, autonomic control, emotion, speech articulation and swallowing.

title: Where does the cerebrum lie, and what separates it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does the cerebrum lie, and what separates it?
body.back: In the skull, in the cerebral lodge bounded by dura: the vault above, the anterior and middle cranial fossae and tentorium below. The falx cerebri separates the hemispheres; the tentorium cerebelli separates cerebrum from cerebellum; the fissure of Bichat separates it from the brainstem.

title: Describe the pyramidal tract.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the pyramidal tract.
body.back: The corticospinal tract, the main pathway for voluntary movement. It starts mainly in the primary motor cortex, runs through the internal capsule and cerebral peduncles, and most fibres cross in the medulla before descending the cord to the limbs.

title: Name the localising signs of a cerebral lesion.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the localising signs of a cerebral lesion.
body.back: Aphasia, blindness, proportional or non-proportional hemiplegia, behavioural disorders, and epilepsy, whose type depends on the cortical site.

title: How does the dura divide the cranial cavity?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How does the dura divide the cranial cavity?
body.back: A vertical extension, the falx cerebri, incompletely separates the hemispheres. A horizontal extension, the tentorium cerebelli, divides it into a supratentorial compartment for the cerebrum and an infratentorial one for the cerebellum and brainstem.

title: Give the dimensions of the cerebrum.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the dimensions of the cerebrum.
body.back: Ovoid; width 14 cm, length 16 cm, height 12 cm; weight 1200 to 1400 g; greyish white; soft and crumbly.

title: Describe the faces of a hemisphere.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the faces of a hemisphere.
body.back: Triangular with three faces: a convex external face against the vault, a concave underside on the skull base and tentorium, and a flat internal face separated from the other hemisphere by the falx.

title: What are fissures and gyri?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are fissures and gyri?
body.back: The cortex is furrowed by grooves: the deepest, fissures or sulci, delimit the lobes; shallower grooves delimit the convolutions or gyri.

title: Name the sulci of the lateral face.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the sulci of the lateral face.
body.back: The central sulcus of Rolando, between frontal and parietal; the lateral sulcus of Sylvius, between frontal-parietal and temporal; the parieto-occipital sulcus; and the inconstant pre-occipital notch. The insula is folded deep in the lateral sulcus.

title: Name the sulci of the internal face.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the sulci of the internal face.
body.back: The calloso-marginal fissure parallel to the corpus callosum, the internal parieto-occipital sulcus, and the calcarine fissure from the occipital pole to the parieto-occipital sulcus, separating the fifth from the sixth occipital gyrus.

title: Which lobe is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which lobe is highlighted?
body.back: The frontal lobe, about 40 percent of the hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus.

title: Which lobe is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which lobe is highlighted?
body.back: The parietal lobe, between the central, lateral and parieto-occipital sulci.

title: Which lobe is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which lobe is highlighted?
body.back: The temporal lobe, below the lateral sulcus, holding Wernicke's area, memory and hearing.

title: Which lobe is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which lobe is highlighted?
body.back: The occipital lobe, at the back, which interprets vision.

title: Which sulcus is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which sulcus is at the arrow?
body.back: The central sulcus of Rolando, separating the frontal and parietal lobes.

title: Which sulcus is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which sulcus is at the arrow?
body.back: The lateral sulcus of Sylvius, separating the frontal and parietal lobes from the temporal lobe. The insula lies deep inside it.

title: Which gyrus is at the arrow, and what does it do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which gyrus is at the arrow, and what does it do?
body.back: The precentral gyrus, the primary motor area, where the corticospinal tract begins.

title: Which area is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which area is at the arrow?
body.back: Broca's area, in the inferior frontal lobe, for speech production.

title: Which area is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which area is at the arrow?
body.back: Wernicke's area, in the posterior superior temporal region, for understanding language.

title: Where does the pathway at the arrow begin?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does the pathway at the arrow begin?
body.back: The primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4, from the Betz cells of layer V.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The posterior limb of the internal capsule, where the corticospinal fibres converge behind the geniculate tract.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The cerebral peduncle of the midbrain, whose middle part carries the corticospinal fibres.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and what gives it its name?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and what gives it its name?
body.back: The medullary pyramid, formed by the corticospinal fibres, which gives the pyramidal tract its name.

title: What happens at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What happens at the arrow?
body.back: The pyramidal decussation: about 90 percent of the fibres cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

title: Which tract is at the arrow, and what does it supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which tract is at the arrow, and what does it supply?
body.back: The lateral corticospinal tract, the crossed fibres, supplying the limb muscles.

title: Which tract is at the arrow, and what does it supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which tract is at the arrow, and what does it supply?
body.back: The anterior corticospinal tract, uncrossed at the medulla, supplying the axial trunk muscles.

title: What is functional neuroanatomy for?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is functional neuroanatomy for?
body.back: It studies how nervous system structure relates to control of sensation, movement and behaviour. It bridges structure and clinical function, helping interpret symptoms and localise lesions.

title: Describe the corticobulbar tract.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the corticobulbar tract.
body.back: The pyramidal tract for the cranial nerve motor nuclei. The corticonuclear or geniculate pathway links the ascending frontal cortex to the somatic nuclei of the cranial nerves, passing through the genu of the internal capsule and the middle of the cerebral peduncle, between the substantia nigra and the interpeduncular space. It supplies the striated muscles of head and neck.

title: Where do corticobulbar fibres end?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where do corticobulbar fibres end?
body.back: They synapse on motor neurons in the cranial nerve nuclei, crossing gradually as they descend. One group ends in the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nuclei; others in the motor nuclei of V, VII, IX, X and XI.

title: What is the extrapyramidal system?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the extrapyramidal system?
body.back: A network of nuclei and tracts influencing skeletal muscle for involuntary movement, balance, posture and coordination. It includes the basal ganglia, cerebellum and brainstem nuclei, which receive cortical input and project to brainstem and spinal motor neurons.

title: Name the components of the extrapyramidal system.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the components of the extrapyramidal system.
body.back: Cerebral cortex, mostly the motor area and nearby frontal and parietal gyri. Basal ganglia: striatum, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus. Diencephalon: the subthalamus, with the entopeduncular nucleus, zona incerta and subthalamic nucleus, none projecting directly to the cord. Cerebellum. Brainstem nuclei: reticular formation, red nucleus, vestibular nuclei.

title: Name the five extrapyramidal tracts and which cross.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the five extrapyramidal tracts and which cross.
body.back: Uncrossed, ipsilateral: vestibulospinal, olivospinal and reticulospinal. Crossed, contralateral: rubrospinal and tectospinal. It is a multisynaptic system controlled by a basal ganglia motor loop.

title: Describe the vestibulospinal tracts.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the vestibulospinal tracts.
body.back: Medial and lateral, from the vestibular nuclei, which receive balance input. They stay ipsilateral and control balance and posture by innervating the anti-gravity muscles, flexors of the arm and extensors of the leg.

title: Describe the reticulospinal tracts.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the reticulospinal tracts.
body.back: Medial, from the pons: facilitates voluntary movement and increases tone. Lateral, from the medulla: inhibits voluntary movement and reduces tone.

title: Describe the rubrospinal and tectospinal tracts.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the rubrospinal and tectospinal tracts.
body.back: Rubrospinal: from the red nucleus of the midbrain, crosses and descends contralaterally; thought to help fine hand control. Tectospinal: from the superior colliculus, which receives optic input, crosses quickly and ends at cervical levels, coordinating head movements with vision.

title: Describe the olivospinal tract.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the olivospinal tract.
body.back: From the olive of the medulla, involved in synergistic muscle activity for upper limb movement, and present only at the cervical enlargement.

title: How do the basal ganglia and cerebellum interact?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How do the basal ganglia and cerebellum interact?
body.back: Classically seen as separate loops through the cortex and thalamus, they in fact have rich direct connections both ways, plus a multisynaptic route through the thalamus for coordination, and they influence dopamine release.

title: What are the descending tracts?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the descending tracts?
body.back: Pathways carrying motor signals from the brain to the lower motor neurons in the cord, controlling voluntary and involuntary movement. They start mainly in the cortex and brainstem nuclei. Two groups: pyramidal and extrapyramidal, working together on alpha and gamma motor neurons.

title: Alpha versus gamma motor neurons.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Alpha versus gamma motor neurons.
body.back: Both in the ventral horn. Alpha: the largest motor neurons, supplying skeletal muscle. Gamma: supplying the intrafusal fibres of muscle spindles. Arranged somatotopically: medial neurons supply proximal muscles, lateral neurons distal ones.

title: Summarise the descending control system.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Summarise the descending control system.
body.back: Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex plan, initiate and direct voluntary movement; brainstem centres handle basic movement and posture. The basal ganglia gate the proper initiation of movement; the cerebellum coordinates ongoing movement. All act on local circuits and lower motor neurons in the cord and brainstem, which drive the muscles.

title: Describe dopamine in the extrapyramidal system.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe dopamine in the extrapyramidal system.
body.back: Made by the substantia nigra pars compacta, acting mainly on the striatum. It smooths coordinated voluntary movement and balances excitation and inhibition. Deficiency in Parkinson's disease gives rigidity, tremor and bradykinesia; excess, as in some psychoses, gives involuntary movements.

title: Describe acetylcholine in the basal ganglia.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe acetylcholine in the basal ganglia.
body.back: Excitatory in the striatum, from cholinergic interneurons, working in balance with dopamine. In Parkinson's disease dopamine falls, so acetylcholine is relatively high, giving tremor and rigidity; anticholinergic drugs help restore balance.

title: Describe GABA and glutamate in the basal ganglia.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe GABA and glutamate in the basal ganglia.
body.back: GABA: the main inhibitory transmitter, in the striatum, globus pallidus and substantia nigra pars reticulata, suppressing unwanted movement; dysfunction gives chorea or dystonia. Glutamate: the main excitatory transmitter, from subthalamic and cortical neurons, needed for movement initiation; overactivity can cause excitotoxicity.

title: What role do serotonin and noradrenaline play?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What role do serotonin and noradrenaline play?
body.back: Modulating motor control through brainstem projections, influencing tone, arousal and motor stability. Serotonin imbalance can contribute to movement and psychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's disease.

title: Pyramidal versus extrapyramidal tracts.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Pyramidal versus extrapyramidal tracts.
body.back: Pyramidal: voluntary control of body and face muscles. Extrapyramidal: involuntary, automatic control of all muscles: tone, balance, posture and locomotion.

title: Describe the two neurons of the pyramidal pathway.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the two neurons of the pyramidal pathway.
body.back: A fast pathway of two neurons. N1: the upper motor neuron, the pyramidal cells. N2: the lower motor neuron, the radicular cells of the ventral horn or the cells of the brainstem motor nuclei.

title: Where do the corticospinal tracts start?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where do the corticospinal tracts start?
body.back: In the cerebral cortex: mainly the primary motor cortex, plus the premotor cortex and the supplementary motor area. The voluntary motor cortex is the precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4.

title: What sets the size of a motor area?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What sets the size of a motor area?
body.back: The complexity and precision of movement, not muscle size, so the hand and tongue areas are the largest.

title: Describe the architecture of the motor cortex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the architecture of the motor cortex.
body.back: Six layers, I to VI from the surface. Layer IV, well developed in the parietal cortex, is almost absent in the motor cortex. Layer V contains the large Betz cells, the origin of the pyramidal tract.

title: Trace the corticospinal tract from the cortex to the medulla.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the corticospinal tract from the cortex to the medulla.
body.back: From the upper two thirds of the precentral gyrus and its medial extension, the fibres converge and descend through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, behind the geniculate tract. They occupy the middle part of the cerebral peduncle, split into fascicles in the pons, and reconverge as the pyramidal eminence in the medulla. Decussation occurs at the bulbospinal junction.

title: Lateral versus anterior corticospinal tract.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Lateral versus anterior corticospinal tract.
body.back: Lateral: about 90 percent of fibres cross in the lower medulla and descend to end in the ventral horn at all levels, supplying the limbs. Anterior: stays ipsilateral, then crosses and ends in the ventral horn of cervical and upper thoracic segments, supplying the axial muscles.

title: What is the diencephalon?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the diencephalon?
body.back: The central brain around the third ventricle, above the brainstem and below the corpus callosum and cortex. Four parts: epithalamus, thalamus, subthalamus and hypothalamus. A primary relay and processing centre for sensation and autonomic control.

title: Describe the hypothalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the hypothalamus.
body.back: Below the thalamus, forming the floor of the third ventricle; a small cone projecting down to the pituitary infundibulum. It holds control centres for the autonomic nervous system and acts on the endocrine system through the pituitary.

title: Name the regions of the hypothalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the regions of the hypothalamus.
body.back: Supraoptic, tuberal and mammillary.

title: Give the functions of the hypothalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the functions of the hypothalamus.
body.back: Homeostasis: hunger, thirst, body temperature, blood pressure and heart rate. It interfaces the nervous and endocrine systems, regulates sexual activity and controls the stress response.

title: What happens when the hypothalamus is damaged?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What happens when the hypothalamus is damaged?
body.back: Aggression, acute stress, hypothermia or hyperthermia, fatigue, weight gain or loss, and high or low sex drive.

title: Describe the epithalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the epithalamus.
body.back: The posterior segment of the diencephalon, related to the back of the roof of the third ventricle. It includes the stria medullaris, posterior commissure, habenular nuclei, pineal body and paraventricular nuclei. It links the limbic system to the rest of the brain, secretes melatonin and regulates motor pathways and emotion.

title: Describe the stria medullaris and habenula.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the stria medullaris and habenula.
body.back: The stria medullaris thalami runs from near the anterior pole of the thalamus back to the habenular trigone. The habenular commissure links the amygdaloid and hippocampal complexes of both sides. The habenula is a pair of small nuclei above the back of the thalamus near the midline.

title: Describe the pineal gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the pineal gland.
body.back: A small piriform outgrowth of the back wall of the third ventricle, below the splenium, in the groove between the superior colliculi, beside the back of both thalami. Its pinealocytes secrete melatonin in response to darkness.

title: What is linked to epithalamic dysfunction?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is linked to epithalamic dysfunction?
body.back: Major depression, schizophrenia and sleep disorders; low melatonin tends to cause mood disorders. Also tumours of the pineal gland.

title: Describe the subthalamus and its boundaries.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the subthalamus and its boundaries.
body.back: A small region between thalamus and midbrain, important in motor control through the basal ganglia. Below the thalamus, above the midbrain; medially the hypothalamus, laterally the internal capsule, posteriorly the red nucleus and substantia nigra.

title: Name the structures of the subthalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the structures of the subthalamus.
body.back: The subthalamic nucleus, lens-shaped, medial to the internal capsule, part of the basal ganglia circuit; the zona incerta above it, for sensorimotor integration; the fields of Forel, linking pallidus, thalamus and subthalamus; and the subthalamic fasciculus to the pallidus and substantia nigra.

title: Describe the thalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the thalamus.
body.back: A paired grey matter structure between cortex and midbrain: interconnected nuclei separated by laminae of white matter, connecting to the cortex in all directions. The two thalami are joined by the interthalamic adhesion. Ovoid, narrowest in front.

title: How does the subthalamic nucleus control movement?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How does the subthalamic nucleus control movement?
body.back: Its glutamatergic neurons excite the internal globus pallidus, whose GABAergic neurons inhibit the thalamus and so inhibit movement. A lesion releases that brake, producing hemiballismus. It is a deep brain stimulation target.

title: Why is the thalamus the gateway to the cortex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why is the thalamus the gateway to the cortex?
body.back: Every sensation except smell is filtered in the thalamus before reaching the cortex, so it controls what the cortex receives.

title: How is the thalamus subdivided?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How is the thalamus subdivided?
body.back: A Y-shaped white matter sheet, the internal medullary lamina, divides it into anterior, medial and lateral parts. Each part has nuclei relaying sensation and modulating motor responses via the basal ganglia. The pulvinar is the posterior nuclear group.

title: Describe the geniculate bodies.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the geniculate bodies.
body.back: Paired nuclei on the posterior inferior thalamus near the midbrain. Lateral geniculate body: vision, from the retina via the optic tract to the occipital cortex via the optic radiations. Medial geniculate body: hearing, from the inferior colliculus to the temporal auditory cortex.

title: Give the anterior and medial relations of the thalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the anterior and medial relations of the thalamus.
body.back: Anterior: its pole forms the posterior wall of the foramen of Monro, where five veins join as the internal cerebral vein. Medial: its medial wall forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle.

title: Give the superior relations of the thalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the superior relations of the thalamus.
body.back: The choroid plexus of the third ventricle, the body of the fornix, the internal cerebral vein, the caudate nucleus and the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

title: Give the posterior and inferior relations of the thalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the posterior and inferior relations of the thalamus.
body.back: Posterior: the pulvinar, lateral to the pineal gland, habenula, posterior commissure, corpora quadrigemina and splenium of the corpus callosum. Inferior: the hypothalamus, the cerebral aqueduct and the midbrain tegmentum.

title: Give the functions of the thalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the functions of the thalamus.
body.back: Maintaining consciousness, wakefulness and sleep; filtering sensory information for the cortex, all senses except smell; and modulating motor responses via the basal ganglia.

title: Describe the blood supply of the thalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the blood supply of the thalamus.
body.back: Branches of the posterior cerebral artery, in four regions: anterior, inferolateral, paramedian and posterior.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The thalamus, the gateway to the cortex, its medial wall forming the side of the third ventricle.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The hypothalamus, forming the floor of the third ventricle and controlling homeostasis.

title: Which gland is at the arrow, and what does it secrete?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which gland is at the arrow, and what does it secrete?
body.back: The pineal gland, in the epithalamus, secreting melatonin in response to darkness.

title: Which gland is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which gland is at the arrow?
body.back: The pituitary gland, joined to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum.

title: Which cavity is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cavity is at the arrow?
body.back: The third ventricle, around which the whole diencephalon is organised.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The mammillary body, part of the hypothalamus, receiving the anterior columns of the fornix.

title: Which region is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which region is at the arrow?
body.back: The subthalamus, between thalamus and midbrain, containing the subthalamic nucleus.

title: What is the ear, and what are its parts?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the ear, and what are its parts?
body.back: The organ of hearing, which also plays an important role in maintaining balance. It has three parts, external, middle and inner, mostly within the petrous part of the temporal bone.

title: What is the middle ear?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the middle ear?
body.back: An air cavity in the thickness of the temporal bone, with a central tympanic cavity, continued behind by the mastoid cells and forward by the Eustachian tube to the nasopharynx. Three cavities: the Eustachian tube, the tympanic cavity and the mastoid.

title: Describe the tympanic cavity.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the tympanic cavity.
body.back: A six-sided box: five bony walls and a sixth membranous one, the tympanic membrane. Length 15 mm, height 15 to 7 mm, width 3 to 6 mm. It contains the ossicular chain. In coronal section it is a biconcave disc, like a red blood cell.

title: Describe the tympanic membrane.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the tympanic membrane.
body.back: Thin, semi-transparent, pearly white or slightly pink. Height 10 mm, width 9 mm, thickness 0.05 to 0.09 mm. Surface features: the malleus, its lateral process, the cone of light and the sulcus tympanicus. Two parts: pars tensa and pars flaccida.

title: Give the three layers of the tympanic membrane.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the three layers of the tympanic membrane.
body.back: Outer cuticular layer of stratified squamous epithelium, continuous with the canal skin. Middle fibrous layer enclosing the handle of the malleus, with outer radiating and inner circular fibres. Inner mucosal layer of low columnar epithelium, continuous with the middle ear lining.

title: Pars tensa versus pars flaccida.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Pars tensa versus pars flaccida.
body.back: Pars tensa forms most of the membrane; its periphery thickens into the annulus tympanicus, fitting the tympanic sulcus. Pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane) is a small triangle above the lateral process of the malleus between the malleal folds; thin and lax because the fibrous layer is replaced by loose areolar tissue; slightly pinkish.

title: Describe the medial wall of the tympanic cavity.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the medial wall of the tympanic cavity.
body.back: The labyrinthine wall, separating the cavity from the inner ear. Divided into two levels by the prominence of the facial canal. Upper level: the prominence of the lateral semicircular canal. Lower level: the promontory, the oval window (fenestra vestibuli) and the round window (fenestra cochleae).

title: Describe the roof and floor of the tympanic cavity.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the roof and floor of the tympanic cavity.
body.back: Roof, the tegmen tympani: a thin plate of bone separating the cavity from the middle cranial fossa. Floor: a thin plate separating the cavity from the jugular bulb. It is sometimes congenitally deficient, so the bulb projects into the middle ear covered only by mucosa.

title: Describe the anterior and posterior walls.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the anterior and posterior walls.
body.back: Anterior: a thin plate separating the cavity from the internal carotid artery below; above, two canals, the upper for tensor tympani and the lower for the auditory tube. Posterior: separates the cavity from the mastoid antrum and cells; presents the aditus ad antrum; the vertical part of the facial canal runs in it behind the pyramid down to the stylomastoid foramen; its lower part is the retrotympanum.

title: Name the parts of the three ossicles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the three ossicles.
body.back: Malleus: head, neck, manubrium, lateral process, anterior process. Incus: body, short process, long process, lenticular process. Stapes: the smallest and lightest, about 2 mg, with head, anterior crus, posterior crus and footplate.

title: Describe the mastoid cells.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the mastoid cells.
body.back: A component of the middle ear: air cells dug into the mastoid bone, part of the temporal bone. The antrum is the most developed. All cells communicate with each other and with the tympanic cavity.

title: What are the functions of the external ear?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the functions of the external ear?
body.back: Localisation of sound, a contribution to amplification for better auditory perception, and protection. It is also of major aesthetic importance, hence reconstructive and aesthetic surgery of the auricle.

title: Describe the Eustachian tube.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the Eustachian tube.
body.back: An osseocartilaginous tube from the tympanic cavity to the nasopharynx, running downwards, forwards and medially. A superior and posterior bony portion and an anterior cartilaginous portion. Length 31 to 38 mm, diameter 2 mm. Functions: equalising air pressure, protection and drainage.

title: What forms the tympanic plexus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What forms the tympanic plexus?
body.back: On the promontory of the medial wall: the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson's nerve), sympathetic fibres from the plexus around the internal carotid artery, and a branch from the geniculate ganglion.

title: What does the external ear do in hearing?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the external ear do in hearing?
body.back: The pinna captures sound and funnels it into the canal; its shape helps localise sound. The canal acts as a resonator, amplifying frequencies important for speech, around 2000 to 5000 Hz. Cerumen traps dust and debris, protecting the eardrum.

title: Why does the middle ear need to amplify sound?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why does the middle ear need to amplify sound?
body.back: Sound passes from air in the canal to fluid in the cochlea, an impedance mismatch that would reflect most of the energy. The ossicles form a lever system amplifying the vibrations of the drum and transmitting them to the oval window.

title: How does the ossicular chain work as a lever?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How does the ossicular chain work as a lever?
body.back: The malleus, attached to the drum, receives vibrations and passes them to the incus, which pivots and transmits them to the stapes at the oval window. The mechanical advantage comes from the relative lengths of the malleus and incus, increasing force on the oval window. The lever action and the hydraulic pressure ratio together give the transformer function of the middle ear, which reconstructive surgery must preserve.

title: What is the acoustic (stapes) reflex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the acoustic (stapes) reflex?
body.back: Contraction of the muscles attached to the ossicles in response to loud sounds, reducing transmission of sound energy to the inner ear and protecting it.

title: How does the Eustachian tube equalise pressure?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How does the Eustachian tube equalise pressure?
body.back: It opens during swallowing or yawning, letting air flow in or out of the middle ear. This keeps the pressure equal on both sides of the drum, essential for hearing and for preventing barotrauma.

title: Where is the external ear situated?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where is the external ear situated?
body.back: Behind the temporomandibular joint and the parotid region, in front of the mastoid, below the temporal region. The pinna is joined to the skull by its anterior third; the posterior two thirds are mobile.

title: What makes up the auricle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What makes up the auricle?
body.back: A lateral surface, a medial (cranial) surface, a skin covering, a cartilaginous framework and a musculo-ligamentary system.

title: Describe the lateral surface of the auricle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the lateral surface of the auricle.
body.back: Projections and depressions formed by cartilage and skin. Four constant projections: the helix around the upper two thirds; the anthelix, bifid and concentric to it, separated by the scapha; the tragus; and the antitragus. The concha is a depression bounded by the anthelix behind and above, the root of the helix and the tragus in front and the antitragus below: its upper posterior part is the cymba conchae, its lower anterior part the cavum conchae. The lobe is a skin fold without cartilage.

title: Describe the muscles of the auricle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the muscles of the auricle.
body.back: Rudimentary in humans. Extrinsic, from scalp or skull to the auricle: auricularis anterior and superior from the epicranial aponeurosis, auricularis posterior from the mastoid process to the eminentia conchae. Intrinsic: small muscles between the cartilaginous parts. They may position the auricle to localise sound, rarely seen in humans but used by animals.

title: Describe the external auditory canal.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the external auditory canal.
body.back: Cylindrical, closed internally by the tympanic membrane and open outside. Length 25 mm, average width 8 mm, elongated S-shaped course. A tight zone, the isthmus, lies at the junction of its outer two thirds and inner third. Cartilaginous part: outer third. Bony part: inner two thirds.

title: Compare the cartilaginous and bony parts of the canal.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Compare the cartilaginous and bony parts of the canal.
body.back: Cartilaginous: outer third (8 mm), continuous with the auricular cartilage; thick skin with hair and ceruminous glands that secrete wax. Bony: inner two thirds (16 mm); thin skin continuous with the cuticular layer of the drum, with no hair or ceruminous glands; contains the isthmus.

title: Blood and nerve supply of the external ear.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Blood and nerve supply of the external ear.
body.back: Arteries: the superficial temporal and posterior auricular, from the external carotid. Nerves: the superficial cervical plexus, the nervus intermedius (VII bis) and the trigeminal nerve.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The external auditory canal: 25 mm long, S-shaped, cartilaginous in its outer third and bony in its inner two thirds.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The tympanic membrane, forming four fifths of the lateral wall of the tympanic cavity.

title: Which ossicle is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which ossicle is at the arrow?
body.back: The malleus. Its handle is enclosed in the fibrous layer of the eardrum.

title: Which ossicle is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which ossicle is at the arrow?
body.back: The incus: body, short, long and lenticular processes. It pivots to pass vibrations from malleus to stapes.

title: Which ossicle is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which ossicle is at the arrow?
body.back: The stapes, the smallest and lightest bone, about 2 mg. Its footplate sits in the oval window.

title: Which opening is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which opening is at the arrow?
body.back: The oval window (fenestra vestibuli), on the lower level of the medial wall, receiving the stapes footplate.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The Eustachian tube, 31 to 38 mm long, running down, forward and medially to the nasopharynx.

title: Which structures are at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structures are at the arrow?
body.back: The mastoid air cells. The antrum is the largest, and all communicate with the tympanic cavity through the aditus ad antrum.

title: Which space is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which space is highlighted?
body.back: The tympanic cavity: a six-sided box with five bony walls and the eardrum laterally, containing the ossicular chain.

title: What is the inner ear, and where is it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the inner ear, and where is it?
body.back: A set of highly differentiated organs with complex functions, hearing and balance, placed inside the massive petrous bone. Two main parts: the bony labyrinth, a complex of bony cavities, and the membranous labyrinth, a set of membranous cavities.

title: Describe the semicircular canals.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the semicircular canals.
body.back: Three bony canals, anterior (superior), posterior and lateral, in three planes at 90 degrees. Each is about two thirds of a circle, dilated at one end into the ampulla. The anterior and posterior lie in vertical planes, the lateral horizontally.

title: How do the semicircular canals open into the vestibule?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How do the semicircular canals open into the vestibule?
body.back: The anterior canal's ampullated end opens anterolaterally; its non-ampullated end joins the upper non-ampullated end of the posterior canal as the crus commune. The posterior canal's lower ampullated end opens into the vestibule. The lateral canal opens by both ends. So three canals open by five openings.

title: How are the parts of the membranous labyrinth connected?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How are the parts of the membranous labyrinth connected?
body.back: The cochlear duct lies in the bony cochlea, the saccule and utricle in the vestibule, the three semicircular ducts in the canals. The cochlear duct joins the saccule by the ductus reuniens. The saccule and utricle are joined by the Y-shaped utriculo-saccular duct, which expands into the endolymphatic duct and sac. The utricle connects to the semicircular ducts by five openings.

title: Name the sensory receptors of the inner ear and their roles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the sensory receptors of the inner ear and their roles.
body.back: Spiral organ of Corti in the cochlear duct: hearing, via the cochlear nerve. Maculae in the saccule and utricle: static balance. Cristae ampullaris in the semicircular ducts: kinetic balance. Both balance signals travel in the vestibular nerve.

title: Describe the cochlear duct.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the cochlear duct.
body.back: The spiral anterior part of the membranous labyrinth, two and three quarter turns, a 30 mm tube. It lies in the middle of the cochlear canal between scala vestibuli and scala tympani and contains the organ of Corti.

title: Describe the organ of Corti.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the organ of Corti.
body.back: It sits on the basilar membrane. Hair cells, the receptors of hearing, carry stereocilia at their apices overlaid by the tectorial membrane. Inner hair cells are richly supplied by cochlear nerve fibres and transmit auditory impulses. Outer hair cells take efferent fibres and modulate the inner hair cells. There are also supporting cells and the tectorial membrane.

title: What is the travelling wave?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the travelling wave?
body.back: The sound wave begins at the oval window and travels up the scala vestibuli toward the apex. Its amplitude grows with sound frequency and peaks at particular sites, where the receptors of the organ of Corti are stimulated and transduction occurs.

title: Trace the central auditory pathway.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the central auditory pathway.
body.back: Cochlea, cochlear nuclei, olivary nuclei, nuclei of the lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculi, medial geniculate, acoustic radiation, auditory cortex in the transverse temporal gyrus. The main pathway is contralateral; a minor pathway is ipsilateral.

title: Saccule versus utricle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Saccule versus utricle.
