body.back: The saccule is a small globular sac; the utricle is an oblong sac, larger than the saccule. The saccule connects in front to the basal turn of the cochlear duct by the ductus reuniens, and behind to the utricle by the Y-shaped utriculo-saccular duct.

title: How does the vestibular system connect centrally?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How does the vestibular system connect centrally?
body.back: Via the vestibular nuclei to the cerebellum, to the oculomotor and abducens nuclei through the medial longitudinal fasciculus for the eye-movement (vestibulo-ocular) reflex, and to the spinal cord through the vestibulospinal tract for posture.

title: Endolymph versus perilymph.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Endolymph versus perilymph.
body.back: Endolymph fills the membranous labyrinth, a closed system of intercommunicating sacs and ducts. Perilymph fills the space between the membranous and bony labyrinths. The sensory receptors in the membranous labyrinth are responsible for hearing and balance.

title: Describe the cochlear nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the cochlear nerve.
body.back: CN VIII divides in the internal auditory canal into an anterior cochlear nerve and a posterior vestibular nerve. The cochlear nerve is voluminous, travels through the IAC into the cochlear fossa and ends in the spiral canal at the spiral ganglion of Corti, whose cells are spread along the two and a half turns.

title: Inner versus outer hair cells.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Inner versus outer hair cells.
body.back: Inner hair cells perform mechano-bioelectrical transduction of the tectorial membrane's vibrations and connect to about 45,000 afferent fibres, 90 to 95 percent of the cochlear nerve, carrying the message to the cochlear nuclei. Outer hair cells are not true sensory receptors: they are contractile, react to sound and increase frequency selectivity.

title: Give the branches of the vestibular nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the branches of the vestibular nerve.
body.back: It quickly divides into three. Superior vestibular nerve: the utricular nerve to the utricular macula, the superior ampullary nerve to the crest of the superior canal, and the lateral ampullary nerve to the crest of the lateral canal. Inferior vestibular nerve: the saccular nerve to the saccular macula. And the posterior ampullary nerve.

title: What supplies blood to the labyrinth?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What supplies blood to the labyrinth?
body.back: The labyrinthine artery, arising from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery or directly from the basilar trunk.

title: Name the parts of the bony labyrinth.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the bony labyrinth.
body.back: It derives from the otic capsule: a series of intercommunicating cavities in the petrous temporal bone, lined by periosteum and containing perilymph. Three parts: the cochlea, the vestibule and the semicircular canals.

title: Name the parts of the membranous labyrinth.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the membranous labyrinth.
body.back: The semicircular ducts, the cochlear duct, the utricle and the saccule, filled with endolymph. The anterior labyrinth, for hearing, is the cochlear duct; the posterior labyrinth, for balance, is the utricle, saccule, semicircular ducts and endolymphatic system.

title: Describe the bony cochlea.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the bony cochlea.
body.back: Just in front of the vestibule, shaped like a snail shell: a bony tube 30 mm long, 1 to 2 mm in diameter, around a central pillar, the modiolus. Each turn of the spiral attaches to the previous one to form the spiral wall.

title: Describe the modiolus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the modiolus.
body.back: The axial bony stem around which the cochlear canal spirals, like an elongated cone. Its base lies at the fundus of the internal acoustic meatus, its apex points toward the middle ear and is overlaid by the apical turn. Its base is perforated spirally by the cochlear nerve fibres.

title: Describe the cochlear canal and spiral lamina.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the cochlear canal and spiral lamina.
body.back: The canal spirals around the modiolus, two and three quarter turns, and its basal turn bulges into the tympanic cavity as the promontory. The spiral lamina, a bony ridge like a screw thread, partly divides it into scala vestibuli above and scala tympani below, which communicate at the apex through the helicotrema.

title: What features lie near the basal turn of the cochlea?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What features lie near the basal turn of the cochlea?
body.back: The scala vestibuli communicates with the vestibule. The scala tympani presents the round window (fenestra cochleae), below and behind the promontory and closed by the secondary tympanic membrane, and the start of the aqueduct of the cochlea, a narrow canal connecting cochlear perilymph with the CSF.

title: Describe the vestibule.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the vestibule.
body.back: The central ovoid cavity of the bony labyrinth, between the cochlea in front and the semicircular canals behind, medial to the middle ear. Its lateral wall communicates with the middle ear by the oval window, closed by the stapes footplate and the annular ligament.

title: Which part of the bony labyrinth is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the bony labyrinth is at the arrow?
body.back: The cochlea: a 30 mm snail-shaped tube spiralling around the modiolus, for hearing.

title: Which cavity is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cavity is at the arrow?
body.back: The vestibule, the central ovoid cavity between the cochlea in front and the semicircular canals behind, containing the utricle and saccule.

title: Which canal is at the arrow, and in which plane does it lie?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which canal is at the arrow, and in which plane does it lie?
body.back: The lateral semicircular canal, in the horizontal plane. Both its ends open directly into the vestibule.

title: Which canal is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which canal is at the arrow?
body.back: The anterior (superior) semicircular canal, in a vertical plane. Its non-ampullated end joins the posterior canal's to form the crus commune.

title: What is the dilated structure at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the dilated structure at the arrow?
body.back: An ampulla, the dilated end of a semicircular canal, which holds the crista ampullaris, the receptor for kinetic balance.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and what does it detect?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and what does it detect?
body.back: The utricle, an oblong sac larger than the saccule. Its macula detects static balance.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The saccule, a small globular sac joined to the cochlear duct by the ductus reuniens. Its macula detects static balance.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The modiolus, the central bony pillar of the cochlea, perforated at its base by the cochlear nerve fibres.

title: Which opening is at the arrow, and what closes it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which opening is at the arrow, and what closes it?
body.back: The round window (fenestra cochleae), closed by the secondary tympanic membrane.

title: Where does the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex begin?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex begin?
body.back: At the retina. Light stimulates the photoreceptors and the retinal ganglion cells transmit the signal into the optic nerve.

title: Which nerve is at the arrow, and which limb of the light reflex is it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which nerve is at the arrow, and which limb of the light reflex is it?
body.back: The optic nerve (CN II): the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex and step II of the seven.

title: What happens to the reflex fibres at the structure marked?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What happens to the reflex fibres at the structure marked?
body.back: The optic chiasm. The nasal retinal fibres cross to the contralateral optic tract; the temporal fibres stay ipsilateral. This crossing is part of why the reflex is consensual.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and where do its reflex fibres go?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and where do its reflex fibres go?
body.back: The optic tract. Fibres for the light reflex leave it to synapse in the pretectal nuclei of the dorsal midbrain, not in the lateral geniculate nucleus.

title: What is the structure at the arrow, and what is it for?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the structure at the arrow, and what is it for?
body.back: The lateral geniculate nucleus, the relay for conscious vision and for the afferent limb of the accommodation reflex. The light reflex bypasses it and uses the pretectal nuclei instead.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and which reflex needs it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and which reflex needs it?
body.back: The primary visual cortex. The accommodation reflex passes through it on its afferent limb; the pupillary light reflex does not.

title: Give the lecture's mnemonic for cranial nerve types.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the lecture's mnemonic for cranial nerve types.
body.back: 128: sensory nerves. 346, 11, 12: motor nerves. The rest are mixed: 5, 7, 9, 10. Parasympathetic fibres run in 3, 7, 9 and 10.

title: Why does the lens become spherical when relaxed?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why does the lens become spherical when relaxed?
body.back: In a young person the lens has a strong elastic capsule filled with viscous, proteinaceous but transparent fluid. With no tension on the capsule it assumes an almost spherical shape, mainly through the elastic retraction of the capsule.

title: Name the four parts of the near response.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the four parts of the near response.
body.back: Lens changes (accommodation), changes in the pupil, the near response itself, and convergence of the eyes. Goal: clear vision of a nearby object.

title: Give the six steps of accommodation for a near object.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the six steps of accommodation for a near object.
body.back: 1. Ciliary muscles contract. 2. The suspensory ligament relaxes. 3. The lens becomes more convex. 4. The dioptric power of the eye increases. 5. The near object is focused on the retina.

title: Give the steps for looking from near to far.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the steps for looking from near to far.
body.back: 1. The far object is focused on the retina. 2. The dioptric power of the eye decreases. 3. The lens becomes less convex (flat). 4. The suspensory ligament contracts (becomes taut).

title: Summarise near vision and far vision.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Summarise near vision and far vision.
body.back: Near vision (accommodation): parallel rays from a close object would focus behind the retina if the ciliary muscle stayed relaxed, giving blurred vision. The solution is to increase the curvature and refractive power of the lens. Far vision (at rest): the ciliary muscles are relaxed and the ligaments taut, so the lens is flat.

title: Trace the accommodation reflex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the accommodation reflex.
body.back: Afferent: retina, optic nerve, optic chiasma, optic tract, lateral geniculate body, visual cortex. Efferent: oculomotor nucleus, parasympathetic fibres, ciliary ganglion, ciliary muscle, circular pupillary muscle.

title: Trace the afferent pathway of the pupillary light reflex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the afferent pathway of the pupillary light reflex.
body.back: Light enters the pupil and stimulates the retina. Retinal ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve. At the optic chiasm the nasal retinal fibres cross to the contralateral optic tract while the temporal fibres stay ipsilateral. Fibres from the optic tracts project to and synapse in the pretectal nuclei in the dorsal midbrain, in the collicular region. The pretectal nuclei project to the ipsilateral Edinger-Westphal nucleus and also to the contralateral one via the posterior commissure.

title: Trace the efferent pathway of the pupillary light reflex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the efferent pathway of the pupillary light reflex.
body.back: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus projects preganglionic parasympathetic fibres, which exit the midbrain and travel along the oculomotor nerve (CN III), then synapse on postganglionic parasympathetic fibres in the ciliary ganglion. The postganglionic fibres, the short ciliary nerves, innervate the sphincter muscle of the pupil, producing pupillary constriction.

title: Direct versus consensual pupillary light reflex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Direct versus consensual pupillary light reflex.
body.back: Because of the bilateral projections, light shone in one eye constricts the pupil of that eye (direct reflex) and of the other eye (consensual reflex). In darkness the reflex is inhibited, which results in dilation of the pupil in both eyes.

title: Give the seven numbered steps of the pupillary light reflex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the seven numbered steps of the pupillary light reflex.
body.back: I. Projection of light. II. Optic nerve. III. Pretectal nucleus. IV. Edinger-Westphal nucleus. V. Oculomotor nerve. VI. Ciliary ganglion. VII. Short ciliary nerve.

title: Why is the optic nerve different from other cranial nerves?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why is the optic nerve different from other cranial nerves?
body.back: It is sheathed by the meninges (dura, arachnoid and pia) with CSF in the subarachnoid space around it, so it behaves like a tract of the brain rather than an ordinary peripheral nerve.

title: Describe the corneal reflex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the corneal reflex.
body.back: Touch on the cornea travels in the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V) to the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, then to the facial motor nucleus on both sides. The temporal branch of the facial nerve (VII) makes the orbicularis oculi contract, so both eyes blink.

title: Which nerve supplies the orbicularis oculi?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which nerve supplies the orbicularis oculi?
body.back: The facial nerve (CN VII), through its temporal and zygomatic branches.

title: Trace the autonomic control of the lacrimal gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the autonomic control of the lacrimal gland.
body.back: Parasympathetic: from the facial nerve through the greater superficial petrosal nerve, the pterygoid canal (joined by the deep petrosal nerve), to the pterygopalatine ganglion, then along the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves to the gland, stimulating secretion. Sympathetic: from the internal carotid plexus through the deep petrosal nerve, following the same route, inhibiting secretion.

title: Which fibres pass through the ciliary ganglion?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which fibres pass through the ciliary ganglion?
body.back: Parasympathetic fibres (which synapse there), sympathetic fibres from the carotid plexus, and sensory fibres from the nasociliary nerve. The sympathetic and sensory fibres pass straight through without synapsing.

title: Where do the ciliary ganglion's roots come from?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where do the ciliary ganglion's roots come from?
body.back: The sensory root from the nasociliary nerve, the motor (parasympathetic) root from the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve, and the sympathetic root from the carotid plexus. Its branches are the short ciliary nerves.

title: Name the three orders of neuron in the visual pathway.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three orders of neuron in the visual pathway.
body.back: First order: cone and rod photoreceptors. Second order: bipolar cells, leading to the ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve. Third order: the neuron running from the lateral geniculate body to the cerebral cortex.

title: Give the visual pathway as a chain.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the visual pathway as a chain.
body.back: Cones and rods, bipolar cells, ganglion cells, optic nerve (axons of the ganglion cells), optic chiasma, optic tract, lateral geniculate body in the thalamus, axons of the geniculocalcarine tract, optic radiation, visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) in the occipital cortex.

title: List the motor supply and reflexes of the eye covered in this lecture.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: List the motor supply and reflexes of the eye covered in this lecture.
body.back: Motor supply CN III, parasympathetic supply CN III, motor supply CN IV, motor supply CN VI, the pupillary light reflex, the accommodation reflex, the corneal reflex, and autonomic control of the lacrimal gland.

title: What does a left trochlear nerve palsy follow from, in the lecture's example?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does a left trochlear nerve palsy follow from, in the lecture's example?
body.back: An infarct in the left midbrain, giving a left CN IV palsy, with the trochlear nucleus in the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus.

title: What two cell types are in the abducens nucleus, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What two cell types are in the abducens nucleus, and why does it matter?
body.back: Motor neurons that control the lateral rectus on the same side, and interneurons that cross the midline to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus, which controls the medial rectus of the opposite eye. That is how the two eyes look sideways together.

title: What is the medial longitudinal fasciculus for?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the medial longitudinal fasciculus for?
body.back: It links CN III, IV, VI and the vestibular nuclei, producing conjugate movement of the eyes and coordinating eye movement with head movement.

title: Photopic versus scotopic vision.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Photopic versus scotopic vision.
body.back: Photopic: bright light vision, served by cones, high visual acuity for colours and details, low sensitivity to light (needs a high visual threshold to be stimulated). Scotopic: night and dim light vision, served by rods, low visual acuity, no colours or details, great sensitivity to light.

title: Which layer is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which layer is highlighted?
body.back: The sclera, forming five sixths of the outer fibrous coat. Relatively avascular, less sensitive than the cornea, and it provides insertion for the extraocular muscles.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The optic nerve, leaving the back of the eye at the optic disc, where there are no photoreceptors: the blind spot.

title: What is the structure at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the structure at the arrow?
body.back: The macula, with the fovea at its centre. It is densely packed with cones, lacks blood vessels, and is responsible for high-acuity vision.

title: Which structure is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is highlighted?
body.back: The cornea, forming one sixth of the outer coat. Completely avascular, highly sensitive (CN V1), and the site of maximum refraction.

title: Which layer is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which layer is highlighted?
body.back: The choroid, the posterior part of the vascular layer (uvea), lying between the sclera and the retina.

title: Which layer is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which layer is highlighted?
body.back: The retina, the neural layer. Its light-receptive neural layer ends anteriorly at the ora serrata.

title: Which structure is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is highlighted?
body.back: The lens: transparent, biconvex, enclosed in a capsule suspended by zonular fibres. It thickens for near vision when CN III makes the ciliary muscle contract.

title: Which structure is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is highlighted?
body.back: The iris, a pigmented diaphragm with the pupil at its centre. Sphincter pupillae narrows the pupil (parasympathetic); dilator pupillae widens it (sympathetic).

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The ciliary body. It alters the shape and thickness of the lens for accommodation, and its ciliary processes secrete the aqueous humour.

title: Which space is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which space is highlighted?
body.back: The vitreous humour, filling about 80 percent of the posterior segment. It transmits light and holds the retina and lens in place.

title: Which space is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which space is highlighted?
body.back: The anterior chamber, between the cornea and the iris. Aqueous fluid reaches it through the pupil and drains at the angle.

title: What is Tenon's capsule?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is Tenon's capsule?
body.back: The fascial sheath of the eyeball: a thin membrane that envelops the eye from the optic nerve to the corneal limbus, separating it from the orbital fat and forming a socket in which it moves.

title: Describe the iris and how the pupil responds.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the iris and how the pupil responds.
body.back: A pigmented diaphragm with a central aperture, the pupil, on the anterior surface of the lens. Sphincter muscles within the iris adjust pupil size in response to light and the autonomic nervous system. Light and parasympathetic stimulation: narrows the pupil (miosis), sphincter pupillae. Darkness and sympathetic stimulation: widens it (mydriasis), dilator pupillae.

title: What is the aqueous fluid and what does it do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the aqueous fluid and what does it do?
body.back: A clear plasma-derived ultrafiltrate, normally devoid of proteins, cells or macromolecules. It delivers oxygen and nutrients and removes waste, inflammatory products and cellular debris from the posterior cornea and crystalline lens; provides a low refractive index transparent medium between the lens and cornea; and maintains intraocular pressure for the optimal shape and alignment of ocular structures.

title: How is the aqueous fluid formed?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How is the aqueous fluid formed?
body.back: By diffusion, ultrafiltration and active secretion. Diffusion and ultrafiltration form a reservoir of plasma in the ciliary stroma. Active secretion from that ultrafiltrate occurs across the ciliary epithelium and is relatively pressure independent. Ascorbic acid, amino acids and glucose are transported into the aqueous to supply the cornea and lens.

title: Trace the passage of the aqueous fluid.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the passage of the aqueous fluid.
body.back: Formed by the ciliary body and secreted into the posterior chamber. It traverses the pupil into the anterior chamber, then exits by one of two routes: the trabecular meshwork route or the uveoscleral route.

title: Describe the trabecular meshwork route.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the trabecular meshwork route.
body.back: Aqueous traverses the trabecular meshwork, crosses the inner wall of Schlemm's canal, then passes into collector channels, aqueous veins and episcleral veins. It accounts for most aqueous drainage, 50 to 75 percent. It is pressure sensitive: outflow increases with greater intraocular pressure.

title: Describe the uveoscleral route.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the uveoscleral route.
body.back: Aqueous passes freely from the anterior chamber angle into the connective tissue spaces within the ciliary muscle, via the iris root and anterior face of the ciliary body. Its flow is intraocular pressure independent, so it keeps draining despite pressure fluctuations. Inflammation can clog the trabecular meshwork, but locally produced prostaglandins enhance uveoscleral drainage and prevent dangerously high pressure.

title: What is intraocular pressure?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is intraocular pressure?
body.back: The fluid pressure inside the eye. The anterior chamber, between the cornea and iris, holds aqueous humour, which is thinner and more watery than the vitreous humour behind the lens. The body constantly makes and drains aqueous, and pressure reflects that balance. It is measured with a tonometer.

title: Name the four refractive media of the eye.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the four refractive media of the eye.
body.back: The cornea, the aqueous humour, the lens and the vitreous humour. Maximum refraction occurs through the cornea.

title: Describe the lens.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the lens.
body.back: Transparent, biconvex, enclosed in a capsule suspended by zonular fibres, the suspensory ligament of the lens. It sits next to the anterior surface of the eye. With no nerve stimulation, more distant objects come into focus.

title: What happens to the lens in accommodation?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What happens to the lens in accommodation?
body.back: CN III parasympathetic stimulation causes sphincter-like contraction of the ciliary muscles, the ring becomes smaller, the zonules relax, and the lens relaxes and thickens, focusing on near vision. Lens thickness increases with age, reducing the ability to accommodate.

title: What is the episclera?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the episclera?
body.back: The outermost layer of the sclera, of loose fibrous elastic tissue, attaching to Tenon's capsule. A vascular plexus lies between the bulbar conjunctiva and the sclera, with superficial and deep episcleral vessels.

title: Name the three histological components of the lens.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three histological components of the lens.
body.back: 1. Lens capsule: a thick, homogeneous, refractile, carbohydrate-rich coating on the outer surface of the epithelial cells, a very thick basement membrane of type IV collagen and glycoprotein. 2. Subcapsular epithelium: a single layer of cuboidal cells, present only on the anterior surface. 3. Lens fibres: highly differentiated cells filled with crystallins.

title: How do the lens fibres allow accommodation?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How do the lens fibres allow accommodation?
body.back: They permit focusing on near and far objects by changing the curvature of the lens. At rest or far gaze the lens is stretched or flat; to focus near, the lens thickens.

title: What is a cataract, and what are its symptoms?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is a cataract, and what are its symptoms?
body.back: The eye's natural lens becoming cloudy as proteins in the lens break down. Symptoms: cloudy, blurry, foggy or filmy vision; changes in colour perception; sensitivity to bright sunlight, headlights or lamps; glare including halos or streaks around lights; and difficulty seeing at night.

title: Describe the vitreous humour.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the vitreous humour.
body.back: A watery fluid enclosed in the meshes of the vitreous body, a jelly-like substance filling about 80 percent of the posterior segment of the eyeball, also called the postremal or vitreous chamber. It transmits light and holds the retina and lens in their respective places.

title: Name the parts of the visual retina.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the visual retina.
body.back: Neural layer (light-receptive, ending anteriorly at the ora serrata), pigmented cell layer (a single layer of cells absorbing light to reduce scattering), optic disc or papilla, macula and fovea.

title: What is the optic disc?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the optic disc?
body.back: The papilla, known as the blind spot because it has no photoreceptors. Located in the fundus of the retina, it is where the sensory fibres of the optic nerve enter the eyeball.

title: Macula and fovea: what are they for?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Macula and fovea: what are they for?
body.back: The macula contains special photoreceptor cones for visual acuity and lacks blood vessels. The fovea, at the centre of the macula, is responsible for high-acuity vision and is densely saturated with cone photoreceptors.

title: How do signals travel through the retina?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How do signals travel through the retina?
body.back: Photoreceptors and bipolar cells produce graded potentials rather than action potentials. Ganglion cells generate action potentials, and their axons join together to form the optic nerve, which exits through the back of the eye at the optic disc.

title: Rods versus cones.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Rods versus cones.
body.back: Rods: vision at low light levels (scotopic), no colour vision, low spatial acuity, about 120 million per retina. Cones: active at higher light levels (photopic), colour vision, high spatial acuity, about 6 million per retina. The central fovea is populated exclusively by cones.

title: Describe the structure of a rod cell.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the structure of a rod cell.
body.back: Thin and elongated, in two portions. The external part has numerous flattened membrane disks stacked like coins; the inner segment is rich in glycogen and mitochondria and lies near a constriction. The disks contain rhodopsin (visual purple), bleached by light to initiate the visual stimulus. The outer segment is the site of photosensitivity; the inner segment holds the metabolic machinery.

title: Name the three layers (coats) of the eyeball.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three layers (coats) of the eyeball.
body.back: Fibrous layer (sclera and cornea), vascular layer or uvea (iris, ciliary body, choroid) and neural layer (retina).

title: Describe the structure of a cone cell.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the structure of a cone cell.
body.back: Similar to rods, with outer and inner segments, a basal body with a cilium, and an accumulation of mitochondria and ribosomes. There are three functional types that cannot be distinguished morphologically. Each type has a photopigment called iodopsin, with maximum sensitivity in the red, green or blue region. Cones are sensitive only to light of higher intensity but are believed to permit better visual acuity than rods.

title: How is the outer coat divided between cornea and sclera?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How is the outer coat divided between cornea and sclera?
body.back: The cornea forms one sixth of the outer coat; the sclera forms the other five sixths.

title: Compare the cornea and the sclera.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Compare the cornea and the sclera.
body.back: Cornea: higher convexity, completely avascular, nourished by the lacrimal gland outside and aqueous humour inside, highly sensitive (CN V1). Sclera: relatively avascular, provides insertion for the muscles, less sensitive, and its collagen arrangement needs less hydration.

title: What is scleral icterus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is scleral icterus?
body.back: Yellowing of the white of the eye, also called icteric sclera, associated with hepatitis and other liver diseases.

title: What is scleritis?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is scleritis?
body.back: Inflammation of both the episclera and the underlying sclera. Up to 50 percent of cases involve an underlying systemic disease such as rheumatoid arthritis. Onset is gradual, with severe piercing pain over several days that worsens with eye movement, usually starting in one area and spreading.

title: Describe the uvea.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the uvea.
body.back: The uveal tract: iris, ciliary body and choroid. It lies between the sclera and the retina. Anterior portion: iris and ciliary body. Posterior portion: choroid.

title: What does the ciliary body do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the ciliary body do?
body.back: A muscular structure connecting the choroid with the circumference of the iris. It alters the shape and thickness of the lens (accommodation), and its ciliary processes secrete aqueous humour.

title: Which bone is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bone is highlighted?
body.back: Frontal bone. It forms the forehead and the roof of the orbits, and is one of the 8 cranial bones.

title: Which bone is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bone is highlighted?
body.back: Parietal bone. There are two, and they form the sides and roof of the skull.

title: Which bones build the cavity at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones build the cavity at the arrow?
body.back: The orbit, built by 7 bones: frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid, zygomatic, lacrimal, maxilla and palatine.

title: Which bone is highlighted, on both sides?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bone is highlighted, on both sides?
body.back: Zygomatic bone (the cheekbone). It has frontal, temporal and maxillary processes and joins the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch.

title: Which bone is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bone is highlighted?
body.back: Maxilla, the upper jaw. Its body holds the maxillary sinus, and it has four processes: frontal, zygomatic, alveolar and palatine.

title: Which bone is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bone is highlighted?
body.back: Mandible, the lower jaw, and the only skull bone that moves. It articulates with the temporal bone at the temporomandibular joint.

title: Which bones are highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones are highlighted?
body.back: The nasal bones, which form the bridge of the nose and meet at the internasal suture.

title: What is the opening at the arrows?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the opening at the arrows?
body.back: The supraorbital notch (or foramen), in the superior orbital margin of the frontal bone. It transmits the supraorbital nerve and vessels.

title: What is the opening at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the opening at the arrow?
body.back: The infraorbital foramen, in the maxilla just below the inferior orbital margin. The infraorbital nerve and vessels emerge here onto the face.

title: What is the opening at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the opening at the arrow?
body.back: The mental foramen, on the outer surface of the body of the mandible. It transmits the mental nerve and vessels.

title: What is the opening at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the opening at the arrow?
body.back: The piriform aperture, the bony opening of the nasal cavity, bounded by the nasal bones and the maxillae.

title: How many bones are in the skull, and how is it divided?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How many bones are in the skull, and how is it divided?
body.back: 22 bones: the neurocranium (8 bones, protects the brain) and the viscerocranium (14 facial bones, including the mandible).

title: What does the cribriform plate do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the cribriform plate do?
body.back: It forms the roof of the nasal cavity and part of the anterior cranial fossa. Its foramina carry the olfactory nerve fibres (CN I).

title: What do the ethmoidal labyrinths contain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What do the ethmoidal labyrinths contain?
body.back: The ethmoidal air cells, the lamina papyracea (orbital plate), and the superior and middle nasal conchae.

title: Name the parts of the temporal bone.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the temporal bone.
body.back: Squamous, petrous, tympanic and mastoid parts, plus the styloid process.

title: What do the mandibular fossa and zygomatic process of the temporal bone do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What do the mandibular fossa and zygomatic process of the temporal bone do?
body.back: The mandibular fossa receives the head of the mandible (temporomandibular joint). The zygomatic process joins the zygomatic bone to form the zygomatic arch.

title: Which bones does the zygomatic bone articulate with, and what are its processes?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones does the zygomatic bone articulate with, and what are its processes?
body.back: Articulates with the frontal, sphenoid (greater wing), temporal and maxilla. Processes: frontal, temporal and maxillary.

title: Describe the maxilla: body and processes.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the maxilla: body and processes.
body.back: A pyramid-shaped body containing the maxillary sinus, plus four processes: frontal, zygomatic, alveolar and palatine.

title: Which maxillary features carry nerves or drain the sinus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which maxillary features carry nerves or drain the sinus?
body.back: Infraorbital foramen: infraorbital nerve and vessels emerge on the face. Maxillary ostium: the sinus opens into the nasal cavity at the hiatus semilunaris.

title: Describe the palatine bone.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the palatine bone.
body.back: L-shaped, with a horizontal plate (posterior part of the hard palate and nasal floor) and a perpendicular plate (lateral nasal wall). It also adds a small part of the orbital floor.

title: What forms the bony nasal septum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What forms the bony nasal septum?
body.back: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid (upper part) and the vomer (lower and posterior part), with septal cartilage in front.

title: Name the parts of the mandible.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the mandible.
body.back: Body (with the alveolar part and mental foramen), two rami joined to the body at the angle, and on each ramus the coronoid process (front), condylar process (back) and the mandibular notch between them.

title: Name the 8 cranial bones.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the 8 cranial bones.
body.back: Frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, occipital (one each), parietal (2) and temporal (2).

title: Mental foramen vs mandibular foramen: where and what passes?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Mental foramen vs mandibular foramen: where and what passes?
body.back: Mental foramen: on the outer surface of the body, transmits the mental nerve and vessels. Mandibular foramen: on the inner surface of the ramus, where the inferior alveolar nerve enters.

title: Name the four paired paranasal sinuses.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the four paired paranasal sinuses.
body.back: Frontal, ethmoidal (air cells), sphenoid and maxillary. The maxillary is the largest.

title: Where do the paranasal sinuses drain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where do the paranasal sinuses drain?
body.back: Middle meatus: frontal, anterior ethmoid and maxillary sinuses. Superior meatus: posterior ethmoid cells. Sphenoid: the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha. (The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct.)

title: Give the functions of the paranasal sinuses.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the functions of the paranasal sinuses.
body.back: They lighten the skull, humidify and warm inhaled air, help the immune response of the nose and add resonance to the voice (some of these roles are debated).

title: What is the pterion and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the pterion and why does it matter?
body.back: The H-shaped junction of the frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of the sphenoid on the side of the skull. It is the thinnest part of the skull wall and overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.

title: Sublingual vs submandibular fossa on the mandible?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Sublingual vs submandibular fossa on the mandible?
body.back: Both are on the inner surface of the body. Sublingual fossa: above the mylohyoid line, near the midline, holds the sublingual gland. Submandibular fossa: below the line, holds the submandibular gland.

title: What does the mandibular (glenoid) fossa do, and which bone is it on?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the mandibular (glenoid) fossa do, and which bone is it on?
body.back: It is on the squamous part of the temporal bone and receives the head of the mandible, forming the temporomandibular joint.

title: Name the 14 facial bones.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the 14 facial bones.
body.back: 6 paired: maxilla, zygomatic, palatine, nasal, lacrimal, inferior nasal concha. 2 unpaired: mandible and vomer.

title: Which joints let the skull nod and rotate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which joints let the skull nod and rotate?
body.back: Atlanto-occipital joint (skull on the atlas): nodding, 'yes'. Atlanto-axial joint (atlas on the axis): rotation, 'no'.

title: Name the parts of the sphenoid.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the sphenoid.
body.back: Body, two greater wings, two lesser wings, two pterygoid processes (each with a medial and a lateral plate).

title: What is the sella turcica and where is it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the sella turcica and where is it?
body.back: A saddle-shaped depression on the upper surface of the sphenoid body. It holds the pituitary gland (hypophysial fossa, with the tuberculum sellae in front and the dorsum sellae behind).

title: Which nerves or vessels go through foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which nerves or vessels go through foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum?
body.back: Foramen rotundum: maxillary nerve (V2). Foramen ovale: mandibular nerve (V3). Foramen spinosum: middle meningeal vessels. All three are in the greater wing of the sphenoid.

title: Which sphenoid wing forms the optic canal and the superior orbital fissure?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which sphenoid wing forms the optic canal and the superior orbital fissure?
body.back: The lesser wing forms the lateral border of the optic canal (the body forms the medial border). The superior orbital fissure is the gap between the lesser and greater wings.

title: Name the 4 parts of the ethmoid.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the 4 parts of the ethmoid.
body.back: Cribriform plate, crista galli, perpendicular plate, and the two ethmoidal labyrinths.

title: What do the muscles of facial expression do, and how are they built?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What do the muscles of facial expression do, and how are they built?
body.back: They control expression and act as sphincters and dilators of the openings of the face. They are subcutaneous, in the superficial fascia, arising from bone or fascia and inserting into the skin. All are supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

title: Procerus: origin, insertion, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Procerus: origin, insertion, action.
body.back: A small pyramidal slip. Origin: nasal bone and upper part of the lateral nasal cartilage. Insertion: skin of the lower forehead between the eyebrows. Action: draws down the medial angle of the eyebrows, making transverse wrinkles over the bridge of the nose, as in anger.

title: Name the dilators of the nose and what they do.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the dilators of the nose and what they do.
body.back: Depressor septi pulls the nasal septum inferiorly, helping the alar part of nasalis open the nares. The dilator naris (anterior and posterior parts) enlarges the opening of the nares and resists the nostrils closing under atmospheric pressure in ordinary breathing.

title: Orbicularis oris: origin, insertion, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Orbicularis oris: origin, insertion, action.
body.back: A complex muscle encircling the mouth. Some fibres arise near the midline from the maxilla above and the mandible below, others come from the buccinator, the cheek and the surrounding lip muscles. It forms an ellipse around the mouth and inserts into the skin and mucous membrane of the lips. It narrows and closes the mouth, as in whistling or pursing the lips.

title: Buccinator: origin, insertion, actions.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Buccinator: origin, insertion, actions.
body.back: A thin quadrilateral muscle filling the gap between the maxilla and the mandible at the side of the face. Origin: posterior parts of the maxilla and mandible and the pterygomandibular raphe, which separates it from the superior constrictor of the pharynx. Insertion: blends with orbicularis oris and into the lips. It compresses the cheeks to keep food under the teeth, expels air as in blowing a trumpet, and helps with whistling, smiling and suckling.

title: Name the lower group of oral muscles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the lower group of oral muscles.
body.back: Depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris and mentalis.

title: Mentalis: origin, insertion, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Mentalis: origin, insertion, action.
body.back: A small conical bundle at the tip of the chin, the deepest muscle of the lower group. Origin: mandible below the incisor teeth. Insertion: skin of the chin. It raises and protrudes the lower lip, wrinkling the chin, as when drinking from a cup or pouting.

title: Name the upper group of oral muscles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the upper group of oral muscles.
body.back: Risorius, zygomaticus major, zygomaticus minor, levator labii superioris, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi and levator anguli oris.

title: Risorius and zygomaticus major: origin, insertion, nerve, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Risorius and zygomaticus major: origin, insertion, nerve, action.
body.back: Risorius: from the masseteric fascia to the skin at the angle of the mouth (buccal branch of CN VII), pulling the angle laterally. Zygomaticus major: from the lateral surface of the anterior part of the zygomatic bone to the skin at the angle of the mouth, blending with levator anguli oris and orbicularis oris (zygomatic and buccal branches), elevating the corners of the mouth to smile.

title: Zygomaticus minor and levator labii superioris: what do they do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Zygomaticus minor and levator labii superioris: what do they do?
body.back: Zygomaticus minor: from the front of the zygomatic arch to the skin of the lateral upper lip, extending to the nasolabial sulcus; elevates and everts the upper lip. Levator labii superioris: from the infraorbital margin of the maxilla to the skin of the upper lip; retracts and everts the upper lip. Both take the buccal branch of CN VII.

title: Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi and levator anguli oris?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi and levator anguli oris?
body.back: Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi: from the frontal process of the maxilla to the skin of the lateral nostril and upper lip (zygomatic branches); dilates the nostril and elevates the wing of the nose and the upper lip. Levator anguli oris: from the canine fossa on the anterior surface of the maxilla to the skin at the angle of the mouth (buccal branch); raises the angle of the mouth while smiling.

title: Name the functional groups of facial muscles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the functional groups of facial muscles.
body.back: Scalp (occipitofrontalis), eyelid (orbicularis oculi, corrugator supercilii, levator palpebrae superioris), nose (nasalis, procerus, depressor septi, dilator naris anterior and posterior), mouth (orbicularis oris, buccinator and the upper and lower groups), ear (anterior, superior and posterior auricular) and platysma.

title: Name the muscles of the ear and the platysma's attachments.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the muscles of the ear and the platysma's attachments.
body.back: Ear: anterior, superior and posterior auricular. Platysma: origin the upper part of the pectoral and deltoid fascia; insertion the base of the mandible and the skin of the lower face and lip; it depresses the mandible and pulls the angle of the mouth downward.

title: Which branch of the facial nerve supplies which muscles?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which branch of the facial nerve supplies which muscles?
body.back: Temporal: frontalis, orbicularis oculi, corrugator supercilii. Zygomatic: orbicularis oculi. Buccal: orbicularis oris, buccinator, zygomaticus. Marginal mandibular: mentalis, depressor labii inferioris, depressor anguli oris. Cervical: platysma.

title: Name the four muscles of mastication and their nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the four muscles of mastication and their nerve.
body.back: Temporalis, masseter, lateral pterygoid and medial pterygoid, all supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).

title: Temporalis: origin, insertion, actions.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Temporalis: origin, insertion, actions.
body.back: Origin: floor of the temporal fossa and the deep temporal fascia. Insertion: coronoid process and anterior border of the ramus of the mandible. Actions: elevates the mandible; its posterior fibres retract it.

title: Masseter: origin, insertion, actions.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Masseter: origin, insertion, actions.
body.back: Origin: zygomatic arch. Insertion: angle of the mandible and coronoid process. Actions: elevates and protrudes the mandible; its deep fibres retract it.

title: Lateral pterygoid: origin, insertion, actions.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Lateral pterygoid: origin, insertion, actions.
body.back: Origin: superior head from the infratemporal surface of the greater wing of the sphenoid; inferior head from the lateral pterygoid plate. Insertion: pterygoid fovea of the neck of the mandible, and the capsule and articular disc of the TMJ. Bilaterally it protracts the mandible; unilaterally it pushes it to the opposite side.

title: Medial pterygoid: origin, insertion, actions.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Medial pterygoid: origin, insertion, actions.
body.back: Origin: deep head from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and the palatine bone; superficial head from the tuberosity of the maxilla. Insertion: medial surface of the ramus, up to the mandibular foramen. Bilaterally it pushes the mandible forward and elevates it; unilaterally it pushes it to the opposite side. Acting alternately with the other side, it produces a grinding motion.

title: Name the articular components of the temporomandibular joint.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the articular components of the temporomandibular joint.
body.back: The mandibular fossa and the articular tubercle of the temporal bone, and the condyle (head) of the mandible.

title: What is unusual about the temporomandibular joint?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is unusual about the temporomandibular joint?
body.back: An articular disc splits the joint into two synovial cavities, each with its own synovial membrane, so the bones never touch. The articular surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage.

title: Name the three extracapsular ligaments of the TMJ.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three extracapsular ligaments of the TMJ.
body.back: Lateral ligament (a thickening of the capsule, from the articular tubercle to the mandibular neck, preventing posterior dislocation), sphenomandibular ligament (from the spine of the sphenoid to the mandible) and stylomandibular ligament (a thickening of the parotid fascia).

title: Describe the epicranius (occipitofrontalis).
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the epicranius (occipitofrontalis).
body.back: A broad musculofibrous layer covering the vertex from the occipital bone to the eyebrows. Two parts, occipitalis and frontalis, joined by the galea aponeurotica.

title: How are the movements of the TMJ divided?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How are the movements of the TMJ divided?
body.back: Upper part of the joint: protrusion and retraction, the forward and backward movements of the jaw. Lower part: elevation and depression, opening and closing the mouth. Depression is mostly caused by gravity, helped by the digastric, geniohyoid and mylohyoid against resistance; elevation is a strong movement by the muscles of mastication.

title: What happens in a dislocation of the TMJ?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What happens in a dislocation of the TMJ?
body.back: A blow to the side of the face, yawning or taking a large bite can make the head of the mandible slip out of the mandibular fossa and be pulled anteriorly, so the patient cannot close the mouth. The facial and auriculotemporal nerves run close to the joint and can be damaged.

title: Name the important relations of the temporomandibular joint.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the important relations of the temporomandibular joint.
body.back: Anteriorly: the mandibular notch with the masseteric nerve and artery. Posteriorly: the tympanic plate of the external acoustic meatus. Laterally: the parotid gland, fascia and skin. Medially: the maxillary artery and vein and the auriculotemporal nerve. Superiorly: the middle cranial fossa with the temporal lobe.

title: Occipital belly: origin, insertion, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Occipital belly: origin, insertion, action.
body.back: Origin: tendinous fibres from the lateral two-thirds of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone and the mastoid part of the temporal bone. Insertion: galea aponeurotica. It draws the scalp backward.

title: Frontal belly: attachments and action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Frontal belly: attachments and action.
body.back: No bony attachment. Origin: galea aponeurotica. Insertion: skin of the eyebrows, its medial fibres blending with procerus and its lateral fibres with corrugator and orbicularis oculi. Action: wrinkles the forehead and raises the eyebrows.

title: Orbicularis oculi: parts and action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Orbicularis oculi: parts and action.
body.back: Surrounds the orbital opening and extends into each eyelid. Orbital part (thicker, a complete ellipse; origin nasal part of the frontal bone, frontal process of maxilla and medial palpebral ligament) closes the eye forcefully. Palpebral part (thin; from the medial palpebral ligament to the lateral palpebral raphe) closes the lids gently, as in blinking or sleep.

title: Corrugator supercilii: origin, insertion, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Corrugator supercilii: origin, insertion, action.
body.back: Origin: medial end of the superciliary arch. Insertion: skin of the medial half of the eyebrow. Action: draws the eyebrows medially and downward, making vertical wrinkles above the nose. The frowning muscle.

title: Levator palpebrae superioris: origin, insertion, nerve, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Levator palpebrae superioris: origin, insertion, nerve, action.
body.back: Origin: lesser wing of the sphenoid, above and anterior to the optic canal. Insertion: anterior surface of the tarsal plate, with fibres to the skin and the superior conjunctival fornix. Nerve: oculomotor (CN III). Action: raises the upper eyelid.

title: Nasalis: parts and actions.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Nasalis: parts and actions.
body.back: Transverse part: origin maxilla just lateral to the nose, insertion an aponeurosis across the dorsum of the nose. It compresses the nasal aperture. Alar part: origin maxilla over the lateral incisor, insertion alar cartilage. It draws the cartilage downward and opens the nostril laterally.

title: Which muscle arises from the highlighted area?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which muscle arises from the highlighted area?
body.back: Temporalis, from the floor of the temporal fossa and the deep temporal fascia. It elevates the mandible, and its posterior fibres retract it.

title: Which muscle arises from the highlighted bone?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which muscle arises from the highlighted bone?
body.back: Masseter, from the zygomatic arch. It inserts on the angle of the mandible and the coronoid process, and elevates the mandible.

title: What is the structure at the arrow, and what inserts there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the structure at the arrow, and what inserts there?
body.back: The coronoid process of the mandible. The temporalis inserts on its tip and medial surface and on the anterior border of the ramus.

title: What is the structure at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the structure at the arrow?
body.back: The condylar process of the mandible, with its head and neck. The lateral pterygoid inserts on the pterygoid fovea of the neck.

title: What is the joint at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the joint at the arrow?
body.back: The temporomandibular joint, between the head of the mandible and the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone. An articular disc splits it into two synovial cavities.

title: What is the highlighted part, and which muscles attach to it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the highlighted part, and which muscles attach to it?
body.back: The ramus of the mandible. The masseter inserts on its lateral surface; the medial pterygoid inserts on its medial surface, up to the mandibular foramen.

title: Which muscles arise from the highlighted plates?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which muscles arise from the highlighted plates?
body.back: The pterygoid plates of the sphenoid. The lateral pterygoid arises from the lateral plate and the greater wing; the medial pterygoid from the medial surface of the lateral plate.

title: What is the structure at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the structure at the arrow?
body.back: The angle of the mandible, where the body meets the ramus. The masseter inserts here.

title: Which cartilage is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cartilage is at the arrow?
body.back: The thyroid cartilage, shaped like an open book with two quadrilateral laminae. Its superior border carries the superior thyroid notch.

title: Which cartilage is at the arrow, and what is unique about it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cartilage is at the arrow, and what is unique about it?
body.back: The cricoid cartilage, at C6: the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway, signet-shaped with a narrow anterior arch and a broad posterior lamina. The foundation stone of the larynx.

title: Which cartilage is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cartilage is at the arrow?
body.back: The epiglottis, shaped like a tennis racket. Its foot inserts into the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage through the thyroepiglottic ligament.

title: Which bone is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bone is at the arrow?
body.back: The hyoid bone. It is closely associated with the larynx but is usually considered a separate structure.

title: Which membrane is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which membrane is at the arrow?
body.back: The thyrohyoid membrane, from the upper edge of the thyroid cartilage to the lower edge of the hyoid. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces it with the superior laryngeal artery.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The median cricothyroid ligament, between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages. Its intrinsic part forms the vocal ligament.

title: Which landmark is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which landmark is at the arrow?
body.back: The laryngeal prominence, the Adam's apple, formed where the two laminae of the thyroid cartilage meet in the midline.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and what connects it to the larynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and what connects it to the larynx?
body.back: The trachea. The cricotracheal ligament runs between the lower edge of the cricoid and the upper edge of the first tracheal ring.

title: Define the larynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Define the larynx.
body.back: The upper expanded part of the lower respiratory tract, modified for producing voice, also called the organ of phonation. An unpaired median tube of fibro-muscular-cartilaginous constitution: several cartilages linked by joints, muscles and ligaments, lined on their deep surface by a mucous membrane.

title: Describe the cricoid cartilage.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the cricoid cartilage.
body.back: A signet-shaped ring with a narrow anterior arch and a broad posterior lamina, at the level of C6. It completely encircles the lumen of the larynx and is the foundation stone of the larynx. The posterior surface of the lamina has a median ridge with a depressed area on each side.

title: Describe the arytenoid cartilages.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the arytenoid cartilages.
body.back: Right and left, shaped like triangular pyramids, arranged vertically, about 15 mm high. The apex articulates with the corniculate cartilage and the concave base with the articular facet of the cricoid lamina. The anterior angle of the base is extended by the vocal process, giving insertion to the vocal ligament. The lateral angle bears the muscular process, where the posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles insert. The posterior side gives insertion to the transverse arytenoid muscle.

title: Name the accessory cartilages.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the accessory cartilages.
body.back: Corniculate: rest on the apices of the arytenoids. Cuneiform: in the aryepiglottic fold. Others: posterior and anterior sesamoids and interarytenoid.

title: Describe the cricoarytenoid joint and its movements.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the cricoarytenoid joint and its movements.
body.back: The most important functionally: an elliptical synovial articulation reinforced by the posterior cricoarytenoid ligament, uniting the base of the arytenoid with the upper edge of the cricoid lamina. 1. Rotatory movement: the arytenoid moves around a vertical axis, abducting or adducting the vocal cords. 2. Gliding movement: one arytenoid glides toward or away from the other, closing or opening the posterior part of the glottis.

title: Describe the cricothyroid joint.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the cricothyroid joint.
body.back: A flat synovial joint reinforced by ligaments, joining the lower cornu of the thyroid cartilage and the lateral face of the cricoid. Movement: tilting of the cricoid around a transverse axis, the arch up and the lamina down, tensing the vocal cords.

title: Name the extrinsic ligaments and membranes.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the extrinsic ligaments and membranes.
body.back: The thyrohyoid membrane, from the upper edge of the thyroid cartilage to the lower edge of the hyoid, with a medial thickening (medial thyroid ligament) and two lateral thickenings (lateral thyroid ligaments). The thyroepiglottic ligament, attaching the lower narrow end of the epiglottis to the posterior surface of the thyroid angle. The hyoepiglottic ligament, connecting the posterior aspect of the hyoid with the anterior surface of the upper epiglottis. The cricotracheal ligament, between the lower edge of the cricoid and the upper edge of the first tracheal ring.

title: Name the intrinsic ligaments.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the intrinsic ligaments.
body.back: They are parts of a broad sheet of fibroelastic tissue forming the inner tube of the laryngeal cavity outside its mucous lining. The cricothyroid ligament, stretched between the thyroid cartilage and the vocal process, forms the vocal ligament. The vestibular ligament is tense between the thyroid angle and the anterolateral aspect of the arytenoid.

title: Classify the intrinsic muscles by action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Classify the intrinsic muscles by action.
body.back: 1. Vocal cord tensors: cricothyroid (paired), elevating the cricoid arch and lowering the thyroid cartilage. 2. Dilator of the glottis: the posterior cricoarytenoid, the only one. 3. Constrictors of the glottis: lateral cricoarytenoid, interarytenoid, superior thyroarytenoid and inferior thyroarytenoid (the vocal muscle), which tilts the arytenoid forward, tensing the cord.

title: Which muscles abduct and which adduct the vocal cords?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which muscles abduct and which adduct the vocal cords?
body.back: Abduct: the posterior cricoarytenoids. Adduct: the lateral cricoarytenoids and the transverse arytenoid.

title: Which muscles change the tension of the vocal cords?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which muscles change the tension of the vocal cords?
body.back: Tense: the cricothyroid and the vocalis. Relax: the thyroarytenoid.

title: Why does the larynx matter, anatomically and physiologically?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why does the larynx matter, anatomically and physiologically?
body.back: Anatomically, for its relations with the pharynx, trachea, thyroid, oesophagus and vascular axis. Physiologically, for phonation, breathing, protection and deglutition.

title: Give the three exceptions worth remembering about the intrinsic muscles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the three exceptions worth remembering about the intrinsic muscles.
body.back: The cricothyroid is the only muscle lying on the outer aspect of the larynx. All the intrinsic muscles are paired except the transverse arytenoid (interarytenoid), which is unpaired. All of them adduct the vocal cords except the posterior cricoarytenoids, which abduct them.

title: Why are the posterior cricoarytenoids called the safety muscles?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why are the posterior cricoarytenoids called the safety muscles?
body.back: They are the only intrinsic muscles that abduct the vocal cords, allowing air through the rima glottidis. When they contract, the muscular processes of both arytenoids rotate medially so the vocal processes rotate laterally, giving a wide diamond-shaped opening. If they are paralysed the adductors take the upper hand and the person may die from lack of air.

title: Name the extrinsic muscles of the larynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the extrinsic muscles of the larynx.
body.back: They ensure laryngeal mobility, especially during swallowing. Elevators: thyrohyoid, mylohyoid and digastric. Depressors: sternothyroid, sternohyoid and omohyoid.

title: Describe the supraglottic compartment.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the supraglottic compartment.
body.back: Vestibule: a pyramidal space extending from the laryngeal margin to the ventricular bands. Laryngeal or Morgagni ventricle: the cavity between the ventricular bands (false vocal cords) above and the plane of the vocal cords below. Interarytenoid region: the posterior part of the supraglottic stage, where the mucous membrane covers the fibres of the interarytenoid muscle.

title: Describe the glottis.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the glottis.
body.back: Two pearly white vocal cords stretched between the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage in front and the arytenoid cartilage behind, made of vocal ligament and muscle. Anteriorly they unite at the anterior commissure, attached directly to the thyroid cartilage and containing vessels and lymphatics. Posteriorly they are separated by the interarytenoid region, the posterior commissure. The glottis is triangular and narrower than the vestibular cleft. It is a narrow zone in children, so obstructive oedema causes respiratory distress very rapidly.

title: Describe the infraglottic compartment.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the infraglottic compartment.
body.back: The cavity below the vocal cords, surrounded by the cricoid and the cricothyroid ligament.

title: Give the histology of the larynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the histology of the larynx.
body.back: The laryngeal mucosa is thin, smooth and pale pink, continuous above with the pharyngeal mucosa and below with the tracheal mucosa. Epithelium: respiratory type (cylindric stratified) throughout, except at the vocal cords and the upper half of the epiglottis, which are non-keratinized stratified squamous.

title: Name the relations of the larynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the relations of the larynx.
body.back: Above: the base of the tongue. Below: the trachea. In front: the musculoaponeurotic planes of the subhyoid region and the covering planes, where the larynx is very superficial. Behind: the hypopharynx and cervical spine. Laterally: the piriform sinuses medial to the thyroid cartilage, then the thyroid lobes, and further out the elements of the carotid region.

title: Give the arterial supply of the larynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the arterial supply of the larynx.
body.back: Superior laryngeal artery, a branch of the superior thyroid artery, supplying the supraglottic part and anastomosing with the posteroinferior laryngeal artery. Anteroinferior laryngeal artery, also from the superior thyroid artery, supplying the anterior infraglottic stage. Posteroinferior laryngeal artery, from the inferior thyroid artery, supplying the posterior laryngeal mucosa.

title: Give the venous and lymphatic drainage.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the venous and lymphatic drainage.
body.back: Veins are satellite to the arteries: the superior and inferior laryngeal veins drain to the superior thyroid vein, then the thyro-linguo-facial trunk, then the internal jugular vein; the posterior laryngeal vein drains to the inferior thyroid vein and the subclavian vein. Lymphatics are very rich in the supraglottic zone, thinner in the subglottic zone and absent at the vocal cords. Supraglottic: the internal jugular chain. Infraglottic: pretracheal and paratracheal nodes and the internal jugular chain.

title: Name the four functions of the larynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the four functions of the larynx.
body.back: Phonation, respiration, protection and deglutition. It acts as a sphincter at the inlet of the lower respiratory tract to protect the trachea and bronchial tree from anything other than air. Laryngeal incompetence means food and fluid may be aspirated. Its upward and downward movements also help in swallowing.

title: Describe the superior laryngeal nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the superior laryngeal nerve.
body.back: A branch of the vagus, mixed but essentially sensory, descending against the pharyngeal wall. It divides behind the greater horn of the hyoid into two branches. Internal: enters the larynx with the superior laryngeal artery by perforating the thyrohyoid membrane, giving sensory innervation to the supraglottic mucosa. External: innervates the cricothyroid muscle and perforates the cricothyroid membrane, giving sensory innervation of the subglottic stage.

title: Describe the recurrent (inferior) laryngeal nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the recurrent (inferior) laryngeal nerve.
body.back: It originates from the vagus, on the right at the base of the neck and on the left at the level of the thorax. It innervates all the intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid, and gives sensory innervation of the subglottis through an ascending branch that anastomoses with the superior laryngeal nerve: Galen's loop.

title: What happens when the recurrent laryngeal nerve is damaged?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What happens when the recurrent laryngeal nerve is damaged?
body.back: It is often damaged accidentally during partial thyroidectomy. Unilateral: the cord on the affected side lies in the paramedian position, between abduction and adduction, and does not vibrate; usually the other cord compensates and phonation is not much affected. Bilateral: both cords lie in the paramedian position, with loss of phonation and difficulty breathing. If the recurrent and external laryngeal nerves are damaged on both sides, all intrinsic muscles are paralysed and the cords are further abducted and fixed: the cadaveric position.

title: What is laryngeal obstruction, and how is it relieved?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is laryngeal obstruction, and how is it relieved?
body.back: The mucous membrane of the superior larynx is very sensitive: a foreign body entering the laryngeal inlet causes immediate explosive coughing. If that reflex is slowed or absent, as in a neurological lesion or after alcohol, a foreign body may enter and cause choking. The Heimlich manoeuvre relieves it: stand behind the victim, pass your arms under theirs, place your hands in front of the epigastrium with one hand as a fist and the other over it, then give three or four abdominal thrusts directed upwards and backwards.

title: What are vocal nodules?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are vocal nodules?
body.back: Singer's or screamer's nodules. During vibration the area of maximum contact between the cords is at the junction of their anterior one third and posterior two thirds, which takes the most friction. People who overuse the voice, such as teachers and pop singers, develop inflammatory nodules there. They are bilateral and symmetrical, varying from pin head to split pea size, soft, reddish and oedematous early, later greyish or whitish.

title: Define phonation.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Define phonation.
body.back: The set of mechanisms allowing vibration at the free edge of the vocal fold, transforming aerodynamic energy into acoustic energy. The sound produced is immediately modified and filtered by the supralaryngeal air cavities to become vowels and consonants: the bucco-pharyngeal resonators.

title: Give the three acoustic parameters of the voice.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the three acoustic parameters of the voice.
body.back: Frequency, in Hertz, depending on the vibration speed of the vocal folds (opening and closing cycles per second). Intensity, in dB, depending on the force of pulmonary expiration (subglottic pressure). Pitch, depending on the accommodation of the vocal folds but especially on the shape of the supralaryngeal cavities.

title: Describe the vibratory cycle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the vibratory cycle.
body.back: 1. Putting into phonatory position: the vocal folds close as the arytenoids come together. 2. Opening: when the subglottic pressure is sufficient to overcome the muscular and elastic forces of resistance, a puff of air passes at high speed, an acoustic impulse. 3. Closure of the vocal folds.

title: What do the supralaryngeal cavities do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What do the supralaryngeal cavities do?
body.back: A filter role: resonance and enrichment of certain frequencies and suppression of others, with two areas of particular enhancement, the pharynx and the oral cavity; the basic laryngeal frequency is enriched with harmonics giving the pitch. An articulation role: under the effect of the articulatory muscles, the tongue, pharyngolarynx, jaws, lips and soft palate. Dry or cold ambient air can change the voice through mucous changes in the walls.

title: Why is a man's voice louder but lower pitched?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why is a man's voice louder but lower pitched?
body.back: Loudness depends on the amplitude of the vibrating vocal folds, pitch on their frequency. The vocal cords are usually longer in males than females, so they vibrate with greater amplitude but lower frequency.

title: Describe the situation of the larynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the situation of the larynx.
body.back: In the middle part of the visceral sheath of the neck. Above: the hyoid bone and base of the tongue. Below: the trachea. Behind: the hypopharynx. In front: the thyroid. It is higher in children (C2 to C3) than in adults; in newborns it contacts the veil, which is why they breathe exclusively through the nose until about four months.

title: Give the extension, shape and dimensions of the larynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the extension, shape and dimensions of the larynx.
body.back: Superior: the upper border of the thyroid cartilage at the body of C4. Inferior: the lower edge of the cricoid at the lower edge of C6. A triangular pyramid with a posterosuperior base (hyoid bone, pharynx) and a lower vertex (trachea). In men, length 4.5 cm, transverse diameter 4 cm, sagittal diameter 3.5 cm; smaller in women.

title: How is the larynx fixed in place?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How is the larynx fixed in place?
body.back: It is mobile in the vertical and transverse directions but held by its continuity with the pharynx and trachea, and by its union with the hyoid bone and the thoracic skeleton through muscles and ligaments.

title: Name the nine laryngeal cartilages.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the nine laryngeal cartilages.
body.back: Unpaired and large: thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis. Paired and small: arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform. The principal cartilages are the cricoid, the thyroid and the two arytenoids.

title: Describe the thyroid cartilage.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the thyroid cartilage.
body.back: Shaped like an open book, open backwards, protecting the elements of the larynx, with two vertical quadrilateral laminae. Each has an anterolateral side, a posteromedial side (smooth, related to the piriform sinus), a superior border with the superior thyroid incisure, an inferior border with the inferior thyroid incisure, and a vertical thick posterior margin extended by the superior and inferior cornua, the inferior one carrying a cricoid articular surface.

title: Describe the epiglottis.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the epiglottis.
body.back: Shaped like a tennis racket with a curved lower handle forming its foot. Laryngeal or posterior side: respiratory-type mucosa with numerous cribriform depressions, facing the laryngeal vestibule. Lingual or anterior side: concave, facing the base of the tongue and the hyoid bone. Base: superior and free. Vertex or foot: inferior, inserting into the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage through the thyroepiglottic ligament.

title: What is the nose, and what is rhinology?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the nose, and what is rhinology?
body.back: The uppermost part of the respiratory tract, containing the peripheral organ of smell. It consists of the external nose and the nasal cavity. The Greek word for nose is rhinos, so the study of the nose and its diseases is termed rhinology.

title: Name the parts of the external nose.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the external nose.
body.back: Tip (apex), the lower free end; root or bridge, the upper narrow part continuous with the forehead; dorsum, the round border between tip and root; nostrils or nares, the two piriform apertures at the broad lower end; and ala, the lower flared part on the side.

title: Describe the choana.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the choana.
body.back: The posterior orifice: oval with a large vertical axis, limited above by the body of the sphenoid, below by the horizontal plate of the palate, laterally by the pterygoid process, and medially by the vomer, which separates the two choanae.
