title: Which six bone pieces form the lateral wall?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which six bone pieces form the lateral wall?
body.back: The medial side of the maxillary body, the medial side of the frontal process of the maxilla, the medial aspect of the ethmoid, the lacrimal bone, the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone and the medial plate of the pterygoid process.

title: How is the lateral wall divided topographically?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How is the lateral wall divided topographically?
body.back: Into three portions: the anterior pre-turbinal area, the turbinal area (with the bony conchae or turbinates and the meatuses) and the posterior retroturbinal area.

title: Describe the conchae in general.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the conchae in general.
body.back: Thin bone plates rolled up on themselves, each with an anterior head, an intermediate body and a posterior tail. Each delimits a space with the corresponding side wall: the meatus. The upper and middle turbinates detach from the medial aspect of the ethmoid. There are three, sometimes four.

title: Describe the inferior turbinate.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the inferior turbinate.
body.back: An independent bone, the most extended and elongated. Its medial side faces the septum and its lateral side the inferior meatus. It has three processes: lacrimal, ethmoidal and maxillary.

title: Describe the middle, superior and supreme turbinates.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the middle, superior and supreme turbinates.
body.back: Middle: inserted on the internal face of the lateral mass of the ethmoid, delineating the middle meatus. Superior: inserts on the posterior half of the lateral mass of the ethmoid, almost horizontal, bounding the superior meatus. Supreme: inconstant.

title: What opens into each meatus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What opens into each meatus?
body.back: Superior meatus (overhanging the posterior half of the middle turbinate): the posterior ethmoidal cells, the sphenoidal sinus and the sphenopalatine foramen. Middle meatus: the anterior ethmoidal cells, the ostium of the maxillary sinus and the frontal sinus. Inferior meatus (close to the floor): the nasolacrimal duct.

title: Give the arterial supply of the nasal septum.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the arterial supply of the nasal septum.
body.back: Septal branches of the anterior ethmoidal artery and the posterior ethmoidal artery (both from the ophthalmic artery), the sphenopalatine artery and the greater palatine artery (both from the maxillary artery), and the superior labial artery (from the facial artery).

title: Give the arterial supply of the lateral wall by quadrant.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the arterial supply of the lateral wall by quadrant.
body.back: Anterosuperior: the anterior ethmoidal artery, from the ophthalmic. Anteroinferior: branches of the facial and greater palatine arteries. Posterosuperior: the sphenopalatine artery, from the maxillary. Posteroinferior: branches of the greater palatine artery, which pierces the perpendicular plate of the palatine. Both the internal and external carotid systems contribute.

title: Name the six functions of the nose.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the six functions of the nose.
body.back: Respiration, olfaction, protection of the lower respiratory passages, air conditioning of the inspired air, vocal resonance, and nasal reflex functions such as sneezing.

title: Describe the venous drainage of the nasal cavity.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the venous drainage of the nasal cavity.
body.back: Two networks, a deep periosteal one and a superficial mucous one, draining to the internal maxillary vein, the ophthalmic vein and the facial vein.

title: Give the innervation of the nasal cavity.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the innervation of the nasal cavity.
body.back: Rich, from branches of V and I. Sensory nerves from V: the spheno-palatine nerve (V2) and the internal nasal nerve. Olfactory nerves (CN I), with a yellowish pigmented zone on the convex face of the upper concha and the upper part of the septum, and a sensory area, the olfactory spot, containing the olfactory cells.

title: Name the relations of the nasal cavity.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the relations of the nasal cavity.
body.back: Roof: front to back, the frontal sinus, anterior cerebral fossa and sphenoidal sinus. Choana: the rhinopharynx. Floor: the oral cavity and palate. Internal wall: the contralateral nasal cavity. External wall: upper ethmoidal stage, the ethmoidal cells and orbit; maxillary lower stage, the maxillary sinus and nasolacrimal duct.

title: What is rhinitis?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is rhinitis?
body.back: Inflammation of the mucous membrane lining the nasal cavity. Hypertrophy of the mucosa over the inferior concha is a common feature of allergic rhinitis. It presents as nasal blockage, sneezing and watery discharge from the nose (rhinorrhea). Excessive rhinorrhea from vasomotor and allergic rhinitis can be controlled by sectioning the Vidian nerve.

title: What is Little's area?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is Little's area?
body.back: An area in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum just above the vestibule. It is highly vascular: the septal branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries anastomose there to form a vascular plexus, Kiesselbach's plexus. It is the commonest site of epistaxis in children and young adults, usually from fingernail trauma after picking the nose.

title: What is sinusitis, and how does it look on imaging?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is sinusitis, and how does it look on imaging?
body.back: Infection of a paranasal air sinus, presenting as headache and persistent thick purulent discharge from the nose. On standard radiological images normal sinuses are radiolucent, whereas diseased sinuses show varying degrees of opacity. CT gives very clear images that significantly aid diagnosis.

title: Name the three domains of nasal physiology.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three domains of nasal physiology.
body.back: Ventilation, immunity and olfaction.

title: Give the four ventilatory functions.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the four ventilatory functions.
body.back: Airflow control (rheostat), filtration, humidification (hygrostat) and heating (thermostat).

title: How is airflow regulated?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How is airflow regulated?
body.back: Inspired air passes down the nasal corridor, meeting obstacles that create resistance and converting laminar flow into turbulent flow. Three valves modify the size of the nasal fossa: the nostril valve, the nasal valve and the septo-turbinal valve.

title: How does the nose filter, humidify and warm air?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How does the nose filter, humidify and warm air?
body.back: Filtration: the role of mucus, its adhesiveness, the mucociliary movement and the slope of the nasal floor and meatus, evacuating contaminated mucus, which is swallowed. Humidification: contact and exchange between inspired air and the mucus layer. Warming: about 70 percent happens in the nasal cavity, by slowing the flow and by local heat from the mucous surface and the conchae.

title: Why does the nasal cavity matter clinically?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why does the nasal cavity matter clinically?
body.back: Its relationships with the skull base and the orbits, its rich blood supply (epistaxis), rhinosinusitis, rhinitis and sinonasal tumors, and the endoscopic surgical approach.

title: Describe the immune function of the nose.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the immune function of the nose.
body.back: Three lines of defence: non-specific inflammation, the epithelial line, and the specific line, NALT and IgA.

title: What do the sinus ostia ensure?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What do the sinus ostia ensure?
body.back: Sinus ventilation, by gas diffusion, and sinus drainage, by mucociliary function. Ostium obstruction leads to transudate and exudate, ciliary slowdown, hypoxia, oedema and rhinosinusitis.

title: Describe the embryological development of the nose.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the embryological development of the nose.
body.back: The nose and nasal cavities are formed by five facial prominences derived from the first branchial arch, appearing at the end of the fifth week. The nasal cavities derive from the nasal placodes, which invaginate to form the primitive nasal cavity, the primitive olfactory gutter. Initially the oronasal membrane separates the nasal from the primary oral cavity; the two are later separated by the maturation of the primary and secondary palate. The paranasal sinuses develop from diverticula in the lateral wall.

title: Describe the situation of the nasal cavities.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the situation of the nasal cavities.
body.back: Two narrow cavities separated by a thin sagittal wall, located in the centre of the facial bones, in front of the rhinopharynx, above the oral cavity, below the skull base and between the orbits. They communicate with the outside through the nostrils and open back into the rhinopharynx via the choanae. The two cavities are often asymmetric, given the frequency of septal deviations.

title: Give the general constitution of the nasal cavity.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the general constitution of the nasal cavity.
body.back: An osteo-cartilaginous framework, cartilaginous in front and bony behind, lined by respiratory (pituitary) mucosa. Shape: two long sagittal corridors, with four walls (roof, floor, medial and lateral) and two apertures (anterior and posterior).

title: What forms the medial wall?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What forms the medial wall?
body.back: The nasal septum, an osteo-cartilaginous structure: the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, the vomer bone and the septal cartilage.

title: What forms the roof and the floor?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What forms the roof and the floor?
body.back: Roof: anterior nasal, superior ethmoidal, posterior sphenoidal. Floor: anterior two thirds the palatine process of the maxillary bone, posterior third the horizontal plate of the palatine bone.

title: Describe the anterior opening.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the anterior opening.
body.back: The bony piriform aperture, circumscribed above by the nasal bones and below and laterally by the frontal process of the maxillary bone. More anteriorly lies the vestibule of the nasal cavity, with the major alar cartilage and the septal cartilage.

title: Which meatus is at the arrow, and what opens into it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which meatus is at the arrow, and what opens into it?
body.back: The inferior meatus, close to the floor of the nasal cavity. The nasolacrimal duct opens into it.

title: Which meatus is at the arrow, and what opens into it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which meatus is at the arrow, and what opens into it?
body.back: The middle meatus. The anterior ethmoidal cells, the ostium of the maxillary sinus and the frontal sinus open here.

title: Which meatus is at the arrow, and what opens into it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which meatus is at the arrow, and what opens into it?
body.back: The superior meatus, overhanging the posterior half of the middle turbinate. The posterior ethmoidal cells, the sphenoidal sinus and the sphenopalatine foramen open here.

title: Which concha is at the arrow, and what is special about it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which concha is at the arrow, and what is special about it?
body.back: The inferior concha: an independent bone, the most extended and elongated, with lacrimal, ethmoidal and maxillary processes.

title: Which concha is at the arrow, and where does it attach?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which concha is at the arrow, and where does it attach?
body.back: The middle concha, inserted on the internal face of the lateral mass of the ethmoid. It delineates the middle meatus.

title: Which concha is at the arrow, and where does it attach?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which concha is at the arrow, and where does it attach?
body.back: The superior concha, inserting on the posterior half of the lateral mass of the ethmoid. It is almost horizontal and bounds the superior meatus.

title: Which space is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which space is at the arrow?
body.back: The sphenoethmoidal recess, where the sphenoidal sinus opens through the sphenoid ostium.

title: Which duct is at the arrow, and where does it open?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which duct is at the arrow, and where does it open?
body.back: The nasolacrimal duct, opening into the anterior part of the inferior meatus.

title: Why does the neck lend itself to triangles?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why does the neck lend itself to triangles?
body.back: From the anatomic and surgical point of view the neck is where vital functional units meet and transit. The operating field is on a favourable scale for the surgeon's hands: not so small that it needs a microscope, nor so large as to require ample movements of the arms. Added surgical landmarks are always helpful when dealing with the neck.

title: What are the contents of the submandibular triangle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the contents of the submandibular triangle?
body.back: The submandibular gland is the main content, in the anterior part, superficial to which is the anterior facial vein. Beneath the gland, on the surface of mylohyoid, are the submental artery and the mylohyoid nerve and vessels. In the posterior part is the external carotid artery, ascending deep into the substance of the parotid gland.

title: Which forgotten triangles lie within the submandibular triangle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which forgotten triangles lie within the submandibular triangle?
body.back: Beclard's, Lesser's and Pirogoff's triangles.

title: Describe Lesser's triangle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe Lesser's triangle.
body.back: Named after the German surgeon Ladislaus Leon Lesser (1846 to 1925). Contained within the submandibular triangle. Its boundaries are the hypoglossal nerve and the anterior and posterior bellies of digastric. The anterior belly and the intermediate tendon of digastric form the inferior boundary, the hypoglossal nerve the superior border, and the posterior margin of mylohyoid at the intermediate tendon of digastric the posterior border. Its floor is formed by hyoglossus and mylohyoid.

title: Describe Pirogoff's triangle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe Pirogoff's triangle.
body.back: Named after the Russian surgeon and scientist Nikolai I Pirogoff (1810 to 1881), who first described this area. Superior boundary: the hypoglossal nerve. Inferior boundary: the intermediate tendon of digastric. Posterior border: the posterior border of mylohyoid. It is considered the posterior continuation of Lesser's triangle, and Deaver called it both Pinaud's and the hypoglossohyoid triangle. The lingual artery can sometimes be found in it, underneath the fibres of hyoglossus.

title: Describe Beclard's triangle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe Beclard's triangle.
body.back: Named after the French anatomist Pierre A. Beclard (1785 to 1825). The greater cornu of the hyoid bone forms the inferior boundary, the posterior belly of digastric the superior boundary, and the posterior border of hyoglossus the posterior boundary and its base.

title: What does Beclard's triangle contain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does Beclard's triangle contain?
body.back: Also known as the posterior triangle of the lingual artery. Its contents are the lingual artery and the hypoglossal nerve. Sometimes the arcus raninus, the anastomosis between the right and left end branches of the deep lingual artery, is also present. This triangle also helps in ligating the external carotid artery.

title: What are these triangles useful for in surgery?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are these triangles useful for in surgery?
body.back: They are reliable and constant landmarks for head and neck surgeons: identifying the common carotid artery, ligating the lingual artery, identifying the hypoglossal nerve for certain measures, and recognising the common facial vein.

title: Describe the neck and its well-known landmarks.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the neck and its well-known landmarks.
body.back: The neck connects the head with the rest of the body and is the most mobile part of the trunk. It is cylindrical, of constant length but uneven diameter. The well-known landmarks are the thyroid cartilage, the hyoid bone, the trachea and the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

title: Give the boundaries of the anterior triangle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the boundaries of the anterior triangle.
body.back: Laterally the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, medially the midline, and superiorly the lower border of the mandible.

title: Give the boundaries of the posterior triangle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the boundaries of the posterior triangle.
body.back: Anteromedially the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid, posterolaterally the anterior border of trapezius, and inferiorly the clavicle.

title: How are the two major triangles subdivided?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How are the two major triangles subdivided?
body.back: Both are covered by the deep fascia of the neck, and only after its removal do the secondary triangles appear. The anterior triangle is subdivided into three paired triangles, the carotid (superior carotid), submandibular (submaxillary or digastric) and muscular (inferior carotid), plus the unpaired submental triangle below the chin between the anterior bellies of digastric. The posterior triangle is subdivided into the occipital and subclavian (omoclavicular) triangles.

title: Give the boundaries of the carotid triangle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the boundaries of the carotid triangle.
body.back: Below and anteroinferiorly the superior belly of omohyoid, above the stylohyoid and posterior belly of digastric, and posteriorly sternocleidomastoid. It contains the triangle of Farabeuf.

title: Describe Farabeuf's triangle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe Farabeuf's triangle.
body.back: Named after the French surgeon Louis Hubert Farabeuf (1841 to 1910). Bounded posteriorly by the internal jugular vein, anteroinferiorly by the common facial vein, and superiorly by the hypoglossal nerve, which forms its base.

title: What does Farabeuf's triangle contain, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does Farabeuf's triangle contain, and why does it matter?
body.back: One branch of the common carotid artery, or the carotid bifurcation, and the jugulodigastric lymph node. It is described as a useful and neglected feature of carotid anatomy, an admirable rallying point of the neck, and a well-known sign for identifying the common carotid artery and its bifurcation.

title: Describe the submandibular triangle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the submandibular triangle.
body.back: Bordered superiorly by the inferior border of the body of the mandible, lying between the anterior and posterior bellies of digastric. It is subdivided into anterior and posterior parts by the stylomandibular ligament.

title: Which triangle is highlighted, and what bounds it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which triangle is highlighted, and what bounds it?
body.back: The anterior triangle: laterally the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, medially the midline, superiorly the lower border of the mandible.

title: Which triangle is highlighted, and what bounds it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which triangle is highlighted, and what bounds it?
body.back: The posterior triangle: anteromedially the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid, posterolaterally the anterior border of trapezius, inferiorly the clavicle.

title: Which triangle is at the arrow, and what does it contain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which triangle is at the arrow, and what does it contain?
body.back: The carotid triangle, bounded below by the superior belly of omohyoid, above by stylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric, and posteriorly by sternocleidomastoid. It contains Farabeuf's triangle.

title: Which triangle is at the arrow, and what is its main content?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which triangle is at the arrow, and what is its main content?
body.back: The submandibular triangle. Its main content is the submandibular gland. Lesser's, Pirogoff's and Beclard's triangles are housed within it.

title: Which triangle is at the arrow, and what is unusual about it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which triangle is at the arrow, and what is unusual about it?
body.back: The submental triangle: the only unpaired triangle of the neck, below the chin between the anterior bellies of digastric of both sides.

title: Which triangle is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which triangle is at the arrow?
body.back: The muscular triangle, also called the inferior carotid triangle, one of the three paired subdivisions of the anterior triangle.

title: Which triangle is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which triangle is at the arrow?
body.back: The occipital triangle, the upper subdivision of the posterior triangle.

title: Which triangle is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which triangle is at the arrow?
body.back: The subclavian, or omoclavicular, triangle: the lower subdivision of the posterior triangle, just above the clavicle.

title: Which muscle is at the arrow, and why does it matter here?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which muscle is at the arrow, and why does it matter here?
body.back: Sternocleidomastoid. Its anterior border bounds the anterior triangle and its posterior border bounds the posterior triangle, so it divides the neck in two.

title: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
body.back: Diencephalon: becomes the thalamus, hypothalamus and epithalamus; its cavity is the third ventricle.

title: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
body.back: Metencephalon: becomes the pons and cerebellum.

title: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
body.back: Midbrain, from the mesencephalon; its cavity is the cerebral aqueduct.

title: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
body.back: Myelencephalon: becomes the medulla oblongata.

title: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
body.back: Prosencephalon (forebrain): divides into the telencephalon and diencephalon.

title: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
body.back: Rhombencephalon (hindbrain): divides into the metencephalon and myelencephalon.

title: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and what does it become?
body.back: Telencephalon: becomes the cerebral hemispheres; its cavities are the lateral ventricles.

title: What are the two components of the CNS?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the two components of the CNS?
body.back: The brain and the spinal cord.

title: What protects the CNS?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What protects the CNS?
body.back: The skull and vertebral column, reinforced by the meninges and cushioned by CSF.

title: From which germ layer does the nervous system derive?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: From which germ layer does the nervous system derive?
body.back: Ectoderm (except its blood vessels and some neurological elements).

title: What is the sequence of neurulation?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the sequence of neurulation?
body.back: Neural plate → neural groove → neural tube (closure days 18 to 28).

title: When do the neuropores close?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: When do the neuropores close?
body.back: Anterior ~day 25, posterior ~day 27.

title: Name the 3 primary and 5 secondary brain vesicles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the 3 primary and 5 secondary brain vesicles.
body.back: Primary: prosencephalon, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon. Secondary: telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, myelencephalon.

title: What does the lumen of the neural tube become?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the lumen of the neural tube become?
body.back: The ventricular system (lateral, third and fourth ventricles, cerebral aqueduct) and the central canal.

title: Which flexure is the most prominent, and where is it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which flexure is the most prominent, and where is it?
body.back: The cephalic flexure, at the level of the midbrain.

title: What does the pontine flexure do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the pontine flexure do?
body.back: Thins the roof of the fourth ventricle, makes space for the cerebellum and separates metencephalon from myelencephalon.

title: Spina bifida vs anencephaly?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Spina bifida vs anencephaly?
body.back: Spina bifida: failure of caudal neural tube closure. Anencephaly: failure of cranial closure; not survivable.

title: How many pairs of cranial and spinal nerves are there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How many pairs of cranial and spinal nerves are there?
body.back: 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

title: What are the three steps of nervous system function?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the three steps of nervous system function?
body.back: Sensory input, integration (brain and spinal cord), motor output.

title: What is the difference between the somatic and autonomic systems?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the difference between the somatic and autonomic systems?
body.back: Somatic: voluntary actions. Autonomic: automatic responses to internal and external changes (sympathetic and parasympathetic).

title: Which cells make myelin in the CNS and in the PNS?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cells make myelin in the CNS and in the PNS?
body.back: Oligodendrocytes in the CNS; Schwann cells in the PNS.

title: Which glial cells act as the brain's immune cells?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which glial cells act as the brain's immune cells?
body.back: Microglia (phagocytosis of debris).

title: Which glial cells line the ventricles and produce CSF?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which glial cells line the ventricles and produce CSF?
body.back: Ependymal cells.

title: What is grey matter made of? Give two examples.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is grey matter made of? Give two examples.
body.back: Neuron cell bodies, dendrites and synapses. Cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus, the cord's butterfly-shaped centre.

title: What is white matter made of? Give two examples.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is white matter made of? Give two examples.
body.back: Myelinated axons. Corpus callosum, internal capsule, the cord's outer layer.

title: Where does the ophthalmic artery come from and where does it go?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does the ophthalmic artery come from and where does it go?
body.back: It is the first branch off the internal carotid as it emerges from the cavernous sinus on the medial side of the clinoid process. It passes through the optic canal, runs along the medial wall of the orbit and divides into its terminal branches.

title: Describe the central retinal artery.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the central retinal artery.
body.back: It branches off the posterior third of the ophthalmic artery and enters the dural sheath of the optic nerve about 13 mm behind the globe. It supplies the retina.

title: Describe the muscular arteries.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the muscular arteries.
body.back: They split into superior and inferior branches. The superior branch supplies the levator palpebral muscle, superior rectus, superior oblique and a portion of the lateral rectus. The inferior branch supplies the medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique, and also gives off most of the anterior ciliary arteries.

title: Describe the venous drainage of the orbit.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the venous drainage of the orbit.
body.back: Superior ophthalmic vein: the main venous drainage. It originates in the superonasal quadrant, extends posteriorly through the medial part of the superior orbital fissure into the cavernous sinus. Inferior ophthalmic vein: originates at the floor and medial wall and drains the inferior orbit. Vortex veins: drain the uveal tract and pierce the sclera posterior to the globe's equator, draining into the two main veins.

title: What is strabismus, and what causes it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is strabismus, and what causes it?
body.back: A squint: the eyes don't point in the same direction. It is caused by nerve damage or problems in the eye muscles. When some muscles are weaker than others they cannot work together, so one eye looks at one object while the other turns in a different direction. Squints affect about one in 20 children.

title: Name the four types of strabismus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the four types of strabismus.
body.back: Esotropia: inward turning. Exotropia: outward turning. Hypotropia: downward turning. Hypertropia: upward turning.

title: What is nystagmus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is nystagmus?
body.back: A vision condition in which the eyes make repetitive, uncontrolled movements, often resulting in reduced vision and depth perception, and affecting balance and coordination. Movements can be side to side (horizontal), up and down (vertical), or circular (rotary). It is caused by a miscommunication between the eye and the brain, typically from brain injury, and is sometimes called dancing eyes.

title: Myopia versus hyperopia.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Myopia versus hyperopia.
body.back: Myopia (nearsightedness): near objects are clear, distant objects blurred; the image focuses in front of the retina. Hyperopia (farsightedness): the image focuses behind the retina, which may be caused by the eyeball being too small or the focusing power being too weak.

title: Which orbital wall is most prone to blowout fracture, and what happens?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which orbital wall is most prone to blowout fracture, and what happens?
body.back: The floor (inferior wall). In about half of cases the medial wall fractures too. Prolapse of orbital fat into the maxillary sinus may be seen, sometimes with inferior rectus muscle prolapse. Most orbital floor fractures occur in the posteromedial portion of the bone in relation to the infraorbital groove.

title: Which is the strongest orbital wall, and which is thinnest?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which is the strongest orbital wall, and which is thinnest?
body.back: The lateral wall is the strongest and thickest; the medial wall (lamina papyracea) is the thinnest. Fractures to the superior border of the orbit are rare, and those to the lateral walls are even rarer, because the latter border is fortified with thicker bone and more muscle.

title: What does leakage of clear fluid into the orbit suggest?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does leakage of clear fluid into the orbit suggest?
body.back: A superior blowout fracture. These may involve the neighbouring sinus as well as the anterior cranial fossa, presenting with leakage of cerebrospinal fluid.

title: Name the orbital branches of the ophthalmic artery.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the orbital branches of the ophthalmic artery.
body.back: Internal palpebral, frontal, nasal, lacrimal, supraorbital, anterior ethmoidal and posterior ethmoidal arteries.

title: What is ptosis, and what causes it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is ptosis, and what causes it?
body.back: Drooping of the eyelid. The levator palpebrae superioris, supplied by the oculomotor nerve, raises the lid; its smooth superior tarsal part is sympathetic. Damage to either gives ptosis, more marked with CN III.

title: What happens to the eye in facial nerve palsy?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What happens to the eye in facial nerve palsy?
body.back: The person cannot wrinkle the brow or raise the eyebrow on one side, the eyelid droops and the eye is difficult to close completely, the smile is asymmetrical, and the corner of the mouth droops.

title: Chalazion versus stye.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Chalazion versus stye.
body.back: A chalazion is a blocked meibomian gland within the lid; a stye is a blocked oil gland on the edge of the eyelid.

title: What is corneal abrasion?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is corneal abrasion?
body.back: Damage to the surface of the eye, generally from trauma: a fingernail scratching the eye, walking into something, getting grit in the eye, particularly if rubbed. It can also be caused by contact lens insertion and removal. Most heal in a few days; those that don't can lead to infections or scarring, and both can cause loss of vision.

title: Conjunctivitis versus uveitis.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Conjunctivitis versus uveitis.
body.back: Conjunctivitis (pink eye) affects the outer layer; uveitis affects the middle layer. Uveitis may result from inflammation associated with an autoimmune disorder, while conjunctivitis is typically bacterial, viral or fungal. Allergic: itching, redness and swelling of the conjunctiva and eyelid. Viral: redness and periodic itching with increased lacrimation. Bacterial: redness, dryness of the eyes and surrounding skin, and mucopurulent discharge.

title: What is papilloedema?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is papilloedema?
body.back: Optic disc swelling secondary to raised intracranial pressure, seen as a bulging optic disc on fundoscopy. It happens because the subarachnoid space and CSF continue along the optic nerve sheath.

title: What is glaucoma?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is glaucoma?
body.back: A chronic, progressive eye disease caused by damage to the optic nerve, leading to visual field loss. Eye pressure is a major risk factor: an abnormality in the drainage system causes fluid to build up. In open-angle glaucoma the increase in pressure is often small and slow; in closed-angle glaucoma it is often high and sudden. Symptoms can start so slowly they are hardly noticed, and the only way to detect it is a comprehensive dilated eye exam. There is no cure, but early treatment can stop the damage.

title: What is retinal detachment and how is it treated?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is retinal detachment and how is it treated?
body.back: An emergency in which a thin layer of tissue at the back of the eye pulls away from the layer of blood vessels supplying it with oxygen and nutrients, often with flashes and floaters. Treatments: vitrectomy (removing and replacing the jelly inside the eye), scleral buckling (a band around the eye to push the wall and retina together) and pneumatic retinopexy (injecting a gas bubble to push the retina back).

title: Direct versus consensual pupillary light reflex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Direct versus consensual pupillary light reflex.
body.back: A direct pupillary reflex is the response of the pupil to light entering the same (ipsilateral) eye. A consensual reflex is the response of a pupil to light entering the opposite (contralateral) eye.

title: What does absence of the corneal reflex indicate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does absence of the corneal reflex indicate?
body.back: It may indicate deep coma or stroke, either unilaterally or bilaterally. Unilateral loss may also indicate a lesion involving the trigeminal or facial nerve. Repeat the test on the other eye and document the reflex as present or absent, unilateral or bilateral.

title: What does the internal palpebral artery supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the internal palpebral artery supply?
body.back: Its terminal branches, the superior and inferior medial palpebral arteries, supply the lacrimal sac and eyelids, creating an anastomosis with the two lateral palpebral branches from the lacrimal artery.

title: Which cells become the optic nerve?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cells become the optic nerve?
body.back: The retinal ganglion cells. Their axons join together and leave the eye at the optic disc as the optic nerve.

title: Frontal and nasal arteries: what do they supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Frontal and nasal arteries: what do they supply?
body.back: Frontal artery: leaves the orbit at its medial angle above the trochlea and supplies the forehead and scalp, anastomosing with the supraorbital artery's terminal branches. Nasal artery: supplies the superior lacrimal sac and nose.

title: What does the lacrimal artery supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the lacrimal artery supply?
body.back: The lacrimal gland. Its terminal branches supply the lateral upper and lower eyelids and the conjunctiva.

title: What does the supraorbital artery supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the supraorbital artery supply?
body.back: The superior rectus and levator palpebral muscles. It then passes through the supraorbital foramen, and its terminal branches supply the eyebrow and forehead.

title: Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries.
body.back: Anterior: in the orbit it supplies the superior oblique muscle, and also the anterior and middle ethmoidal cells, the frontal sinus, the lateral wall of the nose and the nasal septum. Posterior: passes through the posterior ethmoidal canal, supplying the posterior ethmoidal cells.

title: Name the ocular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the ocular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
body.back: Short ciliary, long ciliary, central retinal and muscular arteries.

title: Short and long ciliary arteries: what do they supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Short and long ciliary arteries: what do they supply?
body.back: Short ciliary: the choroid and ciliary processes. Long ciliary: the anterior segment, forming anastomoses with the extraocular muscle branches.

title: Which structure does the central retinal artery supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure does the central retinal artery supply?
body.back: The retina. The artery enters the dural sheath of the optic nerve about 13 mm behind the globe, and it is an end artery, so occlusion causes sudden painless loss of vision.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and which disease damages it in glaucoma?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and which disease damages it in glaucoma?
body.back: The optic nerve. Glaucoma is a chronic progressive disease caused by damage to the optic nerve, leading to visual field loss. Swelling of its head from raised intracranial pressure is papilloedema.

title: A pituitary tumour compressing the structure at the arrow causes which defect?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: A pituitary tumour compressing the structure at the arrow causes which defect?
body.back: The optic chiasm. Compression of the crossing nasal fibres gives bitemporal hemianopia, a loss of the outer half of the visual field in both eyes.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The optic tract. A lesion here causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia: the same side of the visual field is lost in both eyes.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Damage here causes a homonymous field loss, often with macular sparing.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and where does the pathway start?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and where does the pathway start?
body.back: The retina. The photoreceptors are the first order neurons and the ganglion cells send their axons into the optic nerve.

title: Which part of the pathway is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the pathway is at the arrow?
body.back: The optic nerve (CN II), carrying the axons of the retinal ganglion cells from each eye.

title: What is the structure at the arrow, and what happens there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the structure at the arrow, and what happens there?
body.back: The optic chiasm. The fibres from the medial (nasal) half of each retina cross to the optic tract of the opposite side; the temporal fibres stay on the same side.

title: Which part of the pathway is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the pathway is at the arrow?
body.back: The optic tract, running from the chiasm to the lateral geniculate nucleus. It now carries fibres from both eyes.

title: What is the structure at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the structure at the arrow?
body.back: The lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay centre in the thalamus where the ganglion nerve fibres synapse.

title: Which part of the pathway is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the pathway is at the arrow?
body.back: The optic radiation, the fibres leaving the lateral geniculate nucleus for the primary visual cortex.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The primary visual cortex, in the occipital lobe. It relays information onward to the secondary visual cortex for higher processing.

title: Name the seven muscles that move the eye and the lid.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the seven muscles that move the eye and the lid.
body.back: Levator palpebrae superioris, superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, lateral rectus, superior oblique and inferior oblique.

title: Which muscles produce elevation and depression?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which muscles produce elevation and depression?
body.back: Elevation: superior rectus and inferior oblique. Depression: inferior rectus and superior oblique. The obliques move the eye opposite to their name.

title: Which muscles adduct and which abduct?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which muscles adduct and which abduct?
body.back: Adduction: medial rectus, plus superior and inferior rectus. Abduction: lateral rectus, plus superior and inferior oblique.

title: Describe the visual retina.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the visual retina.
body.back: Neural layer: light-receptive, ending anteriorly along the ora serrata. Pigmented cell layer: a single layer of cells absorbing light to reduce scattering within the eye.

title: What is the non-visual retina?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the non-visual retina?
body.back: The portion of the retina that is not sensitive to light: the anterior continuation of the pigment cell layer plus supporting cells over the ciliary body and the posterior surface of the iris.

title: What is the optic disc?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the optic disc?
body.back: The papilla, known as the blind spot: no photoreceptors. It is located in the fundus of the retina, where the sensory fibres of the optic nerve enter the eyeball.

title: Macula and fovea.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Macula and fovea.
body.back: The macula contains special photoreceptor cones for visual acuity and lacks blood vessels. The fovea, at its centre, is responsible for high-acuity vision and is densely saturated with cone photoreceptors.

title: How do signals move through the retinal layers?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How do signals move through the retinal layers?
body.back: Photoreceptors and bipolar cells produce graded potentials rather than action potentials. Ganglion cells generate action potentials, and their axons join together to form the optic nerve, which exits through the back of the eye at the optic disc. Light travels in the opposite direction to the flow of neuronal communication.

title: Name the landmarks of the visual pathway in order.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the landmarks of the visual pathway in order.
body.back: Eye, optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus (in the thalamus), optic radiation, primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.

title: What happens at the optic chiasm?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What happens at the optic chiasm?
body.back: The fibres from the medial (nasal) half of each retina cross over to the optic tract of the opposite side. The temporal fibres stay on the same side.

title: What is the lateral geniculate nucleus and what leaves it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the lateral geniculate nucleus and what leaves it?
body.back: A relay centre in the thalamus where the ganglion nerve fibres synapse. The fibres leaving it form the optic radiation, which carries the signal to the primary visual cortex.

title: Where do the four recti arise, and where do they insert?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where do the four recti arise, and where do they insert?
body.back: All four arise from the common ring tendon (annulus of Zinn) at the orbital apex. Superior rectus: anterior and superior surface of the eyeball. Inferior rectus: anterior and inferior surface. Medial rectus: anterior and medial surface. Lateral rectus: anterior and lateral surface.

title: Damage at the optic nerve: what is lost?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Damage at the optic nerve: what is lost?
body.back: Site 1, a complete cut: total loss of vision from that eye. Site 2, partial damage to the left optic nerve: information from the nasal visual field of the left eye (the temporal part of the left retina) is lost.

title: Damage at the optic chiasm: what is lost?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Damage at the optic chiasm: what is lost?
body.back: The temporal (lateral) portions of the visual field are lost in both eyes, because the crossing fibres are cut.

title: Damage at the optic tract or the tract from the lateral geniculate to the cortex: what is lost?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Damage at the optic tract or the tract from the lateral geniculate to the cortex: what is lost?
body.back: Sites 4 and 5 cause identical visual loss: in the lecture's example, loss of vision of the right side. Partial damage to these fibre tracts causes other predictable visual problems.

title: Describe the pupillary light reflex pathway.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the pupillary light reflex pathway.
body.back: The afferent limb is the optic nerve. Fibres reach the pretectal area, which projects to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres travel in cranial nerve III to the ciliary ganglion, and postganglionic fibres innervate the pupillary constrictor muscle. Because the pretectal projections are bilateral, light in one eye constricts both pupils.

title: Name the cortical visual areas shown in the lecture.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the cortical visual areas shown in the lecture.
body.back: Primary visual cortex, secondary visual cortex, inferotemporal area and posterior parietal area.

title: Levator palpebrae superioris: origin, insertion, nerve, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Levator palpebrae superioris: origin, insertion, nerve, action.
body.back: Origin: lesser wing of the sphenoid, superior and anterior to the optic canal. Insertion: superior tarsus and skin of the upper eyelid. Nerve: oculomotor (CN III); its deep layer, the superior tarsal muscle, is supplied by sympathetic fibres. Action: elevates the upper eyelid.

title: Superior oblique: origin, course, insertion, nerve, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Superior oblique: origin, course, insertion, nerve, action.
body.back: Origin: body of the sphenoid, at the orbit apex above the common ring tendon. Its tendon passes through the trochlea, which changes its direction, and it inserts into the sclera deep to the superior rectus, in the posterior temporosuperior quadrant. Nerve: trochlear (CN IV). Action: intorsion, depression, abduction.

title: Inferior oblique: origin, insertion, nerve, action.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Inferior oblique: origin, insertion, nerve, action.
body.back: Origin: anterior part of the floor of the orbit (maxilla), behind the lacrimal fossa. Insertion: sclera deep to the lateral rectus, posterior temporo-inferior quadrant. Nerve: inferior branch of CN III. Action: extorsion, elevation, abduction.

title: Which nerve supplies each extraocular muscle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which nerve supplies each extraocular muscle?
body.back: Lateral rectus: abducens (CN VI). Superior oblique: trochlear (CN IV). All the rest, including the levator palpebrae superioris: oculomotor (CN III). Remember LR6 SO4.

title: Primary actions of the four recti.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Primary actions of the four recti.
body.back: Superior rectus: elevation, intorsion, adduction. Inferior rectus: depression, extorsion, adduction. Medial rectus: adduction. Lateral rectus: abduction.

title: Give the lecture's six action lines for the eye muscles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the lecture's six action lines for the eye muscles.
body.back: SO: intorsion, depression, abduction. IO: extorsion, elevation, abduction. IR: depression, adduction, extorsion. SR: elevation, adduction, intorsion. MR: adduction. LR: abduction.

title: Which muscles produce intorsion and extorsion?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which muscles produce intorsion and extorsion?
body.back: Intorsion: superior oblique and superior rectus. Extorsion: inferior oblique and inferior rectus.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and which bones form it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and which bones form it?
body.back: The hard palate: the palatine processes of the maxillae in front and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind. It forms the floor of the nasal cavity.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The soft palate, attached to the posterior border of the hard palate. It is made of muscle fibres, an aponeurosis, lymphoid tissue, glands, vessels and nerves.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and which muscle raises it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and which muscle raises it?
body.back: The uvula, raised by the musculus uvulae, which arises from the posterior border of the hard palate and is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.

title: Which part of the tongue is highlighted, and what covers it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the tongue is highlighted, and what covers it?
body.back: The anterior two thirds, the oral part. Its mucosa is rough with three types of papillae: filiform, fungiform and vallate.

title: Which part of the tongue is highlighted, and what covers it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the tongue is highlighted, and what covers it?
body.back: The posterior third, the pharyngeal part. It has no papillae but a nodular surface from the underlying lymphatic nodules, the lingual tonsils.

title: What is the line at the arrow, and what lies at its apex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the line at the arrow, and what lies at its apex?
body.back: The V-shaped sulcus terminalis, dividing the anterior two thirds from the posterior third. Its apex faces backward and is marked by the foramen cecum, a remnant of the upper end of the thyroglossal duct.

title: Which space is highlighted, and what bounds it laterally?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which space is highlighted, and what bounds it laterally?
body.back: The vestibule, the slit-like space between the cheeks and the gums. Its lateral wall is the cheek, formed by the buccinator. The parotid duct opens into it opposite the upper second molar.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and what opens beside it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and what opens beside it?
body.back: The frenulum of the tongue. On each side of it, a small papilla carries the opening of the submandibular (Wharton's) duct.

title: Which structures are at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structures are at the arrow?
body.back: The palatine tonsils, lying between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal folds at the oropharyngeal isthmus.

title: What are the limits and subdivisions of the oral cavity?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the limits and subdivisions of the oral cavity?
body.back: It extends from the lips to the oropharyngeal isthmus, the junction of mouth and pharynx, bounded above by the soft palate and palatoglossal folds and below by the dorsum of the tongue. It is subdivided into the vestibule and the oral cavity proper.

title: Describe the ventral surface of the tongue.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the ventral surface of the tongue.
body.back: Smooth, with no papillae. In the midline anteriorly, a mucosal fold, the frenulum, connects the tongue with the floor of the mouth. Lateral to the frenulum the deep lingual vein can be seen through the mucosa, and lateral to the lingual vein a fold of mucosa forms the plica fimbriata.

title: Intrinsic versus extrinsic muscles of the tongue.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Intrinsic versus extrinsic muscles of the tongue.
body.back: Intrinsic: confined to the tongue with no bony attachment, consisting of longitudinal, transverse and vertical fibres; they alter the shape of the tongue. Extrinsic: connect the tongue to the surrounding structures, the soft palate and the bones (mandible, hyoid bone, styloid process); they help in movements of the tongue.

title: Name the four extrinsic muscles and their movements.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the four extrinsic muscles and their movements.
body.back: Palatoglossus, genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus. Protrusion: genioglossus on both sides. Retraction: styloglossus and hyoglossus on both sides. Depression: hyoglossus and genioglossus on both sides. Elevation: styloglossus and palatoglossus on both sides.

title: Give the sensory nerve supply of the tongue.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the sensory nerve supply of the tongue.
body.back: Anterior two thirds: general sensation by the lingual nerve (branch of CN V3), special sensation (taste) by the chorda tympani (CN VII). Posterior third: general and special sensation by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Base: general and special sensation by the internal laryngeal nerve (CN X).

title: Give the motor nerve supply of the tongue.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the motor nerve supply of the tongue.
body.back: The hypoglossal nerve supplies all the muscles. The vagus nerve supplies the palatoglossus.

title: Blood supply of the tongue.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Blood supply of the tongue.
body.back: Arteries: the lingual artery, the tonsillar branch of the facial artery and the ascending pharyngeal artery. Veins: the lingual vein, which ultimately drains into the internal jugular vein.

title: Lymphatic drainage of the tongue.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Lymphatic drainage of the tongue.
body.back: Tip: submental nodes bilaterally, then deep cervical nodes. Anterior two thirds: submandibular nodes unilaterally, then deep cervical nodes. Posterior third: deep cervical nodes, mainly the jugulodigastric.

title: What are the functions of the tongue?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the functions of the tongue?
body.back: The most important articulator for speech production: during speech the tongue can make an amazing range of movements. Its primary function is to provide a mechanism for taste. Taste buds are located on different areas of the tongue but are generally found around the edges, sensitive to four main tastes: bitter, sour, salty and sweet.

title: Describe the palate and the hard palate.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the palate and the hard palate.
body.back: The palate lies in the roof of the oral cavity and has two parts: the hard (bony) palate anteriorly and the soft (muscular) palate posteriorly. The hard palate forms the floor of the nasal cavity and is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae in front and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind, bounded by the alveolar arches.

title: Describe the soft palate.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the soft palate.
body.back: Attached to the posterior border of the hard palate and covered on its upper and lower surfaces by mucous membrane. It is composed of muscle fibres, an aponeurosis, lymphoid tissue, glands, blood vessels and nerves.

title: Describe the vestibule.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the vestibule.
body.back: A slit-like space between the cheeks and the gums, communicating with the exterior through the oral fissure. When the jaws are closed it communicates with the oral cavity proper behind the third molar tooth on each side. Superiorly and inferiorly it is limited by the reflection of mucous membrane from lips and cheek onto the gums.

title: What is the palatine aponeurosis?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the palatine aponeurosis?
body.back: A fibrous sheath attached to the posterior border of the hard palate. It is the expanded tendon of tensor veli palatini, splits to enclose the musculus uvulae, and gives origin and insertion to the palatine muscles.

title: Give the muscles of the soft palate with their nerves and actions.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the muscles of the soft palate with their nerves and actions.
body.back: Tensor veli palatini: from the spine of the sphenoid and auditory tube to the palatine aponeurosis, via the medial pterygoid nerve of the mandibular nerve; tenses the soft palate. Levator veli palatini: from the petrous part of the temporal bone and auditory tube to the palatine aponeurosis, pharyngeal plexus; raises the soft palate. Palatoglossus: from the palatine aponeurosis to the side of the tongue, pharyngeal plexus; pulls the root of the tongue upward and backward. Palatopharyngeus: from the palatine aponeurosis to the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage, pharyngeal plexus; elevates the wall of the pharynx. Musculus uvulae: from the posterior border of the hard palate to the mucous membrane of the uvula, pharyngeal plexus; elevates the uvula.

title: Name the three major salivary glands.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three major salivary glands.
body.back: The parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands.

title: Describe the parotid gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the parotid gland.
body.back: Para = around, otic = ear. The largest major salivary gland, purely serous, weighing about 15 grams. Its superficial portion lies in front of the external ear and its deeper part fills the retromolar fossa. Arteries: external carotid, maxillary, superficial temporal and posterior auricular. Veins: the retromandibular vein is formed within the gland by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins. Nerves: the facial nerve enters the gland and divides into its terminal branches within it.

title: Describe the parotid duct.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the parotid duct.
body.back: The main excretory duct, Stensen's duct, crosses the masseter and pierces the buccinator to open at a papilla at the buccal mucosa opposite the maxillary second molar. It measures 4 to 6 mm in length and 5 mm in diameter. A small portion of the parotid accompanies the duct, forming the accessory gland.

title: Describe the submandibular gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the submandibular gland.
body.back: The second largest, also called the submaxillary salivary gland. A mixed gland with both serous and mucous units, but serous units predominate. Its superficial part fills the digastric triangle; its deep part lies deep to the mylohyoid and superficial to the hyoglossus and styloglossus.

title: Describe the submandibular duct.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the submandibular duct.
body.back: Wharton's duct, the main excretory duct. It runs forward above the mylohyoid muscle, lying just below the mucosa and the floor of the mouth, and opens on the sublingual papilla, also called the caruncula sublingualis, lateral to the lingual frenulum.

title: Describe the sublingual gland and its ducts.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the sublingual gland and its ducts.
body.back: The smallest of the major salivary glands. It lies between the floor of the mouth, below the mucosa and above the mylohyoid muscle. A mixed gland, but mucous units predominate. Its duct opens near the submandibular duct, and several small ducts, the ducts of Rivinus, open independently along the sublingual fold.

title: Give the nerve supply of each salivary gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the nerve supply of each salivary gland.
body.back: Parotid: a serous gland innervated by CN IX parasympathetics, coursing via the lesser petrosal nerve, synapsing in the otic ganglion, with postganglionics conveyed to the gland in the auriculotemporal nerve (a branch of CN V3); secretes via the parotid (Stensen's) duct. Submandibular: a seromucous gland innervated by CN VII parasympathetics coursing via the chorda tympani branch of CN VII and joining the lingual nerve to synapse in the submandibular ganglion (a branch of CN V3); secretes via the submandibular (Wharton's) duct. Sublingual: a largely mucous gland innervated by CN VII parasympathetics coursing similar to those supplying the submandibular gland; secretes via many small ducts in the sublingual fold.

title: What forms the lateral wall of the vestibule?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What forms the lateral wall of the vestibule?
body.back: The cheek, composed of the buccinator muscle, covered laterally by the skin and medially by the mucous membrane. A small papilla on the mucosa opposite the upper second molar tooth marks the opening of the parotid duct.

title: Describe the oral cavity proper.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the oral cavity proper.
body.back: The cavity within the alveolar margins of the maxillae and the mandible. Roof: the hard palate anteriorly and the soft palate posteriorly. Floor: the mylohyoid muscle, with the anterior two thirds of the tongue lying on it.

title: Describe the floor of the mouth.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the floor of the mouth.
body.back: Covered with mucous membrane. In the midline a mucosal fold, the frenulum, connects the tongue to the floor. On each side of the frenulum a small papilla carries the opening of the submandibular duct. A rounded ridge extending backward and laterally from the papilla is produced by the sublingual gland.

title: Give the sensory and motor nerve supply of the oral cavity.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the sensory and motor nerve supply of the oral cavity.
body.back: Sensory: roof, the greater palatine and nasopalatine nerves (branches of the maxillary nerve); floor, the lingual nerve (branch of the mandibular nerve); cheek, the buccal nerve (branch of the mandibular nerve). Motor: the buccinator in the cheek and the orbicularis oris in the lip are supplied by branches of the facial nerve.

title: Describe the tongue in general.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the tongue in general.
body.back: A mass of striated muscles covered with mucous membrane, divided into right and left halves by a median septum. Three parts: oral (anterior two thirds), pharyngeal (posterior third) and root. Two surfaces: dorsal and ventral.

title: Describe the dorsal surface of the tongue.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the dorsal surface of the tongue.
body.back: Divided into anterior two thirds and posterior one third by a V-shaped sulcus terminalis. The apex of the sulcus faces backward and is marked by a pit called the foramen cecum, an embryological remnant marking the site of the upper end of the thyroglossal duct.

title: What covers the two parts of the dorsal surface?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What covers the two parts of the dorsal surface?
body.back: Anterior two thirds: the mucosa is rough and shows three types of papillae: filiform, fungiform and vallate. Posterior third: no papillae, but a nodular surface because of underlying lymphatic nodules, the lingual tonsils.

title: What is the structure at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the structure at the arrow?
body.back: Optic canal, at the orbital apex in the lesser wing of the sphenoid. Transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery.

title: Which bones form the highlighted wall?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones form the highlighted wall?
body.back: The floor: orbital surface of the maxilla + zygomatic bone + orbital process of the palatine. It is the roof of the maxillary sinus.

title: Which bones form the highlighted wall?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones form the highlighted wall?
body.back: The lateral wall: zygomatic bone + greater wing of the sphenoid. The strongest wall.

title: Which bones form the highlighted wall?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones form the highlighted wall?
body.back: The medial wall: frontal process of the maxilla + lacrimal bone + orbital plate of the ethmoid (lamina papyracea) + body of the sphenoid. The thinnest wall.

title: What is the slit at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the slit at the arrow?
body.back: Superior orbital fissure, between the lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid, where the roof meets the lateral wall. Carries CN III, IV, VI, the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves (V1) and the superior ophthalmic vein.

title: What is the slit at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the slit at the arrow?
body.back: Inferior orbital fissure, between the greater wing of the sphenoid and the maxilla, where the floor meets the lateral wall. Carries the infraorbital and zygomatic nerves (from V2), infraorbital vessels and a branch of the inferior ophthalmic vein.

title: What is the notch at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the notch at the arrow?
body.back: Supraorbital notch (sometimes a foramen) in the superior margin of the frontal bone, at the junction of the medial third and lateral two-thirds. Transmits the supraorbital nerve and vessels.

title: What is the opening at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the opening at the arrow?
body.back: Infraorbital foramen, just below the inferior orbital margin in the maxilla. The end of the infraorbital groove and canal. The infraorbital nerve and vessels emerge here onto the face.

title: What are the two small openings at the arrows?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the two small openings at the arrows?
body.back: Anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina, at the junction of the roof and the medial wall. They transmit the ethmoidal nerves and vessels.

title: What is the depression at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the depression at the arrow?
body.back: Lacrimal fossa (lacrimal groove) on the medial wall, between the anterior lacrimal crest (maxilla) and the posterior lacrimal crest (lacrimal bone). It holds the lacrimal sac and leads into the nasolacrimal canal.

title: What is the small pit at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the small pit at the arrow?
body.back: Trochlear fossa, superomedial in the roof, about 4 mm behind the margin. It anchors the trochlea, the pulley for the tendon of the superior oblique.

title: Which bones form the highlighted wall?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones form the highlighted wall?
body.back: The roof: orbital plate of the frontal bone + lesser wing of the sphenoid.

title: What passes through the optic canal?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What passes through the optic canal?
body.back: The optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery, with sympathetic fibres.

title: Two 'lacrimal fossae': which holds the gland and which holds the sac?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Two 'lacrimal fossae': which holds the gland and which holds the sac?
body.back: The lacrimal gland sits superolaterally in the fossa of the orbital plate of the frontal bone. The lacrimal sac sits in the lacrimal fossa (groove) on the medial wall, between the anterior and posterior lacrimal crests.

title: Name the 7 bones of the orbit. Which are cranial and which are facial?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the 7 bones of the orbit. Which are cranial and which are facial?
body.back: Cranial (3): frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid. Facial (4): zygomatic, lacrimal, maxilla, palatine.

title: Superior orbital fissure: location and contents (inside vs outside the common tendinous ring)?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Superior orbital fissure: location and contents (inside vs outside the common tendinous ring)?
body.back: Between the lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid, superolateral to the optic canal. Inside the ring: CN III (both divisions), CN VI, nasociliary nerve. Outside the ring: lacrimal nerve, frontal nerve, CN IV, superior ophthalmic vein.

title: Inferior orbital fissure: location and contents?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Inferior orbital fissure: location and contents?
body.back: Between the greater wing of the sphenoid and the maxilla, inferolateral to the optic canal. Connects the orbit to the pterygopalatine fossa. Contents: infraorbital nerve and vessels, zygomatic nerve, a branch of the inferior ophthalmic vein, orbital branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion.

title: What passes through the supraorbital notch and the infraorbital foramen?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What passes through the supraorbital notch and the infraorbital foramen?
body.back: Supraorbital notch (or foramen): supraorbital nerve and vessels. Infraorbital foramen (just below the inferior margin): infraorbital nerve and vessels.

title: Where are the anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina and what do they transmit?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where are the anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina and what do they transmit?
body.back: At the junction of the roof and the medial wall (frontoethmoidal suture). They transmit the anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves and vessels.

title: Origin of each extraocular muscle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Origin of each extraocular muscle?
body.back: Four recti: common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn). Levator palpebrae superioris: lesser wing of the sphenoid. Superior oblique: body of the sphenoid (passes through the trochlea). Inferior oblique: orbital surface of the maxilla.

title: Nerve supply of the extraocular muscles (LR6 SO4)?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Nerve supply of the extraocular muscles (LR6 SO4)?
body.back: Lateral rectus: abducens (CN VI). Superior oblique: trochlear (CN IV). All the others, including levator palpebrae superioris: oculomotor (CN III).

title: Describe the shape of the orbit and where its base and apex point.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the shape of the orbit and where its base and apex point.
body.back: A four-sided pyramid. The base is the orbital margin, opening onto the face. The apex points posteromedially, at the optic canal.

title: How are the two orbits angled to each other?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How are the two orbits angled to each other?
body.back: Medial walls: roughly parallel. Lateral walls: about 90 degrees to each other. Orbital axes: about 45 degrees to each other (each about 22 to 23 degrees from the sagittal plane). Visual axes: parallel, straight ahead.

title: Which bones form the roof of the orbit?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones form the roof of the orbit?
body.back: Orbital plate of the frontal bone + lesser wing of the sphenoid (posteriorly).

title: Which bones form the floor of the orbit? What lies below it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones form the floor of the orbit? What lies below it?
body.back: Orbital surface of the maxilla (most of it) + zygomatic bone + orbital process of the palatine. The maxillary sinus lies below.

title: Which bones form the medial wall? Which part is paper-thin?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones form the medial wall? Which part is paper-thin?
body.back: Frontal process of the maxilla, lacrimal bone, orbital plate of the ethmoid, and the body of the sphenoid. The ethmoid part (lamina papyracea) is the largest and paper-thin.

title: Which bones form the lateral wall? How strong is it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones form the lateral wall? How strong is it?
body.back: Zygomatic bone + greater wing of the sphenoid. It is the strongest, thickest wall.

title: Which bones form each of the four orbital margins?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which bones form each of the four orbital margins?
body.back: Superior: frontal. Lateral: frontal (zygomatic process) + zygomatic (frontal process). Inferior: zygomatic laterally, maxilla medially. Medial: frontal above, frontal process of the maxilla (anterior lacrimal crest) below.

title: Optic canal: where is it and what passes through it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Optic canal: where is it and what passes through it?
body.back: In the lesser wing of the sphenoid, at the orbital apex. Transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery.

title: Which layer of the eyelid is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which layer of the eyelid is highlighted?
body.back: Layer 1: the skin, with the cilia (eyelashes) at the margin.

title: Which layer is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which layer is highlighted?
body.back: Layer 2: loose connective tissue and adipose tissue, containing the sebaceous glands of Zeis and the ciliary glands of Moll.

title: Which layer, and which muscle, is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which layer, and which muscle, is highlighted?
body.back: Layer 3: the muscular layer. The orbicularis oculi closes the lids; the levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper lid.

title: Which layer is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which layer is highlighted?
body.back: Layer 4: the tarsal plate, of dense connective tissue, which gives the eyelid its shape and holds the tarsal (meibomian) glands.

title: Which layer is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which layer is highlighted?
body.back: Layer 5: the palpebral conjunctiva, the mucous membrane lining the inner surface of the eyelid.

title: Which glands are at the arrow, and what do they make?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which glands are at the arrow, and what do they make?
body.back: The tarsal (meibomian) glands, inside the tarsal plate. They produce the oil layer of the tear film, which prevents evaporation.

title: What is the structure at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the structure at the arrow?
body.back: The superior conjunctival fornix, where the palpebral conjunctiva reflects onto the eyeball as the bulbar conjunctiva. The lacrimal ducts empty here.

title: What are the structures at the arrow, and what do they do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the structures at the arrow, and what do they do?
body.back: The cilia (eyelashes). They protect the eye from foreign particles, prevent evaporation of the tear film, and act as sensory receptors.

title: List the contents of the orbit.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: List the contents of the orbit.
body.back: Eyeball (the most essential content), extraocular muscles, fascia bulbi, nerves (optic, oculomotor, trochlear, abducens, ophthalmic), the ciliary ganglion, the ophthalmic artery and ophthalmic veins, the lacrimal gland and orbital fat.

title: Palpebral vs bulbar conjunctiva.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Palpebral vs bulbar conjunctiva.
body.back: The palpebral conjunctiva lines the inner surface of the eyelid; the bulbar conjunctiva covers the front of the eyeball. They are continuous at the superior and inferior conjunctival fornices, enclosing the conjunctival sac. The conjunctiva keeps the surface of the eye and eyelids lubricated and protects the ocular surface from microbial infection.

title: What is the tear film made of and what does it do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the tear film made of and what does it do?
body.back: Water with electrolytes and proteins. It lubricates the eye and protects it from infections.

title: Name the three layers of the tear film, their source and their job.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three layers of the tear film, their source and their job.
body.back: Oil layer: meibomian glands, prevents evaporation. Water layer: lacrimal glands, lubricates, allows blinking, washes away debris, forms a smooth surface. Mucin layer: goblet cells of the conjunctiva, attaches the tear film to the eye and spreads the water evenly.

title: Where is the lacrimal gland and what are its relations?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where is the lacrimal gland and what are its relations?
body.back: Anteriorly in the superolateral aspect of the orbit, in the lacrimal fossa of the orbital plate of the frontal bone. Superiorly: the zygomatic process of the frontal bone. Anteriorly: the orbital septum. Posteriorly: orbital fat. Inferolaterally: the lateral rectus muscle.

title: Describe the structure of the lacrimal gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the structure of the lacrimal gland.
body.back: About 2 cm long, with an orbital part (larger, on the lateral margin of the levator palpebrae superioris) and a palpebral part (smaller, along the inner surface of the eyelid). It is a compound tubuloacinar gland of lobules formed by multiple acini, whose serous cells make the watery lacrimal fluid.

title: How does lacrimal fluid reach the eye?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How does lacrimal fluid reach the eye?
body.back: The acini secrete into excretory ducts that empty into the superior conjunctival fornix. The fluid is then spread over the cornea by blinking.

title: Trace the flow of tears from the gland to the nose.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the flow of tears from the gland to the nose.
body.back: Parasympathetic stimulation (CN VII fibres reaching the gland) makes it secrete fluid into the superior conjunctival fornix, then the conjunctival sac. Gravity and blinking move the tears across the cornea, removing dust. Capillary action draws them through the puncta into the lacrimal sac, and then down the nasolacrimal duct to the inferior nasal meatus.

title: Blood and lymphatic supply of the lacrimal gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Blood and lymphatic supply of the lacrimal gland.
