body.back: Arterial: the lacrimal artery, from the ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid. Venous: the superior ophthalmic vein, emptying into the cavernous sinus. Lymphatic: superficial parotid lymph nodes, which empty into the superior deep cervical nodes.

title: Sensory innervation of the lacrimal gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Sensory innervation of the lacrimal gland.
body.back: The lacrimal nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1), itself derived from the trigeminal nerve.

title: Trace the parasympathetic supply of the lacrimal gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the parasympathetic supply of the lacrimal gland.
body.back: Preganglionic fibres run in the greater petrosal nerve (a branch of the facial nerve), then the nerve of the pterygoid canal, and synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Postganglionic fibres travel with the maxillary nerve and finally the zygomatic nerve. They stimulate fluid secretion.

title: Levator palpebrae superioris: what does it do and who supplies it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Levator palpebrae superioris: what does it do and who supplies it?
body.back: It raises the upper eyelid. Skeletal part: oculomotor nerve (CN III). Its smooth muscle part, the superior tarsal muscle, is supplied by sympathetic fibres.

title: Trace the sympathetic supply of the lacrimal gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the sympathetic supply of the lacrimal gland.
body.back: Fibres originate in the superior cervical ganglion and are carried by the internal carotid plexus and the deep petrosal nerve. They join the parasympathetic fibres in the nerve of the pterygoid canal and follow the same route to the gland. They inhibit fluid secretion.

title: What is the ciliary ganglion?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the ciliary ganglion?
body.back: A peripheral parasympathetic ganglion that relays parasympathetic impulses from the oculomotor nerve to their target structures. It also transports sympathetic impulses from the internal carotid plexus and sensory impulses from the nasociliary nerve. Its branches are the short ciliary nerves.

title: Describe the two parts of the eyelid.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the two parts of the eyelid.
body.back: A medial part and a lateral part. The lateral part carries the eyelashes and is known as the ciliary part. The eyelid is 2 to 3 mm thick.

title: Name the five layers of the eyelid.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the five layers of the eyelid.
body.back: 1. Skin. 2. Loose connective tissue and adipose tissue. 3. Muscular layer: orbicularis oculi and levator palpebrae superioris. 4. Tarsal plate (dense connective tissue). 5. Palpebral conjunctiva.

title: What is the orbital septum and what does it do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the orbital septum and what does it do?
body.back: A fibrous membrane, part of the tarsal plate, that connects the tarsi to the margins of the orbit. It bounds the orbital fat anteriorly and helps limit the spread of infection between the face and the orbit.

title: Which ligaments are associated with the orbital part of orbicularis oculi?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which ligaments are associated with the orbital part of orbicularis oculi?
body.back: The medial and lateral palpebral ligaments.

title: What are the functions of the cilia (eyelashes)?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the functions of the cilia (eyelashes)?
body.back: Protecting the eyes from foreign particles, preventing evaporation of the tear film, and acting as sensory receptors.

title: Name the two glands of the eyelid margin and what they secrete.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the two glands of the eyelid margin and what they secrete.
body.back: Sebaceous glands of Zeis and the ciliary glands of Moll, which are modified apocrine sweat glands. They contribute sebum to the lipid layer of the film across the anterior chamber of the eye.

title: What are the tarsi and what do they do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the tarsi and what do they do?
body.back: The superior and inferior tarsal plates: dense connective tissue that shapes and stiffens the eyelid and contains the tarsal (meibomian) glands.

title: Orbicularis oculi: which part blinks gently and which closes the eye forcefully?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Orbicularis oculi: which part blinks gently and which closes the eye forcefully?
body.back: The palpebral part blinks gently; the orbital part closes the eye forcefully. (The lacrimal part helps drain tears.)

title: Where does the nasolacrimal duct run and where does it open?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does the nasolacrimal duct run and where does it open?
body.back: In the nasolacrimal canal, formed by grooves of the maxilla and the lacrimal bone; it opens into the inferior nasal meatus.

title: Define the pharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Define the pharynx.
body.back: A funnel-shaped fibromuscular tube extending from the base of the skull to the oesophagus, lined throughout with mucous membrane. It acts as a common channel for both food (deglutition) and air (respiration), and contains the tonsils of Waldeyer's ring and the connection to the middle ear.

title: Longitudinal muscles: origins, insertion and nerves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Longitudinal muscles: origins, insertion and nerves.
body.back: Stylopharyngeus: from the medial surface of the base of the styloid process, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX). Palatopharyngeus: by two fasciculi, anterior and posterior, from the upper surface of the palatine aponeurosis. Salpingopharyngeus: from the lower part of the cartilage of the auditory tube. The last two are supplied by the cranial root of the eleventh nerve through the pharyngeal plexus. All three insert on the posterior border of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage.

title: What do the longitudinal muscles do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What do the longitudinal muscles do?
body.back: They elevate the larynx and shorten the pharynx during swallowing. At the same time the palatopharyngeal sphincter, formed by some fibres of palatopharyngeus, closes the nasopharyngeal isthmus.

title: Name the muscles of the soft palate and their nerves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the muscles of the soft palate and their nerves.
body.back: Tensor veli palatini, levator veli palatini, musculus uvulae and palatopharyngeus. All are innervated by the vagus (CN X) except the tensor veli palatini, which takes CN V3.

title: Describe the nasopharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the nasopharynx.
body.back: The region of the pharynx posterior to the nasal cavity. Its features are the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids), the auditory (Eustachian, pharyngotympanic) tube connecting the middle ear and the pharynx, the torus tubarius (a raised ridge above the tube opening) and the salpingopharyngeal fold with the salpingopharyngeus muscle.

title: Describe the oropharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the oropharynx.
body.back: The region posterior to the oral cavity. Its posterior wall is the superior pharyngeal constrictor. It contains the palatine tonsils, between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches, and the lingual tonsil.

title: Describe the laryngopharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the laryngopharynx.
body.back: The region posterior to the larynx. Its posterior wall is the middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors. Its anterior wall presents the laryngeal inlet, and below the inlet it is supported by the cricoid and arytenoid cartilages. Its lateral wall presents the piriform fossa on each side of the laryngeal inlet.

title: What is the piriform fossa?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the piriform fossa?
body.back: A deep recess, broad above and narrow below, in the anterior part of the lateral wall of the laryngopharynx on each side of the laryngeal inlet. It is produced by the bulging of the larynx into the laryngopharynx. Swallowed foreign bodies may lodge there.

title: Give the motor innervation of the pharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the motor innervation of the pharynx.
body.back: The vagus nerve (CN X) innervates all the muscles of the pharynx and soft palate except the tensor veli palatini and the stylopharyngeus. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies the stylopharyngeus, and the mandibular nerve (CN V3) the tensor veli palatini.

title: Give the sensory innervation of the pharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the sensory innervation of the pharynx.
body.back: Upper pharynx: the maxillary nerve (CN V2) and the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Lower pharynx: the vagus nerve (CN X).

title: What is the pharyngeal plexus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the pharyngeal plexus?
body.back: A plexus composed of the glossopharyngeal nerve, the vagus nerve and sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion. It carries the motor and sensory supply of the pharynx.

title: Give the measurements and location of the pharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the measurements and location of the pharynx.
body.back: Length 12 to 14 cm. Width 3.5 cm at its base and 1.5 cm at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction. It lies behind the cavities of the nose, mouth and larynx, with which it communicates.

title: Give the blood supply and drainage of the pharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the blood supply and drainage of the pharynx.
body.back: Arteries: the ascending pharyngeal artery (the second branch of the external carotid), the ascending palatine and tonsillar arteries (from the facial artery), the greater palatine and pharyngeal arteries (from the maxillary artery) and the lingual artery. Veins: the pharyngeal venous plexus, a tributary of the internal jugular vein. Lymph: the jugulodigastric (tonsillar) node.

title: Define deglutition and name its three stages.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Define deglutition and name its three stages.
body.back: The process by which food is transferred from the mouth to the stomach. First stage, in the mouth: voluntary. Second stage, in the pharynx: involuntary. Third stage, in the oesophagus: involuntary.

title: Describe the first stage of swallowing.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the first stage of swallowing.
body.back: The mouth is closed and the anterior part of the tongue is raised against the hard palate in front of the bolus, pushing the masticated food progressively into the posterior part of the oral cavity. The soft palate closes down onto the back of the tongue to help form the bolus. The hyoid bone moves up and the food is pushed from the oral cavity into the oropharynx through the oropharyngeal isthmus.

title: Describe the second stage of swallowing.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the second stage of swallowing.
body.back: Very rapid. The nasopharyngeal isthmus is closed by elevation of the soft palate and contraction of Passavant's ridge, preventing food entering the nasopharynx. The laryngeal inlet is closed by approximation of the aryepiglottic folds. The pharynx and larynx are elevated behind the hyoid bone by the longitudinal muscles, and the bolus is pushed down over the posterior surface of the epiglottis by gravity and contraction of the superior and middle constrictors, passing from oropharynx to laryngopharynx. Rapid downward displacement of the larynx and pharynx by the infrahyoid muscles then reopens the laryngeal orifice.

title: Describe the third stage of swallowing.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the third stage of swallowing.
body.back: The propulsive action of thyropharyngeus, followed by relaxation of cricopharyngeus, pushes the food from the laryngopharynx into the oesophagus. From there it reaches the stomach by peristaltic movements of the oesophageal wall.

title: What happens if the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is damaged?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What happens if the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is damaged?
body.back: Loss of sensation above the vocal folds. This is the question your professor asks on the laryngopharynx slide.

title: Give the boundaries and relations of the pharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the boundaries and relations of the pharynx.
body.back: Superior: the base of the skull, including the posterior part of the body of the sphenoid and the basilar part of the occipital bone in front of the pharyngeal tubercle. Inferior: continuous with the oesophagus at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage anteriorly and the lower border of C6 posteriorly. Posterior: the prevertebral fascia in front of the cervical spine, separated only by loose areolar tissue so the pharynx slides freely during swallowing. Anterior: opens into the nasal cavities, mouth and larynx. Lateral: the neurovascular bundle of the neck and the styloid process with its muscles and ligaments.

title: Name the three layers of the pharyngeal wall.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three layers of the pharyngeal wall.
body.back: A fibrous tunic, a superficial muscular tunic and a deep pharyngeal mucosa. The buccopharyngeal fascia covers the lateral surface of the constrictors; the pharyngobasilar fascia lines their deep surface.

title: With what is the pharyngeal mucosa continuous?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: With what is the pharyngeal mucosa continuous?
body.back: With the mucous membrane of the nasal cavity and auditory tubes in the rhinopharynx, the oral mucosa in the oropharynx, and the laryngeal mucosa in the laryngopharynx.

title: Name the pharyngeal muscles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the pharyngeal muscles.
body.back: Constrictors: superior, middle and inferior. Elevators (longitudinal): stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus.

title: Superior constrictor: origin, insertion, nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Superior constrictor: origin, insertion, nerve.
body.back: Quadrilateral. Origin: the pterygoid hamulus, the pterygomandibular raphe, the medial surface of the mandible at the upper end of the mylohyoid line, and the side of the posterior part of the tongue. Insertion: the pharyngeal tubercle on the base of the skull and the median fibrous raphe. Nerve: the pharyngeal branch of the vagus carrying fibres of the cranial root of the accessory nerve. Action: helps in deglutition.

title: Middle constrictor: origin, insertion, nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Middle constrictor: origin, insertion, nerve.
body.back: Fan shaped. Origin: the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament, the lesser cornu of the hyoid and the upper border of the greater cornu of the hyoid. Insertion: the median fibrous raphe. Nerve: the pharyngeal branch of the vagus carrying fibres of the cranial root of the accessory nerve.

title: Inferior constrictor: its two parts and their nerves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Inferior constrictor: its two parts and their nerves.
body.back: Thyropharyngeus, from the oblique line on the lamina of the thyroid cartilage and the tendinous band between the thyroid tubercle and the cricoid, inserting into the median fibrous raphe, supplied by the pharyngeal plexus and the external laryngeal nerve. Cricopharyngeus, from the cricoid cartilage, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

title: Which subdivision of the pharynx is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which subdivision of the pharynx is highlighted?
body.back: The nasopharynx, behind the nasal cavity. It contains the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids), the auditory tube opening and the torus tubarius.

title: Which subdivision of the pharynx is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which subdivision of the pharynx is highlighted?
body.back: The oropharynx, behind the oral cavity. Its posterior wall is the superior pharyngeal constrictor, and it contains the palatine and lingual tonsils.

title: Which subdivision of the pharynx is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which subdivision of the pharynx is highlighted?
body.back: The laryngopharynx, behind the larynx. Its posterior wall is the middle and inferior constrictors, and its lateral wall presents the piriform fossa.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The pharyngeal tonsil, the adenoids, in the roof of the nasopharynx.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The opening of the auditory tube with the torus tubarius above it, connecting the middle ear to the nasopharynx.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The palatine tonsil, in the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.

title: Which recess is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which recess is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: The piriform fossa, lateral to the laryngeal inlet. Swallowed foreign bodies may lodge there.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and what does it do in swallowing?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and what does it do in swallowing?
body.back: The epiglottis. The bolus is pushed down over its posterior surface, while the aryepiglottic folds close the laryngeal inlet.

title: What is the peripheral nervous system?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the peripheral nervous system?
body.back: All neural structures outside the brain and spinal cord: the cranial nerves, spinal nerves and their branches, plexuses and ganglia. It links the CNS to the body, carrying sensation in and motor commands out. Functionally divided into somatic and autonomic systems.

title: Give the lesion patterns of the visual pathway.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the lesion patterns of the visual pathway.
body.back: Optic nerve: ipsilateral blindness. Optic chiasm: bitemporal hemianopia, as with pituitary tumours. Optic tract: contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Occipital cortex: contralateral homonymous hemianopia, with macular sparing after a posterior cerebral artery stroke.

title: Describe CN III, IV and VI.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe CN III, IV and VI.
body.back: III: from the midbrain, through the cavernous sinus, to the superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique and levator palpebrae superioris. IV: from the dorsal midbrain, crossing ventrally, to the superior oblique for downward and inward movement. VI: from the pons, through the cavernous sinus, to the lateral rectus for abduction.

title: Describe the trigeminal nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the trigeminal nerve.
body.back: The main sensory nerve of the face and motor nerve of mastication, the largest cranial nerve. It emerges from the pons with a large sensory and small motor root; sensory fibres synapse in the Gasserian ganglion in Meckel's cave. Ophthalmic (sensory) via the superior orbital fissure; maxillary (sensory) via the foramen rotundum; mandibular (sensory and motor) via the foramen ovale.

title: Trace the facial motor pathway.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the facial motor pathway.
body.back: From the inferior precentral gyrus, the face area, the upper motor neurons descend through the genu of the internal capsule, the cerebral peduncles and the pons to the facial nucleus. The upper face receives bilateral input, the lower face only contralateral input.

title: Give the course of the facial nerve in the temporal bone.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the course of the facial nerve in the temporal bone.
body.back: It enters the internal auditory canal with CN VIII. Labyrinthine segment: the narrowest, to the geniculate ganglion. Tympanic segment: horizontal, above the oval window. Mastoid segment: gives the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani (taste and parasympathetic). It exits by the stylomastoid foramen.

title: What does the facial nerve do after leaving the skull?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the facial nerve do after leaving the skull?
body.back: It enters the parotid gland and divides into five purely motor terminal branches, the parotid plexus: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical.

title: Supranuclear versus peripheral facial palsy.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Supranuclear versus peripheral facial palsy.
body.back: A supranuclear lesion, such as a stroke, weakens only the lower face on the opposite side, since the upper face has bilateral input. A peripheral facial nerve lesion, such as Bell's palsy, paralyses the whole half of the face, including the eyelid and forehead.

title: Describe the spinal nerves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the spinal nerves.
body.back: All carry combined sensory and motor axons in two roots: sensory axons enter as the dorsal root, motor fibres (somatic and autonomic) leave as the ventral root. The dorsal root ganglion is an enlargement of the spinal nerve. 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal, each leaving through its intervertebral foramen.

title: Name the plexuses and their main nerves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the plexuses and their main nerves.
body.back: Cervical (C1 to C5): posterior neck and head, and the phrenic nerve to the diaphragm. Brachial (C4 to T1): radial, axillary, ulnar and median nerves. Lumbar: pelvis and anterior leg, with the femoral nerve and its saphenous branch. Sacral (L4 to S4): the sciatic nerve.

title: Describe the sciatic nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the sciatic nerve.
body.back: The largest and longest nerve, from L4 to S3. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, usually below piriformis, descends deep to gluteus maximus and down the posterior thigh on adductor magnus, supplying the hamstrings and part of adductor magnus. Near the popliteal fossa it divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves.

title: What is a nerve made of?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is a nerve made of?
body.back: Axons run in bundles called fibres; multiple fibres form a nerve, which also contains connective tissue and blood vessels.

title: What is sciatica?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is sciatica?
body.back: Pain along the sciatic nerve, most commonly caused by a bulging or herniated intervertebral disc.

title: Somatic versus autonomic nervous system.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Somatic versus autonomic nervous system.
body.back: Somatic: voluntary control of skeletal muscle, one motor neuron from CNS to muscle, reflex arcs such as the patellar reflex. Autonomic: involuntary control of smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands, with a two-neuron pathway. Sympathetic is thoracolumbar; parasympathetic is craniosacral.

title: Describe the somatic nervous system.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the somatic nervous system.
body.back: Voluntary movement through skeletal muscle, plus sensation from skin, muscles and joints. Sensory division: touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain and proprioception, with cell bodies in dorsal root or cranial sensory ganglia. Motor division: one neuron from the ventral horn or a cranial motor nucleus directly to the muscle, releasing acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors.

title: Name the five components of a reflex arc.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the five components of a reflex arc.
body.back: 1. Receptor. 2. Sensory neuron. 3. Integration centre in the spinal cord, sometimes with interneurons. 4. Motor neuron. 5. Effector, the skeletal muscle.

title: Describe the patellar reflex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the patellar reflex.
body.back: Stretching the quadriceps activates the muscle spindle; the sensory neuron carries the signal to the cord, synapses directly on the motor neuron, and the muscle contracts. A monosynaptic reflex, used to test the integrity of a spinal segment.

title: Describe the autonomic nervous system.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the autonomic nervous system.
body.back: Involuntary control of organs, smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands, maintaining homeostasis: heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, respiration, temperature. It works below consciousness with the hypothalamus and brainstem centres, through a two-neuron chain: a preganglionic neuron from the CNS and a postganglionic neuron from a ganglion.

title: Which neurotransmitters does the ANS use?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which neurotransmitters does the ANS use?
body.back: Acetylcholine: all preganglionic fibres of both divisions, and parasympathetic postganglionic fibres. Noradrenaline: most sympathetic postganglionic fibres, except those to sweat glands, which use acetylcholine.

title: Describe the sympathetic division's anatomy.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the sympathetic division's anatomy.
body.back: Thoracolumbar, from the lateral horn of T1 to L2. Preganglionic fibres leave via the ventral roots and enter the sympathetic chain through the white rami communicantes. Some synapse in the chain; others pass to the prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric). Postganglionic fibres then reach the organs.

title: List the sympathetic effects.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: List the sympathetic effects.
body.back: Fight or flight: increased heart rate and output, mydriasis, bronchodilation, reduced gut motility and secretion, sweating and piloerection, vasoconstriction in skin and viscera with vasodilation in muscle, glucose release and lipolysis.

title: Describe the parasympathetic division.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the parasympathetic division.
body.back: Craniosacral, from the brainstem nuclei of III, VII, IX and X and from S2 to S4. Long preganglionic fibres synapse in terminal ganglia near or within the organs; postganglionic fibres are short. Both use acetylcholine.

title: Afferent versus efferent nerves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Afferent versus efferent nerves.
body.back: Afferent nerves bring information to the CNS; efferent nerves carry signals from the CNS to organs and muscles.

title: List the parasympathetic effects.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: List the parasympathetic effects.
body.back: Rest and digest: slower heart, miosis, salivation, lacrimation and digestive secretion, increased gut motility, bladder contraction with sphincter relaxation, and erection.

title: Describe the enteric nervous system.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the enteric nervous system.
body.back: Sometimes considered a third division of the ANS: millions of neurons in the gut wall in two plexuses. Myenteric (Auerbach's) controls motility; submucosal (Meissner's) regulates secretion and blood flow. It can work independently but is modulated by both divisions.

title: Who controls autonomic function centrally?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Who controls autonomic function centrally?
body.back: The hypothalamus, the main integration centre; brainstem nuclei for cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes; the spinal cord for visceral reflexes such as urination and defecation; and the limbic cortex for emotional responses.

title: Name the autonomic clinical correlations.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the autonomic clinical correlations.
body.back: Autonomic neuropathy in diabetes: orthostatic hypotension, bladder dysfunction, impotence. Horner's syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis. Vasovagal syncope: an exaggerated parasympathetic response causing fainting. Raynaud's disease: excessive sympathetic vasoconstriction in the extremities.

title: Classify the twelve cranial nerves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Classify the twelve cranial nerves.
body.back: Sensory: I olfactory, II optic, VIII vestibulocochlear. Motor: III oculomotor, IV trochlear, VI abducens, XI accessory, XII hypoglossal. Mixed: V trigeminal, VII facial, IX glossopharyngeal, X vagus.

title: Give the function of each mixed cranial nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the function of each mixed cranial nerve.
body.back: V: facial sensation and muscles of mastication. VII: facial expression, part of taste and saliva. IX: muscles of the mouth and upper throat, part of taste and saliva. X: homeostatic control of thoracic and upper abdominal organs.

title: Which cranial nerves contact autonomic ganglia?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cranial nerves contact autonomic ganglia?
body.back: III (pupillary constriction), VII and IX (salivation), and X (thoracic and upper abdominal ganglia).

title: Describe the olfactory nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the olfactory nerve.
body.back: Axons of bipolar neurons in the olfactory epithelium pass through the cribriform plate and synapse in the olfactory bulbs, then run along the olfactory tracts to the olfactory cortex, amygdala and hypothalamus.

title: Trace the visual pathway.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the visual pathway.
body.back: Retina (rods and cones, with bipolar, ganglion and horizontal cells); optic nerve of ganglion cell axons, wrapped in meninges, through the optic canal; optic chiasm above the pituitary, where nasal fibres cross; optic tract carrying the contralateral field of both eyes; lateral geniculate nucleus; optic radiations; primary visual cortex, V1 or area 17, around the calcarine sulcus.

title: Where do optic tract fibres go besides the LGN?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where do optic tract fibres go besides the LGN?
body.back: A smaller number go to the superior colliculus (reflexes), the pretectal area (pupillary reflex) and the hypothalamus (circadian rhythm).

title: Which plexus is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which plexus is at the arrow?
body.back: The cervical plexus, C1 to C5, supplying the posterior neck and head.

title: Which nerve is at the arrow, and what does it supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which nerve is at the arrow, and what does it supply?
body.back: The phrenic nerve, from the cervical plexus, supplying the diaphragm.

title: Which plexus is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which plexus is at the arrow?
body.back: The brachial plexus, C4 to T1, forming the nerves of the arm.

title: Which plexus is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which plexus is at the arrow?
body.back: The lumbar plexus, whose major nerve is the femoral nerve.

title: Which plexus is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which plexus is at the arrow?
body.back: The sacral plexus, from L4 to S4, giving the sciatic nerve.

title: Which nerve is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which nerve is at the arrow?
body.back: The sciatic nerve, the largest and longest in the body, from L4 to S3, dividing into tibial and common fibular nerves.

title: Which nerves come from the plexus at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which nerves come from the plexus at the arrow?
body.back: The radial, axillary, ulnar and median nerves, from the brachial plexus.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The superior concha. Below it lies the superior meatus, which receives the posterior ethmoidal air cells.

title: Which duct is at the arrow, and where does it open?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which duct is at the arrow, and where does it open?
body.back: The nasolacrimal duct, carrying tears from the lacrimal sac down into the inferior meatus.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The middle concha. Below it lies the middle meatus, into which the maxillary, frontal and anterior and middle ethmoidal sinuses drain.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The inferior concha, a separate facial bone. Below it lies the inferior meatus, which receives the nasolacrimal duct.

title: Which air channel is at the arrow, and what drains into it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which air channel is at the arrow, and what drains into it?
body.back: The middle meatus, between the inferior and middle conchae. The maxillary sinus (via the ethmoidal infundibulum), the frontal sinus (via the frontonasal duct) and the anterior and middle ethmoidal cells all drain here.

title: Which air channel is at the arrow, and what opens into it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which air channel is at the arrow, and what opens into it?
body.back: The inferior meatus, between the inferior concha and the nasal floor. The nasolacrimal duct opens into it, which is why crying makes the nose run.

title: Which space is at the arrow, and which sinus opens there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which space is at the arrow, and which sinus opens there?
body.back: The spheno-ethmoidal recess, between the superior concha and the nasal roof. The sphenoidal sinus opens here at the sphenoidal ostium.

title: Which sinus is at the arrow, and how big is it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which sinus is at the arrow, and how big is it?
body.back: The maxillary sinus, the largest of the paranasal sinuses, about 3.5 x 2.5 x 3.5 cm. It fills the body of the maxilla and is pyramidal in shape.

title: Which sinus is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which sinus is at the arrow?
body.back: The frontal sinus: one on each side, triangular, averaging 2.5 cm, draining onto the lateral wall of the middle meatus via the frontonasal duct.

title: Which sinus is at the arrow, and what lies above it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which sinus is at the arrow, and what lies above it?
body.back: The sphenoidal sinus. Above it lie the hypophyseal fossa, pituitary gland and optic chiasma; laterally the cavernous sinus, internal carotid artery and CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.

title: Describe the nasal cavity in general.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the nasal cavity in general.
body.back: The uppermost parts of the respiratory tract, containing the olfactory receptors. Elongated wedge-shaped spaces with a large inferior base and a narrow superior apex. The skeletal framework consists mainly of bone and cartilage.

title: Describe the ethmoidal sinus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the ethmoidal sinus.
body.back: Three sets of ethmoidal air cells: anterior, middle and posterior, with 3 to 18 cells on each side. The thin-walled, bony, honeycombed spaces collectively form the ethmoidal labyrinth, located between the orbits and the nasal fossae. It may invade any of the other three sinuses.

title: What is the ethmoid bulla?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the ethmoid bulla?
body.back: The swelling on the lateral wall of the middle meatus produced by the middle ethmoid air cells.

title: Innervation, blood supply and lymphatics of the ethmoidal sinus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Innervation, blood supply and lymphatics of the ethmoidal sinus.
body.back: Nerves: the anterior and posterior ethmoidal branches of the nasociliary nerve from V1, and the maxillary nerve (V2) via orbital branches from the pterygopalatine ganglion. Blood: branches of the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries. Lymph: submandibular nodes for the anterior and middle cells, retropharyngeal nodes for the posterior.

title: Describe the maxillary sinus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the maxillary sinus.
body.back: One on each side, the largest paranasal sinus, about 3.5 x 2.5 x 3.5 cm. It completely fills the body of the maxilla and is pyramidal in shape.

title: Give the four boundaries of the maxillary sinus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the four boundaries of the maxillary sinus.
body.back: Roof: the inferior orbital margin. Floor: the alveolus of the maxilla. Base: the lateral wall of the nose. Apex: the zygomatic process of the maxilla.

title: Innervation, blood supply and lymphatics of the maxillary sinus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Innervation, blood supply and lymphatics of the maxillary sinus.
body.back: Nerves: the infraorbital and alveolar branches of the maxillary nerve (V2). Blood: branches from the infraorbital and superior alveolar branches of the maxillary arteries. Lymph: the submandibular nodes.

title: Describe the sphenoidal sinus and its relations.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the sphenoidal sinus and its relations.
body.back: Two large, irregularly shaped cavities separated by a septum. Superior: the hypophyseal fossa, pituitary gland and optic chiasma. Inferior: the nasopharynx and pterygoid canal. Medial: the other sphenoid bone. Lateral: the cavernous sinus, internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.

title: Innervation and blood supply of the sphenoidal sinus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Innervation and blood supply of the sphenoidal sinus.
body.back: Innervated by a branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1) and by the maxillary nerve (V2). Supplied by branches of the pharyngeal arteries from the maxillary arteries.

title: Where does each sinus open? Give the full table.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does each sinus open? Give the full table.
body.back: Maxillary: the maxillary ostium into the middle meatus via the ethmoidal infundibulum (constant), and an accessory maxillary ostium into the middle meatus (inconstant). Frontal: the frontonasal duct and frontal ostium into the frontal recess of the middle meatus (constant), or the middle meatus via the ethmoidal infundibulum (inconstant). Ethmoidal: posterior cells into the superior meatus, middle cells into the middle meatus, anterior cells into the middle meatus via the ethmoidal infundibulum or the frontal recess. Sphenoidal: the sphenoidal ostium into the spheno-ethmoidal recess.

title: What are the nares and choanae?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the nares and choanae?
body.back: Nares: the external opening of the nose. Choanae: openings into the nasopharynx.

title: Name the parts of the external nose.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the external nose.
body.back: Nasal bone, frontal process of the maxilla, lateral process of the septal cartilage, superior margin of the septal cartilage, major alar cartilage, minor alar cartilages, the septal cartilage, and the naris. The lacrimal bone and nasolacrimal groove lie behind.

title: How do the conchae divide the nasal cavity?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How do the conchae divide the nasal cavity?
body.back: Into four air channels: the inferior meatus (between the inferior concha and the nasal floor), the middle meatus (between the inferior and middle conchae), the superior meatus (between the middle and superior conchae) and the spheno-ethmoidal recess (between the superior concha and the nasal roof).

title: What are the paranasal sinuses, and how many are there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the paranasal sinuses, and how many are there?
body.back: Invaginations from the nasal cavity that drain into spaces associated with the lateral nasal wall. Four: ethmoidal cells, sphenoidal, maxillary and frontal sinuses.

title: What are the functions of the paranasal sinuses?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What are the functions of the paranasal sinuses?
body.back: They make the skull lighter and add resonance to the voice. Infection causes sinusitis.

title: How do the sinuses develop with age?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How do the sinuses develop with age?
body.back: Rudimentary or even absent at birth. They enlarge rapidly at the age of 6 to 7 years, then again after puberty. Size increases through enlargement of the bones from birth to adult life, and resorption of bone in old age. All are lined by respiratory epithelium.

title: Describe the frontal sinus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the frontal sinus.
body.back: One on each side. Variable in size and the most superior of the sinuses, averaging 2.5 cm. Each is triangular in shape. Rudimentary at birth and usually well developed by the age of 7 or 8. It drains onto the lateral wall of the middle meatus via the frontonasal duct.

title: Nerve and blood supply of the frontal sinus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Nerve and blood supply of the frontal sinus.
body.back: Nerves: branches of the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves from the ophthalmic nerve (V1). Blood: branches of the anterior ethmoidal, supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries.

title: What is the spinal cord?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the spinal cord?
body.back: The caudal part of the central nervous system, extending down from the brainstem through the vertebral column. It is both a nervous centre and a conduit for ascending and descending pathways.

title: Describe the surface grooves.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the surface grooves.
body.back: A deep anterior median fissure, a shallow posterior median sulcus, and on each side anterolateral and posterolateral sulci, where the root filaments emerge.

title: Describe the grey matter.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the grey matter.
body.back: Central, butterfly or H-shaped, with four horns. Dorsal horns receive sensory input from the dorsal roots. Ventral horns contain motor neurons sending fibres out through the ventral roots. Lateral horns in T1 to L2 for sympathetic outflow and S2 to S4 for parasympathetic outflow.

title: How are the ventral horn motor neurons grouped?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How are the ventral horn motor neurons grouped?
body.back: A lateral group for the limbs and a medial group for the trunk, head and neck.

title: Describe the white matter.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the white matter.
body.back: Peripheral, surrounding the grey matter, made of myelinated axons in tracts, divided on each side into anterior, lateral and posterior funiculi. Ascending: dorsal columns (fine touch, proprioception) and spinothalamic tracts (pain, temperature). Descending: corticospinal (voluntary movement) and vestibulospinal (balance, posture).

title: How is a spinal nerve formed?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How is a spinal nerve formed?
body.back: By a sensory root from the back of the cord and a motor root from the front, merging at the side. The dorsal root ganglion holds the sensory cell bodies. There are 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.

title: Why is the cauda equina important for lumbar puncture?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why is the cauda equina important for lumbar puncture?
body.back: Below the conus medullaris the roots lose their horizontal course and become vertical, forming the cauda equina. This arrangement protects the cord from the needle, since only roots, which move aside, lie below.

title: What bounds the spinal canal?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What bounds the spinal canal?
body.back: Anteriorly the vertebral bodies, reinforced by the discs and the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments. Posteriorly the laminae. Laterally the pedicles, which delimit the intervertebral foramina for the spinal nerves. Diameter 12 to 22 mm cervical, 22 to 25 mm lumbar.

title: What does the spinal canal contain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the spinal canal contain?
body.back: The spinal cord, the meninges, blood vessels, spinal nerve roots and surrounding fatty and connective tissue.

title: Describe the meninges of the spinal cord.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the meninges of the spinal cord.
body.back: From outside in: dura mater (periosteal and meningeal layers), arachnoid mater and pia mater. The subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia holds CSF. The pia sends the denticulate ligament laterally to attach to the dura. The meninges follow the roots to the foramina, becoming nerve sheaths.

title: Describe the blood supply of the spinal cord.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the blood supply of the spinal cord.
body.back: The vertebral artery gives the anterior and posterior spinal arteries. Segmental arteries (deep cervical, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal) give 31 pairs of radicular branches. Anterior and posterior spinal veins drain to radicular veins, then the internal and external vertebral venous plexus, then the vertebral and segmental veins.

title: Name the three layers of the neural tube wall.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the three layers of the neural tube wall.
body.back: Ventricular (ependymal) zone: innermost, giving neuroblasts and glioblasts. Mantle zone: neuroblasts, becoming grey matter. Marginal zone: outermost, nerve fibres, becoming white matter.

title: Name the main functions of the spinal cord.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the main functions of the spinal cord.
body.back: Conduction of sensory input to the brain and motor output to the periphery; reflex activity independent of the brain, such as the withdrawal reflex; and autonomic control of visceral functions. It also modifies and integrates the information passing through.

title: What is a reflex arc?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is a reflex arc?
body.back: A reflex generated in the spinal cord independently of the brain, either monosynaptic or polysynaptic.

title: What is a dermatome?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is a dermatome?
body.back: The area of skin supplied by one spinal segment; each segment also supplies a myotome, a group of muscles. Mapping sensory loss by dermatome localises a spinal or root lesion.

title: Describe spinal cord compression.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe spinal cord compression.
body.back: A neurosurgical emergency, with a localized lesion syndrome at the level, a sublesional syndrome below it and a spinal syndrome. MRI and CT help locate it.

title: Alar plate versus basal plate.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Alar plate versus basal plate.
body.back: Separated by the sulcus limitans. Alar plate (dorsal): sensory, afferent neurons. Basal plate (ventral): motor, efferent neurons. Between them the intermediate zone gives autonomic neurons.

title: Where do the nerve roots come from?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where do the nerve roots come from?
body.back: Ventral (motor) roots from basal plate motor neurons. Dorsal (sensory) roots from neural crest cells outside the neural tube. Together they form the spinal nerve.

title: How does the level of the cord's end change with age?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: How does the level of the cord's end change with age?
body.back: Initially the cord fills the canal. At 6 months of fetal life it reaches S1, at birth L3, in adults the L1/L2 disc. The cord stops growing at about 4, the spine at 14 to 18, so the cord occupies the upper two thirds of the canal. This explains the oblique course of the lower roots, the cauda equina.

title: Give the morphology of the spinal cord.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the morphology of the spinal cord.
body.back: Cylindrical, flattened anteroposteriorly. Cervical curvature concave posteriorly, thoracic concave anteriorly. Length 40 to 45 cm, transverse diameter 10 to 12 mm, anteroposterior about 8 mm, mass 25 to 30 g.

title: Where does the cord extend, and how does it end?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does the cord extend, and how does it end?
body.back: From the foramen magnum to the lower border of L1. It ends as the conus medullaris; the filum terminale runs from its tip to the first coccygeal vertebra, anchoring it. The cauda equina begins below L1. It is enlarged at two sites, cervical and lumbar.

title: What is a myelomere?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is a myelomere?
body.back: A spinal segment or metamere: the anatomical and functional unit of the cord, corresponding to a pair of spinal nerves.

title: Name the parts of the spinal cord.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the spinal cord.
body.back: Cervical (medulla to C7, with the C4 to T1 enlargement for the upper limbs), thoracic (T1 to T12, narrower with less grey matter), lumbar (T12 to L1/L2, with the L1 to S3 enlargement for the lower limbs), sacral, the conus medullaris at L1 to L2, the cauda equina in the lumbar cistern, and the filum terminale.

title: Which part of the grey matter is at the arrow, and what does it do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the grey matter is at the arrow, and what does it do?
body.back: The posterior (dorsal) horn, which receives sensory input from the dorsal roots.

title: Which part of the grey matter is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the grey matter is at the arrow?
body.back: The anterior (ventral) horn, containing motor neurons: a lateral group for the limbs and a medial group for the trunk.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and where is it found?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and where is it found?
body.back: The lateral horn: T1 to L2 for sympathetic outflow and S2 to S4 for parasympathetic outflow.

title: Which tissue is highlighted?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which tissue is highlighted?
body.back: The white matter: myelinated axons in tracts, divided into anterior, lateral and posterior funiculi.

title: Which groove is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which groove is at the arrow?
body.back: The anterior median fissure, the deep groove on the front of the cord.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The central canal, at the centre of the grey matter.

title: Which structures are at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structures are at the arrow?
body.back: The dorsal root and its ganglion, which holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons.

title: Introduce the thyroid gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Introduce the thyroid gland.
body.back: A unique and median endocrine gland located in the neck. It ensures a major metabolic function: the secretion of thyroid hormones and calcitonin. Thyroid pathology is very common, and the anatomical relations with the recurrent nerves and the parathyroid glands are the major risks in thyroidectomy.

title: Why is the thyroid removed with its true capsule?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why is the thyroid removed with its true capsule?
body.back: The dense venous plexus, unlike that of the prostate gland, lies deep to the true capsule. To avoid haemorrhage during thyroidectomy the gland is removed along with the true capsule.

title: What is the thyroid space?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is the thyroid space?
body.back: The cleavage or dissection plane between the thyroid body and its lodge: an important anatomical feature for surgery.

title: Describe the cervical wall in front of the thyroid, from surface to depth.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the cervical wall in front of the thyroid, from surface to depth.
body.back: The skin and adipose pannicle; the fascia superficialis, which laterally envelops the platysma; the subcutaneous tissue; the superficial layer of the cervical fascia, which covers the sternocleidomastoid muscles laterally and contains the anterior jugular veins; and the pretracheal blade of the cervical fascia, made of two sheets enclosing the subhyoid muscles.

title: What marks the tracheostomy landmarks?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What marks the tracheostomy landmarks?
body.back: The medial edges of the sternocleidohyoid and sternothyroid muscles. At the level of this diamond-shaped area lies the white line of the neck.

title: Describe the relation of the isthmus to the trachea.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the relation of the isthmus to the trachea.
body.back: Its posterior aspect covers the 2nd, 3rd and 4th tracheal rings, and it is attached to the trachea by the thyro-tracheal ligament, the median ligament of Berry.

title: What does the inner side of the lateral lobe cover?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the inner side of the lateral lobe cover?
body.back: Forward, the laryngo-tracheal tube: from top to bottom the posteroinferior part of the thyroid cartilage, the lateral surface of the cricoid cartilage, and the lateral face of the first five or six tracheal rings. The posteromedial border is attached to the first three tracheal rings by the thyro-tracheal ligament (the medial lateral ligament of Berry), so the gland follows the larynx and trachea during swallowing. Backwards, the medial side responds to the pharynx and then to the oesophagus.

title: Why does the recurrent laryngeal nerve matter here?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why does the recurrent laryngeal nerve matter here?
body.back: It is the capital nerve for swallowing, phonation and protection of the airways. It has a very intimate relationship with the thyroid tissue, shows anatomical variations, differs between the right and left sides, and is at risk of injury in thyroid surgery.

title: Trace the right recurrent laryngeal nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the right recurrent laryngeal nerve.
body.back: It originates from the pneumogastric (vagus) at the level of the right subclavian artery, gradually approaches the right oesophageal angle, passes in front of the branches of the inferior thyroid artery, then passes under the fibres of the inferior constrictor muscle of the pharynx.

title: Trace the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Trace the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
body.back: It arises from the pneumogastric (vagus) below the aortic arch, has a mediastinal course between the trachea and the aortic arch, runs along the oesotracheal angle in front of the left edge of the oesophagus, passes behind the branches of the inferior thyroid artery and the left inferior parathyroid, then under the fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor.

title: Describe the parathyroid glands and their position.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the parathyroid glands and their position.
body.back: Two small endocrine glands on each side, orange-yellow, flattened, located in the fat of the thyroid space. The inferior parathyroid lies on the posteromedial border of the lateral lobe, outside the inferior laryngeal nerve, below the termination of the inferior thyroid artery. The superior parathyroid lies on the same posteromedial border.

title: Where is the thyroid gland situated?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where is the thyroid gland situated?
body.back: In the infrahyoid region, in front of the upper end of the trachea and the lower part of the larynx, just behind the infrahyoid muscles. It lies in the lower part of the front and side of the neck opposite C5, C6, C7 and T1, clasping the upper part of the trachea.

title: Name the vessels of the thyroid body.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the vessels of the thyroid body.
body.back: The superior thyroid pedicle, the only true pedicle of each lobe, approaching the superior pole and made of the superior thyroid artery and veins. The inferior thyroid artery, reaching the posteromedial border above the base and dividing into three branches. The middle thyroid veins, from the posterolateral border, draining into the internal jugular vein. The inferior thyroid veins, not satellite to the artery, forming at the inferior border of the isthmus and the base of the lateral lobe.

title: Describe the superior thyroid artery.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the superior thyroid artery.
body.back: The first branch of the external carotid artery. It ends at the top of the lateral lobe, dividing into three branches: a lateral branch, a medial (internal) branch that joins the upper border of the isthmus and anastomoses with its contralateral counterpart, and a posterior branch.

title: Describe the inferior thyroid artery.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the inferior thyroid artery.
body.back: A branch of the thyrocervical trunk, a collateral of the subclavian artery. It divides into three branches: a posterior branch ascending on the posterior aspect of the lateral lobe and anastomosing with its counterpart from the superior thyroid artery, an inferior branch anastomosing with its contralateral counterpart along the inferior border of the isthmus, and a middle branch.

title: Describe the venous drainage of the thyroid.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the venous drainage of the thyroid.
body.back: A rich anastomotic network on the surface of the gland drains into three groups. The superior thyroid vein emerges from the upper pole, accompanies the superior thyroid artery and drains into the internal jugular vein, most often via the thyro-linguo-facial (Farabeuf) trunk. The middle thyroid veins arise from the lateral lobe and join the internal jugular directly. The inferior thyroid veins arise from the inferior border of the isthmus and the base of the lateral lobe and descend to the left brachiocephalic vein.

title: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the thyroid.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the thyroid.
body.back: From a fine subcapsular network arise the median collectors, going to either the prelaryngeal or the pretracheal nodes, and the lateral collectors, which subdivide into pedicles going to the jugular nodes.

title: Give the actions of thyroid hormones.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the actions of thyroid hormones.
body.back: Secreted by the follicular cells. Acceleration of enzymatic metabolism, increasing oxygen consumption and heat production. Acceleration of carbohydrate metabolism, lowering blood sugar. Acceleration of lipid catabolism. Acceleration of diuresis. Hypercalcemic action by accelerating bone resorption. Action on cartilage ossification and growth.

title: Describe calcitonin.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe calcitonin.
body.back: Secreted by the C cells. A hypocalcemic hormone that inhibits bone demineralization, preventing the passage of calcium into the blood. It is regulated by the level of calcium in the blood.

title: Describe parathyroid secretion.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe parathyroid secretion.
body.back: Discharged directly into the bloodstream through the capillary network of the connective tissue. It participates in the regulation of phosphocalcic metabolism with vitamin D and calcitonin. It is hypercalcemic, increasing bone resorption and promoting intestinal absorption and renal reabsorption of calcium, and hypophosphoremic, decreasing renal reabsorption of phosphates.

title: Give the take-home messages of the lecture.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the take-home messages of the lecture.
body.back: The thyroid is an endocrine gland contained in the thyroid region, occupying the medial cervical infrahyoid region. The superior thyroid pedicle (the main one) and the inferior thyroid artery ensure its vascularization. It has very important relationships with the parathyroid glands and the inferior laryngeal (recurrent) nerves. Its major metabolic role is the secretion of thyroid hormones.

title: Name the infrahyoid muscles and what they do.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the infrahyoid muscles and what they do.
body.back: Four pairs of strap muscles enclosed in a fascial sheath in the anterior neck: thyrohyoid, sternohyoid, omohyoid and sternothyroid. They fix or depress the hyoid bone during swallowing and speech, supplied by the anterior rami of the upper three cervical nerves.

title: Give the attachments of each infrahyoid muscle.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Give the attachments of each infrahyoid muscle.
body.back: Thyrohyoid: superiorly to the body and greater horn of the hyoid, inferiorly to the body of the thyroid cartilage. Sternothyroid: superiorly to the thyroid cartilage, inferiorly to the back of the manubrium and first costal cartilage, lying deep to sternohyoid. Sternohyoid: superiorly to the body of the hyoid, inferiorly to the manubrium sterni and adjacent clavicle. Omohyoid: superior and inferior bellies united by an intermediate tendon, attached superiorly to the body of the hyoid and inferiorly to the lateral end of the superior border of the scapula by the suprascapular notch.

title: Describe the morphology of the thyroid gland.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the morphology of the thyroid gland.
body.back: Two vertical lateral lobes joined by a horizontal transverse isthmus, looking like an H or a butterfly moulded on the aerodigestive axis. Lateral lobes 6 cm high, 6 cm wide between their lateral edges, isthmus 1 cm wide by 1.5 cm high, weight about 30 g, bigger in women than in men.

title: Describe a lateral lobe.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe a lateral lobe.
body.back: A triangular pyramid with a tapered apex (upper pole) resting against the posterior and inferior part of the thyroid cartilage, a rounded base (lower pole) one or two centimetres from the sternum, and three sides: a peripheral (anterolateral) convex superficial face, a medial (internal) visceral side applied to the lateral side of the trachea and the lower larynx, and a posterior face moulded on the vascular-nervous bundle of the neck.

title: Describe the isthmus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the isthmus.
body.back: A flattened narrowing, higher than wide, with two faces (anterior and posterior) and two concave edges (top and bottom). From the upper edge, to the left of the median line, an inconstant extension of variable length stands out: the pyramidal lobe.

title: Describe the aspect of the thyroid parenchyma.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the aspect of the thyroid parenchyma.
body.back: Reddish brown, of soft consistency, enveloped by a fibrous capsule that adheres to it. The encapsulated gland lies within a cellular layer which extends onto the vascular pedicles, and it is through this sheath that the gland is mobilised in its lodge.

title: Describe the two capsules of the thyroid.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Describe the two capsules of the thyroid.
body.back: True capsule: formed by peripheral condensation of the fibrous stroma of the gland. False capsule: derived from splitting of the pretracheal fascia. Through the false capsule the gland is attached to the oblique lines of the thyroid cartilage and to the body of the hyoid bone in the midline; on the medial surface of the lobe it thickens as the suspensory ligament of Berry, connecting the lobe to the cricoid cartilage.

title: Which part of the gland is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the gland is at the arrow?
body.back: A lateral lobe, shaped like a triangular pyramid, about 6 cm high, with an apex against the thyroid cartilage and a base one or two centimetres from the sternum.

title: Which part of the gland is at the arrow, and what does it cover?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which part of the gland is at the arrow, and what does it cover?
body.back: The isthmus, about 1 cm wide and 1.5 cm high. Its posterior aspect covers the 2nd, 3rd and 4th tracheal rings and is attached by the median ligament of Berry.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The pyramidal lobe: an inconstant extension of variable length from the upper edge of the isthmus, to the left of the median line.

title: Which vessel is at the arrow, and where does it arise?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which vessel is at the arrow, and where does it arise?
body.back: The superior thyroid artery, the first branch of the external carotid. With its veins it forms the superior thyroid pedicle, the only true pedicle of each lobe.

title: Which vessel is at the arrow, and where does it arise?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which vessel is at the arrow, and where does it arise?
body.back: The inferior thyroid artery, a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, itself a collateral of the subclavian artery. It reaches the posteromedial border of the lobe and divides into three branches.

title: Which nerve is at the arrow, and why does it matter here?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which nerve is at the arrow, and why does it matter here?
body.back: The recurrent (inferior) laryngeal nerve. It has a very intimate relationship with the thyroid and is at major risk during thyroidectomy.

title: Which cartilage is at the arrow, and what attaches to it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which cartilage is at the arrow, and what attaches to it?
body.back: The cricoid cartilage. The suspensory ligament of Berry, a thickening of the false capsule, connects the thyroid lobe to it.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The trachea. The medial face of each lateral lobe covers the first five or six tracheal rings, and the isthmus covers rings two to four.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Magendie and Luschka. The median aperture (Magendie, to the cisterna magna) and two lateral apertures (Luschka, to the cerebellopontine cisterns).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cerebral aqueduct. Narrow channel through the midbrain, no choroid plexus; a common site of obstruction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Choroid plexus. Capillary network lined by ependymal cells; makes most of the CSF (about 500 mL a day) and forms the blood-CSF barrier.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fourth ventricle. Tent-shaped cavity behind the pons and medulla, in front of the cerebellum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Arachnoid granulations. Arachnoid projections into the dural sinuses (of Pacchioni) through which CSF returns to the blood.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lateral ventricles. Paired C-shaped cavities in the hemispheres: frontal, temporal and occipital horns, body and atrium.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Foramina of Monro. The interventricular foramina joining each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Subarachnoid space. Between arachnoid and pia; holds most of the CSF and widens into cisterns.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Superior sagittal sinus. Dural venous sinus receiving CSF; the sinuses drain into the internal jugular veins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Third ventricle. Median cleft between the two thalami, in the diencephalon.

title: Name the parts of the ventricular system in order of CSF flow.
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Name the parts of the ventricular system in order of CSF flow.
body.back: Lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramina of Magendie and Luschka → subarachnoid space.

title: Where does CSF leave the fourth ventricle, and into which cisterns?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where does CSF leave the fourth ventricle, and into which cisterns?
body.back: Median aperture of Magendie → cisterna magna; two lateral apertures of Luschka → cerebellopontine cisterns; also the central canal through the obex.

title: CSF volume and daily production?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: CSF volume and daily production?
body.back: About 150 mL (125 subarachnoid, 25 ventricular); about 500 mL a day (400-600).

title: Communicating versus non-communicating hydrocephalus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Communicating versus non-communicating hydrocephalus?
body.back: Communicating: poor absorption or overproduction, pathway open. Non-communicating: obstruction between ventricles, often at the aqueduct.

title: Two surgical treatments of hydrocephalus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Two surgical treatments of hydrocephalus?
body.back: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt; endoscopic third ventriculostomy (floor of third ventricle → interpeduncular cistern).

title: Why lumbar puncture at L3-L4 or L4-L5?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Why lumbar puncture at L3-L4 or L4-L5?
body.back: The adult cord ends at about L1-L2, but the subarachnoid space continues below.

title: Parts of the lateral ventricle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Parts of the lateral ventricle?
body.back: Frontal, temporal and occipital horns, body and atrium.

title: Walls of the frontal horn?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Walls of the frontal horn?
body.back: Medial: septum pellucidum (fornix columns below). Lateral: head of caudate. Roof and front: genu of corpus callosum. Floor: rostrum.

title: Temporal horn: size, end and floor?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Temporal horn: size, end and floor?
body.back: Longest and largest; ends at the amygdala; floor = collateral eminence and hippocampus.

title: Floor of the third ventricle, front to back?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Floor of the third ventricle, front to back?
body.back: Optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies.

title: Anterior and posterior walls of the third ventricle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Anterior and posterior walls of the third ventricle?
body.back: Anterior: fornix columns, anterior commissure, lamina terminalis. Posterior: habenular commissure, pineal gland, posterior commissure.

title: Fourth ventricle: roof, floor, caudal tip?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Fourth ventricle: roof, floor, caudal tip?
body.back: Roof: superior and inferior medullary vela. Floor: rhomboid fossa. Caudal tip: obex.

title: What does the sulcus limitans separate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: What does the sulcus limitans separate?
body.back: Motor nuclei (medial, medial eminence) from sensory nuclei (lateral, vestibular area).

title: Where is there no choroid plexus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.front: Where is there no choroid plexus?
body.back: Frontal and occipital horns, and the cerebral aqueduct.
